"I've come out here several times after a SpaceX launch to document all of the debris," Hinojosa said. "I have photos of metal shrapnel blown up into this area that we're on."

SpaceX did not respond to NPR's questions about the environmental impact of its rocket launches.

Sponsor Message

Sofia Benavides, a Cameron County Commissioner representing the area where Starbase is located, said the law clearly allows Starbase to expand.

"There's nothing that we can do to stop it," Benavides said.

Starbase has until August 18 to hear back from potentially impacted landowners about the annexation plan and determine if they have the necessary signatures needed to move forward. The city then is required to hold two public hearings before voting in September on whether to annex, or not.

Hinojosa's organization is looking into possible legal action to prevent the annexation.

"They call it Starbase. You pull the curtain back, it's the SpaceX annexation," Hinojosa said. "SpaceX threatens the Rio Grande Valley. And that's why we'll continue to resist."

World.title: Advocates worry new bans on student IDs will trip up younger voters
World.content:
Advocates worry new bans on student IDs will trip up younger voters

toggle caption Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images

To vote in the 2024 election, Lia Symer remembers checking in at her polling place with her student ID card.

"I tend to not carry my driver's license on my person when I'm walking around campus. Most students just carry their student IDs to get into buildings," says Symer, who's about to start her senior year at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire — one of about three dozen states with in-person voter ID laws.

But to cast a ballot this year, Symer is going to need to show a state ID, U.S. passport or another accepted identification now that New Hampshire has become the latest of several states to ban registered voters from using a student ID to verify their identity at the polls.

Sponsor Message

Weeks before New Hampshire's student ID ban began in June, a federal appeals court put a similar Indiana law back into effect in April. And earlier that same month, Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis signed into a law an upcoming ban on accepting student IDs when checking in voters at the polls. Florida's restriction is set to start in 2027.

Those state laws come amid President Trump's so-far failed push for a Republican plan to overhaul voting in federal elections in every state, including a proposal that would not allow in-person voters to use student IDs.

New Hampshire's legislature passed its student ID ban as part of a slate of bills "adding security and transparency" to the state's elections, as the House Republican caucus put it.

But this month, the Coalition for Open Democracy, a voter advocacy group, filed a lawsuit, arguing the New Hampshire law is unconstitutional for burdening eligible students' right to vote and discriminating against younger voters for their age.

While the legal fights over the bans in New Hampshire and Indiana continue, voting rights advocates are adding another item to their agenda ahead of this fall's midterm election — helping students navigate these latest hurdles to the ballot box for the U.S. voting-age group that's least likely to vote.

toggle caption Robert F. Bukaty/AP

Student IDs have long been a focus of voting restrictions

While some states ban any student ID for voting, others allow certain kinds to be used depending on what school issues them, for example, or whether they show a photo or address.

Sponsor Message

In North Carolina, for instance, colleges and universities must get approval from the state's board of elections before their student IDs can be accepted as voter ID. And in Georgia, only student IDs from public institutions are allowed, leaving out seven of the state's 10 historically Black colleges and universities, including Morehouse and Spelman Colleges.

The intricacies of state voter ID laws, student voting advocates point out, can trip up many of the country's least experienced voters.

"Student IDs have been a source of attempts at controlling who votes on the part of legislators who want to manipulate the process, and that's not necessarily new," says Michelle Kanter Cohen, policy director at Fair Elections Center, a voting rights group. "I think there's been, this year, an additional wave of that happening. What this really is, is a power grab of legislators saying that they don't want students to vote."

Supporters of the newest state bans on student IDs for voting argue these kinds of rules promote election security.

In Indiana, attorneys for Republican state officials defending the state's ban in court argued that it's needed to increase public confidence and streamline the photo ID requirement "to make the acceptable forms of identification more uniform, objective, and verifiable."

"The last thing I want to do is to keep people from voting," the sponsor of Indiana's student ID ban, Republican state Sen. Blake Doriot, said at a January hearing on the legislation. "The first thing I want to do is to keep people from voting who shouldn't be voting, who do not have the proper ID."

toggle caption Darron Cummings/AP

It's not clear how many voters have used their student IDs to check in at polling places, where local election officials generally don't keep a record of what type of identification voters present.

And there is no evidence of widespread voter fraud involving student IDs.

Sponsor Message

That lack of proof led a federal judge to conclude that Indiana's ban "looks more like a solution in search of a problem" in an April ruling that found the state law is likely unconstitutional after the voter advocacy group Count US IN sued.

U.S. District Judge Richard Young, a nominee of former President Bill Clinton, wrote that by no longer allowing student IDs as voter ID, Indiana officials "selectively excluded a form of identification that otherwise complies with the neutral criteria established by Indiana's voter ID law and that has been accepted as a form of voter identification for nearly two decades."

Young's ruling is now paused and under review by a panel of the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

"It's just taking away an avenue for participation in our democracy"

In states that have stopped allowing student IDs at the polls, some younger voters are left with having to get a state ID, such as a driver's license. But what earlier generations may consider a rite of passage into adulthood is becoming less common.

"Young people are much less likely to obtain a driver's license, more broadly speaking, than in prior generations. Some of that is because of ride-sharing, financial issues and just their life circumstances," Kanter Cohen of Fair Elections Center says.

And getting ahold of supporting documents needed when applying for a state ID, such as a birth or naturalization certificate or U.S. passport, can be complicated for some students, says Kristen Rodriguez, a Florida-based organizer for VoteRiders, an advocacy group that helps eligible people obtain IDs so they can cast ballots.

"It takes a lot of time to get those documents. And in some states. a birth certificate takes six to eight months to come," Rodriguez notes. "It's usually a series of unfortunate events that lead someone to be without the documents that they need. And it can be as simple as things getting lost in the mail. When I was in college, I moved five times in four years. In all of those moves, it's so easy to lose something."

Sponsor Message

With Florida's student ID ban not going into effect until next year, Rodriguez sees an opportunity now to encourage eligible students to consider bringing any documents they do have to campus so VoteRiders can help them get a Florida ID.

"It's about really making sure that as many people know this as possible, as early as possible, so that we have enough time to get all of those documents in place before any sort of voting, registration deadlines," Rodriguez adds.

In New Hampshire, a student civics group that Symer, the Dartmouth senior, helps lead is trying to come up with new ways of informing eligible voters on campus about the state's student ID ban — a change that Symer notes also affects high schoolers who are eligible to vote.

"It doesn't only apply to college students. You could also have used a high school student ID to vote in the past," Symer says. "It's just taking away an avenue for participation in our democracy."

And in a state where student interest in elections has often been spurred by New Hampshire's role as a key campaign stop in federal races, Will Nelson, another fourth-year student who is co-president of Dartmouth Civics Association, says he's concerned the student ID ban could have long-lasting ripple effects.

"College is a very formative time for young minds and the civic traditions that you pick up. And we certainly hope that as many of our peers as possible will be lifelong voters for whomever they choose to vote," Nelson adds. "We're just sad to see that some of our policymakers have decided to make it a little bit more difficult for us to participate in that storied tradition."

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

World.title: Carney says last-minute U.S. tariff negotiations are 'delicate' and 'intense' as deadline looms
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last-minute negotiations with the U.S. to avoid a fresh batch of tariffs due to take effect this week are "delicate" and "intense," and he plans to speak to his American counterpart in the next 48 hours to broker a mutually agreeable deal.

Speaking to reporters in St. John's on Monday, where he announced a landmark hydroelectric deal with Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, Carney said he was reluctant to publicly discuss how talks are going to avoid U.S. President Donald Trump's threatened Section 338 tariffs on billions of dollars' worth of Canadian goods.

"We are involved in very delicate and intense negotiations, this is not the time to negotiate in public," Carney said in French.

"We are in the middle of a negotiation, and we are coming into those negotiations from a position of strength."

WATCH | Carney on the state of negotiations: Carney expects to speak with Trump before Aug. 19 tariff deadline | Duration 1:33 Prime Minister Mark Carney says he'll have 'opportunities over the next 48 hours' to speak to U.S. President Donald Trump before his threat to raise tariffs on a number of Canadian goods takes effect. Carney was speaking to reporters after announcing $10 billion in federal financing for the Churchill Falls hydroelectric agreement between Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador.

Asked if he plans to hit back against Trump if the two sides fail to reach a deal avoiding these new levies, Carney said he is ready for any possible scenario.

"I have plans for any situation that may arise," Carney said.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and Canada's chief trade negotiator, Janice Charette, have held a series of talks with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer over the last three weeks to not only avoid the planned Section 338 tariffs but also lower the existing Section 232 tariffs on industrial products like steel, aluminum, autos and lumber in exchange for some Canadian concessions.

LeBlanc and Charette met with Greer and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Monday afternoon for what was their longest meeting so far, clocking in at about an hour and 45 minutes.

A source with direct knowledge of the negotiations said that is expected to be the final meeting at the ministerial level.

After this, the source said a discussion is expected between Carney and Trump to review next steps.

CBC News is not identifying the source because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the talks.

Speaking briefly to reporters outside Greer's Washington office after the talks, LeBlanc said: "We're going to continue working; our job is not yet done."

At issue in these talks is just how much Canada can get out of the U.S. in exchange for a series of concessions of its own.

The Americans want U.S. liquor back on the shelves of provincially run stores. The Trump administration is also pushing for Canada's retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos removed, and tweaks to how the supply-managed dairy sector allocates quotas.

Canada, in turn, wants Trump to scrap the threatened Section 338 tariffs, which could impose a 50 per cent levy on a whole host of new products as of Aug. 19. Carney's team is also demanding substantial tariff relief for the hard-hit sectors that have endured Trump's levies for over a year.

Greer has repeatedly signalled the U.S. is not open to dropping its tariff regime entirely.

WATCH | Inside details of the tariff talks: Canada-U.S. trade talks stuck as Washington, provinces refuse to budge | Duration 5:14 Sources tell CBC News that Canadian negotiators fear looming new U.S. tariffs may be unavoidable as Washington continues to demand an end to provincial bans on U.S. alcohol — which provinces refuse to do. Canada's push for greater tariff relief on key sectors like lumber is also stalled.

Still, in an interview with CBC News, Erin O'Toole, a member of the prime minister's Canada-U.S. advisory committee, said Canada has made some "progress" with the Americans.

It's just a question of whether Trump will agree to any lower tariff rates brokered by Greer and if those levies are palatable to the Canadian industries most affected, he said.

"We're not just gonna take what they throw at us. We have to forge a deal that is fair for Canadian workers and good for our economy," O'Toole said.

The former Conservative leader said if Trump's latest 50 per cent tariffs take effect this week as planned, Canada will have no choice but to respond in kind. O'Toole said Canada is already drawing up plans to hit back at this "aggressive act" if it comes to pass.

"What's so short-sighted about tariffs is it leads to these tit-for-tat wars of response. It hurts both economies and workers. So let's hope we can avoid that," he said.

World.title: Why is Australian beef the cheaper option in Canadian grocery stores?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Australian beef is on Canadian supermarket shelves at much lower prices than for Canadian beef.

Some producers are concerned about their products being undercut, and some consumers are just happy to have an affordable option.

Tyler Fulton, president of the Canadian Cattle Association, said the Australian option has been around for years.

"Recently there's been an increased visibility to consumers as to that choice, in particular with some of those steak-type cuts," he said.

Many factors contribute to the price difference, Fulton told CBC Saskatchewan.

Canadian Cattle Association president Tyler Fulton says Australian beef is filling a void in the Canadian market. (Google Meets)

"The Australian production model is a grass-based system that commonly has a short grain feeding at the end of it. So the result is really a product that is leaner, doesn't tend to have quite the same marbling and therefore isn't as preferred in Canada as compared to the Canadian-produced beef.

"The other likely big factor here is that retailers will use a 'loss leader' tactic."

Australia has had more access to the Canadian beef market since 2018, when the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) came into effect.

Fulton said the same agreement benefits Canada in a very similar way, allowing preferred access in countries like Japan and Vietnam.

"While we wish it was Canadian, there's an acute purpose for really bringing in some imported beef," he said.

"It fills a short-term need or void in supply. I don't think that there's a big concern from a Canadian beef producer standpoint about seeing a product like Australian beef that — we have confidence in their standards, but quite simply isn't of the same quality."

CBC News talked to shoppers coming and going from the Loblaws-owned Real Canadian Superstore and Independent Grocer in Regina, to hear the consumer perspective.

"I just can't spend that kind of money on one steak," said Karen Novak.

She completely adjusted her diet because of the prices, she said.

"The last time I tasted beef other than ground beef was probably two Christmases ago, when I made beef Wellington instead of turkey … Beef is definitely a luxury. So if any of our friends want to invite us over for a steak, I'll bring a salad."

Karen Novak says other than hamburger meat, she hasn't had a taste of beef since 2024 because of the cost. (Richard Agecoutay/CBC)

Jordan Fieseler said he buys beef in bulk from local producers instead.

"I think it makes sense if the price is so high that people are going to look to something cheaper. Certainly it's not the sustainable option … I'd prefer things to not come from a long distance away. It's not as important to me as it was in the past, but that's only just because sometimes life gets crazy, and you have to just make things work," he said.

"Options are always good. Everyone's going to make their own choices," said Larry Evans. "If the quality is not there, they probably won't, but it comes down to cost. In the future, if beef keeps rising, I'll try some Australian."

Loblaws responded to a CBC request for comment with a statement.

"In recent years, North American cattle supply has tightened while Australian beef production has increased, contributing to differences in market pricing. We remain committed to supporting Canadian beef producers while providing customers with choice and value," the statement said.

As for the Canadian Cattle Association, Fulton said producers are better positioned for further domestic growth.

"I'm really very optimistic about what the opportunities are abroad, but keeping in mind our bread and butter is the domestic Canadian consumer," he said.

"We went darn near two decades with kind of low or negative profitability in the beef sector. Last year, the beef cow herd grew in Canada 2.5 per cent, and my expectation is that we'll continue to see that growth because the incentives are there."

World.title: N.L., Quebec announce new Churchill Falls agreement worth billions — with help from Ottawa
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ottawa is calling it the largest clean energy investment in North American history.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was in St. John’s on Monday to announce a new agreement on Churchill Falls and other electricity projects in Labrador, alongside N.L. Premier Tony Wakeham and Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette.

“We are finally turning the page on one of the darkest chapters in our past, and replacing both the notorious 1969 Churchill Falls agreement and the 2024 MOU with a better deal for all of us," said Wakeham.

The trio of leaders gathered on Pier 17, amid a picturesque ocean background, as details of the new deal were touted.

The deal will provide $10 billion in federal financing to upgrade and expand the Churchill Falls generating station, develop the Gull Island hydroelectric project, build transmission lines and implement a 2,000 MW onshore wind energy project in Labrador — with the exact location and other details for that wind project under consideration by Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro.

According to the federal government, altogether these projects represent the largest clean energy investment in North American history, valued at nearly $70 billion — and will nearly triple the current generating capacity of Churchill Falls, with enough power to light, heat and cool all the homes in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver combined.

“Just put this in context. Tripling the current generation capacity of Churchill Falls to that 14,000 megawatts of renewable power — that's more than the entire generating capacity of B.C. Hydro, it's more than double the output of Bruce Power, the largest nuclear plant on this continent," said Carney.

The projects will create 23,000 jobs, according to both levels of government.

Wakeham calls agreement a ‘win-win-win’

The new agreement between Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro and Hydro-Quebec has some updated figures.

N.L. Hydro says the deal will increase the value for N.L. from the $36 billion estimated in the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in 2024 — to $49 billion in net present value.

This new agreement has an end date of March 31, 2027, unless both parties agree to extend or end it, or unless they sign definitive agreements before that date.

The upcoming Quebec election could complicate that if another party takes power, but today, Wakeham is calling it a “win-win-win.”

He said this guarantees N.L. more power, more value and more transmission — a phrase he has said many times before when he was asked what he wanted to get out of N.L.’s negotiations with Quebec on Churchill River hydroelectric projects.

There's a guaranteed transmission access of 985 megawatts through Quebec. This means Newfoundland and Labrador can sell up to that amount of Churchill River electricity by sending it through Quebec, using Hydro-Quebec’s transmission network, and on to other markets. For example, if Massachusetts or New York needed power, Newfoundland and Labrador could sell it.

The previous Churchill Falls MOU had no guarantees of transmission access and it would be Quebec that would have first access to energy set aside for N.L. but that was not being used within the province.

“Newfoundlanders and Labradorians will finally be the primary beneficiary of our own resources, with complete control over whether we use our power to develop our economy or sell to outside markets,” Wakeham said.

“Today is not about what we can tear up, it’s about what we can build up,” he said, seeming to allude to the 2024 announcement with Quebec when former N.L. premier Andrew Furey ripped up the 1969 Churchill Falls agreement.

“And with a new and better deal finally in our hands, it’s time for us to roll up our sleeves and build a new and brighter future for all of us.”

Within N.L, the original deal has long been criticized as lopsided in Quebec's favour.

On the campaign trail last fall, Wakeham vowed to put the new deal to a referendum. He said on Monday that in place of that, he will convene a special meeting of the House of Assembly on Sept. 14.

He admits people will likely be "disappointed" that he is not going to move forward with his promise of a referendum, but said, "the time is now, the urgency is there."

More power, money for N.L.

The new deal includes upgrades to the existing Churchill Falls facility, increasing its capacity by 23.5 per cent, or 1,275 MW. The MOU signed in 2024 pegged those upgrades at 550 MW.

And while Ottawa says it has funding to expand Churchill Falls, the agreement between N.L. and Quebec says they agree to “study” the “potential” expansion of Churchill Falls with a new powerhouse. This is a change from the original MOU, which said it would expand Churchill Falls.

The agreement also says they will “study” the “potential” development of a new wind project generating facility, but there are few other details.

In total, N.L. Hydro says Newfoundland and Labrador will get about 760 MW more power with this agreement — 2,350 MW versus 1,990 MW agreed in the 2024 MOU. If the wind project is completed, that amount could increase up to 2,750 MW.

Hydro-Quebec gets access to up to 6,915 MW, or up to 8,515 MW if the wind project is completed.

N.L. Hydro says Hydro-Quebec will pay 1.8 cents per kilowatt hour next year — up from the current 0.2 cents — and that price will go up 14 per cent per year, reaching 11.5 cents in 2041.

N.L. Hydro also says N.L. can choose whether or not it wants to use or sell its allotted power from the Churchill Falls base plant.

Expansion of Labrador mining projects

Ottawa says this extra power will help to grow Labrador’s mining industry, and it is also providing money to bolster that development.

Natural Resources Canada says Ottawa will provide more than $2.3 million to complete an engineering and design study for transmission lines that would bring more power to Labrador west.

There is also $439,844 for preconstruction and feasibility planning for the Kami iron ore project southwest of Wabush.

World.title: Canadian icon Jann Arden marries Icelandic author Thordis Elva: 'Wife and wife'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Those who follow Canadian music icon, actor, author and overall delightful human Jann Arden on social media would likely note the dirt road as much as they took in the happy couple posing on it.

"Jann's road," as Arden calls it, is more than a secluded rural stretch near her property in Springbank, Alta., west of Calgary. It's a character in and of itself. It's where she posts video walks and updates, photos of her beloved dogs at various stages in their lives, where she reflected on the heartache and humour of caring for her aging parents, and then grieved them.

Jann's road is also a place of joy, where more recently, the singer has posted smiling photos with her partner, and then fiancée: Icelandic author and digital rights and gender equality advocate Thordis Elva.

So, as many of her followers noted, it was fitting that Arden announced she and Elva had married over the weekend with a photo of the white-clad couple on none other than Jann's road.

"Wife and wife," Arden posted on Instagram Sunday, along with their wedding date: Aug. 15, 2026.

"Well, this is maybe the most joyous #Jannsroad yet!" commented TV host Jessica Allen.

"#Jannsroad has never looked better!" commented TV and radio host Meredith Shaw.

In a statement to CBC News Monday, Arden said she and Elva had a "beautiful, kickass gathering with dear friends and family."

"It could not have been more magical or surreal," she added.

"We are looking forward to doing it all again next weekend!!! We wish!!!”

Couple met at writer's retreat

Arden, 64, who is best known for ballads like Insensitive, Good Mother and Could I Be Your Girl, announced her engagement to Elva on Dec. 31, 2025. The couple initially met at a writer's retreat in Iceland, with former Icelandic first lady Eliza Reid as the inadvertent matchmaker.

Reid was one of many notable guests at the wedding, writing on Instagram that she always joked she started the Icelandic writing retreat "so that two people might meet there, fall in love, and then invite me to the wedding. AND IT HAPPENED!"

Several Canadian celebrities and media personalities also posted images and comments from the wedding, including Syrian Canadian novellist Danny Ramadan, actor Dani Kind, talk show host Cynthia Loyst, MLA Janis Irwin and CBC chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault.

American comedian and actress Chelsea Handler was also evidently in attendance.

"WHAT A BEAUTIFUL DAY," Handler commented on Arden's photo.

"So glad you could make it Chelsea. Meant the world to us," Arden replied.

Congratulations also poured in from Canadian singers k.d. Lang and Bif Naked.

Arden posted a second photo Monday showing the couple holding hands in front of a gazebo laden with colourful flowers.

"What a day!" she wrote.

A screengrab of an Instagram post by Jann Arden from Aug. 17, 2026, showing her Saturday wedding. (@JannArden/Instagram)

'Insistent I carry a bouquet'

Elva was voted Iceland's Woman of the Year in 2015 for her work on gender equality, and Person of the Year in 2017 for her part in the #MeToo movement. Elva is also a playwright, and co-author of the non-fiction book South of Forgiveness.

The couple discussed their upcoming wedding in an Aug. 11 episode of Arden's podcast titled Pre-wedding Jitters and Shitters. They joked that Arden was "the groom," but Elva added that Arden would be the one carrying the bridal bouquet.

"She is insistent that I carry a bouquet," Arden said.

Later in the podcast, Arden said she thought same-sex love should be as normalized as "a sandwich."

"The one thing that I'm very proud of is how much we're just normalizing this.… Normalizing people being in loving relationships and normalizing how society is structured and that we need to do a lot better for all people," Arden said.

"We're both in positions of privilege.... we have power, we have access to media. We're not fu--ing taking any prisoners with us. We don't tolerate it."

They're planning a honeymoon in Edinburgh, Arden said in a previous episode.

World.title: Hayden Panettiere, troubled star of Heroes and Nashville, remembered as 'brave and brilliant soul'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hayden Panettiere, who soared to fame two decades ago as a cheerleader with superpowers in the TV show Heroes and won country music success playing a singer on Nashville, has died. She was 36.

Police said Panettiere was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville, S.C., shortly before 2 p.m. Sunday. Life-saving measures were performed, but she was pronounced dead at the scene.

No cause of death has been determined and Panettiere's death remains under investigation. An autopsy found no signs of trauma and police said officers saw no signs of foul play.

"What an amazing talent you were … so gifted," wrote actress Viola Davis, who co-starred with Panettiere in the 2016 film Custody, on Instagram.

"Sending my love to Hayden and her family," wrote actor David Arquette, who worked with Panettiere on Scream 4, in an Instagram story. "She was such a brave and brilliant soul."

The television and film performer, who would have turned 37 on Friday, had been open about her private battles and wrote at length about them in the memoir This Is Me: A Reckoning, which came out in May.

She described lifelong scars from her early fame, and acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and enduring postpartum depression after the birth of her daughter with Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko in 2014.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden," her father, Skip Panettiere, said in a statement provided to ABC. "She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her on screen."

WATCH | Hayden Panettiere, star of Heroes and Nashville, dead at 36: Hayden Panettiere, star of Heroes and Nashville, dead at 36 | Duration 4:06 American actress Hayden Panettiere, famed for roles in television shows such as Nashville and Heroes, has died at age 36, her family said in a statement.

A publicist for Panettiere did not provide any additional details in response to inquiries from The Associated Press and CBC News.

In her final Instagram post, dated July 27, Panettiere is seen in a black and white photo, smiling and winking alongside director and photographer Randall Slavin.

"Good times and good friends," she said in the post.

Panettiere was one of two children born to Skip Panettiere, a former New York City fire captain, and Lesley Vogel, a former soap opera star who had been the prime force behind her early career, before the two became estranged.

Panettiere began acting in commercials and soap operas, including as the ever-troubled Lizzie Spaulding on Guiding Light. In This Is Me, she wrote that the traumas her character endured, from being kidnapped to killing her mother's boyfriend, led her to associate "catastrophe with adoration."

"Grown-ups gave me positive attention when — as an actor — I failed, got sick, screamed and cried, killed, grieved, and suffered," she wrote. "Is it any wonder why I've faced so many real struggles in my life? I've often wondered whether — unintentionally — I've brought on my traumas because I'm wired to think they're good for me."

She had much warmer memories of her role as a cheerleader with supernatural powers in Heroes, which propelled her to fame in 2006. The series revolved around the mantra "Save the cheerleader, save the world."

Panettiere's role as a cheerleader with superpowers in Heroes propelled her to fame in 2006. (Adam Taylor/NBCU Photo Bank/Getty Images)

"At the core of it are these human stories that people can relate to, very rugged. And it's just grabbed everyone in every age group," Panettiere told The Associated Press in 2008.

She went on to win three Teen Choice Awards for that role and was a Grammy award nominee for a children's spoken word album recorded a few years after the release of the animated movie A Bug's Life.

2 Golden Globe nominations

Panettiere later played a brash country upstart opposite Connie Britton on Nashville, which aired on ABC for four seasons before being cancelled and revived on CMT. She did her own singing in the show, which scored some hits on country charts, spawned U.S. tours and earned Panettiere two supporting actress Golden Globe nominations.

She had 11 songs recorded for Nashville appear on Billboard's Hot Country Songs charts during the show's run, including two featuring Britton.

Panettiere played a country singer opposite Connie Britton, right, on Nashville, which aired on ABC for four seasons before being cancelled and revived on CMT. She did her own singing in the show. (Mark Levine/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty Images)

In an interview with podcaster Jay Shetty after her memoir came out in May, Panettiere talked about the custody arrangement for her 11-year-old daughter, who lives full-time with Klitschko in Ukraine. News of the 2018 decision had prompted headlines about Panettiere giving up custody of her daughter.

"I think there's been this very common misconception that I just gave up my child," she said. "That could not be farther from the truth."

Panettiere worked in film and television beginning as a child. She is shown with Julie Bowen and Tim Allen at the Dec. 19, 2001, premiere in Los Angeles for the film Joe Somebody. (Vince Bucci/Getty Images)

Battled depression, addiction

Panettiere said Klitschko suggested their daughter live with him full-time when the child was two years old, as Panettiere struggled with mental health challenges and addiction.

She entered rehab in 2015, while filming Nashville.

"I was the one who put myself in the first treatment centre. I was drowning," she said in a 2023 interview with Women's Health magazine.

Panettiere had endured numerous family struggles and tragedy.

Her parents' marriage was strained, and eventually ended. Her younger brother, Jansen Panettiere, who was also an actor, died of a heart condition in 2023 at age 28.

Years earlier, Hayden had made the painful decision to part professionally with her mother, who throughout her childhood had "defined and driven her" and watched her "struggle, learn, grow, fall apart, and triumph."

"She and I spent so much time together, so deeply enmeshed in each other's lives, that we started grating on each other," Panettiere wrote in her memoir. "I hated when Mom whispered about other actors during auditions, positive that they could hear her compare them to me. I hated when Mom went to industry parties and got tipsy on the merlot she loved."

In recent years, she had been in a tumultuous relationship with actor Brian Hickerson.

Panettiere poses on the red carpet at the Emmy Awards in Los Angeles in August 2014. (Lucy Nicholson/Reuters)

On Shetty's podcast, Panettiere recalled the explosion of her fame when she was cast on Heroes, including the first time she was tracked by the paparazzi. When she'd imagined the moment as a younger actress, she'd planned to look chic.

Instead, she said, "it was just sheer terror."

Panettiere also appeared in two of the Scream movies, starred as the title character in the 2009 film I Love You Beth Cooper and played the young daughter of a football coach in Remember the Titans.

WATCH | Heroes, Nashville star Hayden Panettiere dead at 36: Heroes, Nashville star Hayden Panettiere dead at 36 | Duration 2:36 Hayden Panettiere, star of popular television series including Heroes and Nashville, has died at the age of 36. Her father, Skip, announced the actor's death in a statement on Sunday, though a cause of death has yet to be announced by the family.

In her memoir, Panettiere described herself as an "optimist to the core" who refused to be defined by tragedy.

"One thing I know from my 36 years in the public eye is this: Life is a process that evolves day by day, year by year and — like it or not — you are engaged in a cycle of growth until the moment you take your last breath."

Remembering a star

News of Panettiere's death prompted a wave of tributes.

"I wish the world had more time with you because I had a burning curiosity about who you were becoming. I saw this beautiful phoenix rising from the ashes," said Viola Davis. "Rest well, Hayden."

"Oh my god — heartbroken," said talk show host and comedian Rosie O'Donnell in an Instagram post.

Shetty, who interviewed Panettiere on his podcast just months ago, said in an Instagram comment, "I was so moved by the conversation we shared earlier this year. My love and condolences to her family and fans."

World.title: Nick Reiner denied access to trust fund ahead of murder trial, as trustees cite ‘slayer statute’
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nick Reiner, who stands accused of killing his parents Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, has been denied access to the $1.5-million US trust fund he was seeking to use to fund his legal defence.

According to a June filing, Reiner had been seeking allegedly unpaid money from a trust fund his parents established for him in 1993.

In court papers obtained by CBC News, trustees rejected Reiner’s request for the funds, citing a portion of California law known as the "slayer statute," which prevents individuals from inheriting money, property, or trusts from someone they have “feloniously and intentionally” killed.

Rob Reiner, a celebrated director and actor, and his wife Michele, a photographer and producer, were stabbed to death in their California home on Dec. 14. Hours later, their son Nick Reiner was arrested.

The 32-year-old was indicted on murder charges on July 20. He has pleaded not guilty.

Nick Reiner pleads not guilty to two counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of his parents, on Feb. 23. (Chris Torres/The Associated Press)

The indictment by a Los Angeles County grand jury, unsealed earlier this month, alleges that Reiner was lying in wait before attacking his parents. This detail, along with other circumstances, means he is eligible for the death penalty. District Attorney Nathan Hochman has said his office has not yet decided whether to seek it.

Reiner is scheduled to return to court for a pretrial hearing in September. He is currently being represented by public defender Kimberly Greene, to whom CBC News has reached out for comment.

Trust fund access denied

The June filing said that apart from the family trust fund, smaller individual trust funds had been established for the Reiner children, in their names. Nick Reiner was entitled to half of his trust fund when he turned 30, according to the document, and the rest at 35.

But he claimed in the petition that he had never received the funds he was meant to at 30, alleging that the trustees were denying him access to money to which he was legally entitled.

Alan Jackson, the attorney for Nick Reiner, speaks after Reiner's arraignment on murder charges, on Jan. 7 in Los Angeles. (Damian Dovarganes/The Associated Press)

"Like anyone accused of a crime, Nick is presumed innocent, and he is entitled to mount his defense with the resources that are lawfully his own,” the petition said, adding that the assets in the fund added up to at least $1.5 million US.

High-profile private lawyer Alan Jackson was originally retained to represent Reiner, but left after less than a month without sharing the reason. The June filing revealed that Reiner’s siblings, Jake and Romy Reiner, had initially agreed to pay their brother's legal fees before reversing course.

Jackson said in a declaration accompanying the petition that he would be willing to rejoin the case if the funds were available to retain him.

The two siblings have not publicly commented on the legal proceedings.

'Slayer statute' principles

The lawyer who was previously overseeing the trust fund, Paul R. Kanin, and incoming trustee Jodi Pais Montgomery both concluded in court documents that the unknown outcome of the criminal case against Reiner meant that funds could not be distributed at this time.

“Nick’s sense of urgency is real, but it did not arise in a vacuum. It arises from the deaths of his parents, the very settlors of the Trust at issue, and Nick is presently accused of causing those deaths," the new filing reads.

"While Nick is presumed innocent of that accusation ... no one, not this Court, nor the parties, knows how the criminal proceedings against Nick will ultimately resolve."

Caption: Rob Reiner and Michelle Reiner arrive on the red carpet at the State Department for the Kennedy Center Honors gala dinner in December 2023 in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Wolf/The Associated Press)

The filing stated that the trust fund can't be accessed until it is clear whether Probate Code Section 250 and any related "slayer statute" principles could affect Reiner’s entitlement to the funds.

Eight months after the killings, many details are still unknown to the public. Authorities have not speculated on motives.

Jake Reiner, the eldest son of Rob and Michele Reiner, opened up in April about enduring the “living nightmare” of his parents' murder, as well as the attention around the case centring on allegations about his brother.

WATCH | Rob Reiner's film legacy: 3 movies that shaped Rob Reiner’s film legacy | Duration 5:01

“Nothing can prepare you for what it feels like to lose both parents instantly at the same time,” he wrote in a Substack essay .

“They were the last people in the world to deserve what happened to them.”

Rob Reiner was known for his decades of work in the film industry, acting in and helming some of the most well-known films of Hollywood at the time. His credits as a director include The Princess Bride, A Few Good Men and Stand By Me.

He met his wife Michele while filming the beloved rom-com When Harry Met Sally, later telling CNN in 2024 that this meeting inspired him to change the ending of the film so that the main characters got together. They were married for 36 years.

World.title: Demand for Canadian citizenship certificates soaring, fuelled by Americans
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Applications from people around the world seeking Canadian citizenship certificates have been rising rapidly in recent months, fuelled by thousands of applications from the United States, CBC News has learned.

The number of people who have already received certificates as a result of Parliament’s adoption of “Lost Canadian” legislation late last year rose nearly 50 per cent between April 1 and May 31, according to new data obtained by CBC.

Bill C-3 allows citizenship for those who can prove they're descended from a Canadian ancestor, even if that ancestor left the country several generations back. It was adopted after the courts ruled that limiting citizenship to the first generation born outside of Canada was too restrictive.

Between mid-December — when Bill C-3 went into effect — and May 31, some 6,100 citizenship certificates were granted by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) to those who now qualify.

That is up from 4,075 certificates issued as a result of Bill C-3 from mid-December until March 31.

Another 17,390 people have received certificates as a result of having a Canadian parent. Prior to the bill's adoption, those who were born outside Canada had to have a Canadian parent to qualify for citizenship.

Tip of the iceberg

The certificates allow the 23,490 newly recognized Canadian citizens to apply for Canadian passports and live and work in Canada.

Elections Canada, however, says they can't vote in federal elections unless they've lived in Canada at some point in their life.

People born in the U.S. account for nearly half of those recognized between mid-December and the end of May. According to the data from IRCC, 3,110 Americans have qualified for Canadian citizenship certificates as a result of Bill C-3, while another 8,125 Americans have been granted certificates because one of their parents was born in Canada.

However, that’s just the tip of a very big iceberg.

The number of citizenship certificate applications waiting for a decision has exploded. In April, around 56,000 applications were waiting to be processed. That climbed to 70,400 in May.

Now, the IRCC’s website says 121,800 people are waiting for a decision. Those applications could be for anything from seeking recognition as a citizen under Bill C-3 to requesting a routine replacement of a lost or stolen certificate.

At the same time, the estimated wait time for a decision has doubled from 12 months in May to 25 months as of Aug. 10.

Estimates of just how many people could qualify for Canadian citizenship as a result of Bill C-3 vary widely.

Some point to a span of over 100 years in the 1800s and 1900s when hundreds of thousands of Canadians — particularly from Quebec — flowed over the border to jobs in the U.S.

The parliamentary budget officer has estimated that 115,000 people could be affected by the change in the law.

Last October, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab told the House of Commons immigration committee that she didn’t expect a flood of applications for citizenship certificates once Bill C-3 went into effect.

“We anticipate volumes in the tens of thousands over time," she said. "We do not expect any surge.”

Taous Ait, spokesperson for Metlege Diab, said IRCC took steps beforehand to prepare for the implementation of Bill C-3 and is working to process applications as quickly as possible while protecting the integrity of the citizenship program.

"We’re closely monitoring application volumes and trends and will adjust our operations as needed to manage demand as efficiently as possible," Ait said.

IRCC has not changed its requirements for documents, she added, but has taken steps to make the requirements clearer on its website and in other information for the public.

Demand soars for genealogical records

Meanwhile, Canada’s archivists are reporting a sharp rise in the number of requests for the genealogical records needed to prove someone seeking a Canadian citizenship certificate under Bill C-3 has an unbroken line of descent from a Canadian ancestor.

Alyssa Hyduk, president of the Association of Canadian Archivists, says her members are swamped, with some institutions seeing requests jump by 100 to 300 per cent.

Some are for documents that go back hundreds of years, she added.

“I think across the board there is this overwhelming feeling of just, of overwhelm and burnout …it’s really having an impact,” Hyduk explained.

“These requests are taking up so much of archivists' time that other reference requests — the [ones from the] rest of the public that we’re trying to still serve and do all our jobs — those are being set back too.”

Hyduk said the requests, most of which appear to be coming from the United States, are often complicated, as the records pre-date Confederation or are located in small church archives.

“We are at the point where [we're] going through boxes and boxes of material to find a single document sometimes,” she said. “You are going through reels of microfilm to find ship manifests with one name.”

“And these aren’t searchable documents,” she added. “We can’t go to Ctrl+F and find a last name. We have to read the handwriting. We have to figure it out.”

Archivists need more funding, says group

Mab Coates-Davies, executive director of the association, says the requests can also take an emotional toll on archivists.

“It is personal, it’s emotionally charged, it’s about family history,” she said. “There’s so many reasons that people, you know, might be looking to leave the States right now or planning for future moves.

“And so, there is that human element to it that archivists are feeling and experiencing, and frankly, IRCC isn’t on that front line in terms of the documentation.”

Another problem archivists are facing is the list of documents that IRCC will accept keeps evolving, said Hyduk. When the association met recently with the department, IRCC didn’t want to provide a definitive list of documents, saying it was likely to change.

The association is calling for more funding for archives across the country to keep up with the demand for records created by Bill C-3.

Coates-Davies said the flood of requests also began just as the Carney government’s budget cuts ended Library and Archives Canada’s $1.5-million-a-year Documentary Heritage Communities program, one that many small-and-medium-sized archives across the country have counted on for funding help.

“This funding package was just cut and then our workload skyrocketed," Coates-Davies said.

Last October, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab said she didn’t expect a flood of applications for citizenship certificates once Bill C-3 went into effect. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

Another wave looms?

During an association meeting last week, some archivists were also bracing for a new wave of requests for genealogical records.

In June, IRCC suddenly suspended an estimated 100 certificates that had already been issued after flagging problems with the documents submitted with the applications. The concern from archivists is that some people who've already applied to IRCC will be sent back to archives to find more genealogical records.

The IRCC says 83 of the suspensions have been resolved and the certificates restored. It has sent procedural fairness letters to another 17 people whose certificates were suspended and given them 60 days to submit the documents necessary to prove their Canadian ancestry.

If they fail to provide acceptable proof, their citizenship certificates could be revoked.

New Democrat immigration critic Jenny Kwan said she has been getting letters and inquiries from people affected by the suspension letters and has written to Metlege Diab, calling for answers.

“It really makes no sense whatsoever, what’s going on," Kwan said. "And the minister is completely ignoring that reality right now.”

World.title: Las Vegas gang leader masterminded Tupac's drive-by killing, prosecutor tells jury
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A former street gang leader orchestrated the 1996 drive-by shooting of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas in retribution for the beating of his nephew, a prosecutor told jurors during opening statements in a murder trial tied to a long-unsolved ‌crime that became a seminal moment in rap history.

Duane (Keffe D) Davis, 63, is charged in Clark County, Nev., with a single count of murder ‌using a deadly weapon. He has pleaded not guilty. Davis is accused of leading a group of men to kill Shakur, 25, one of rap's most commercially successful and influential artists, in a 1996 drive-by shooting near the Las Vegas Strip.

"You will learn that when the opportunity presented itself for ​retribution, Duane Davis made sure that the shooters were armed and ready to execute their plan. ​And remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself," prosecutor Binu Palal told the jurors in a downtown Las Vegas courthouse, referring to recent public statements by Davis that revived the long-dormant case.

Defence lawyer Michael Sandt said that after 30 years, investigators still have very little ​evidence to prove their case.

"At the end of the day you have to ask yourself, is what they are saying truth or ⁠fiction?" Sandt told the jury.

Shakur's killing heightened the image of violence permeating hip-hop culture and its lyrics during "gangsta" rap's golden age, stoking the East Coast-West ​Coast rap feud of that era.

Police said after Davis's 2023 arrest that he ​was a longtime suspect in the killing but that investigators lacked sufficient admissible evidence to charge him until he began implicating himself in a series of public statements.

The trial before Judge Carli Kierny is expected to run ​for up to six weeks. The jury was selected last week.

It may feature testimony from Death Row Records ⁠co-founder Marion (Suge) Knight, a former rap ⁠mogul who was with Shakur the night he was slain and is ‌now serving a 28-year prison sentence on an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction.

Former rap mogul Marion (Suge) Knight appears in court in 2018 to formally receive his 28-year prison sentence for a manslaughter conviction in the fatal 2015 hit-and-run killing of a man he ran down with his pickup truck in Los Angeles. Knight, the only other living witness to Tupac Shakur's shooting, may testify at the murder trial. (David McNew/EPA/Reuters)

Authorities have described Davis as the "shot caller" of a hurried plot to avenge the beating of his nephew by Shakur and members of his entourage inside the MGM Grand casino in Las Vegas the night of Sept. 7, 1996.

The violence at the ⁠casino allegedly stemmed from hostility between two Los Angeles-area street gangs — the South Side Compton Crips, of which Davis was the self-described leader, and Mob Piru, which police say was associated with Knight and Death Row Records. They were in Las Vegas to see a world heavyweight title boxing match ‌between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon.

Davis allegedly obtained the murder weapon and handed it off to two other men in the rear seat of a white Cadillac as they rode around looking for Knight and Shakur's car following the brawl.

Shots were fired when Davis and the others caught up with Knight and Shakur's vehicle. Shakur was struck four times and died in a ​hospital six days later. Knight, who had been driving, suffered a minor injury from a bullet fragment that grazed his head.

Davis described murder in interviews, book

The murder investigation grew cold for years, but ⁠police said statements Davis made in 2018 to various media outlets about his involvement in the shooting reinvigorated the case.

Davis said in interviews ⁠and in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, that he was riding in the front passenger seat of the Cadillac and had ⁠handed the ⁠gun to one of the two men sitting behind ​him, according to police.

But neither Davis's account nor authorities have said who fired the gun at Shakur. The three other men in the ​Cadillac with Davis have all since died.

Rap musician Tupac Shakur, seen in this 1993 file photo, died on Sept. 13, 1996, the victim of a drive-by shooting. Davis, who talked about his role in the shooting in interviews and a book, is on trial facing one count of murder ‌using a deadly weapon. (The Associated Press)

Under ⁠Nevada law, Davis can be charged with murder if he took part in the crime without pulling the trigger.

Tupac fan O'Ron Gordy said he'll never forget the night Tupac died.

“I don’t think we’ll ever find out the truth,” he said in an interview with CBC News outside the courthouse.

“It is what it is at this point. I’m just here to see what they got to say happened, see if I learn anything new, any new developments. [I’m] just here to support my favourite rapper.”

In his book, Davis wrote that he was long considered a suspect in the murders of Shakur and a rival rapper, Christopher Wallace, who performed as the Notorious B.I.G. under the New York-based Bad Boy Entertainment label and was shot dead in Los Angeles in March 1997.

Although the Wallace killing remains unsolved, investigators have long speculated ⁠he was gunned down in retaliation for Shakur's ‌killing months earlier.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: US seeks $1B aid package for Colombia’s new government
World.content:
Th US State Department said it will ask Congress for $1 billion for “deepening our shared and economic partnership” with the government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The funding boost, which resembles that of the first year of Plan Colombia in 2000, seeks to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

In preliminary talks, De la Espriella had already agreed to join the “Shield of the Americas,” a regional initiative of far-right governments to jointly fight crime.

According to a fact sheet, the funds that would require congressional approval would be used to:

Strengthen Colombia’s security forces

Disrupt illegal armed groups and organized crime’s ability to launder money

Significantly expand coca eradication and cocaine interdiction operations

Halt migration

Increase State presence in conflict regions

Combat child recruitment and exploitation by illegal armed groups

The administration of President Donald Trump also seeks to “increase trade and deepen economic ties between our countries.”

In order to do this, nominated US ambassador Nate Morris told the Senate that De la Espriella would withdraw from a memorandum of understanding with the government of China that sought to improve ties with the Asian giant.

Trump’s aid package would help Colombian communities “recover from potential El Niño-related flooding, drought,” which is expected to cause emergencies between December and March.

The US would also support a Bilateral Prosperity Dialogue to “stabilize” Colombia’s economy, “strengthening its energy generation and distribution sectors, exploring critical mineral investments, and creating new opportunities for US investors.”

The aid package would additionally “strengthen Colombian small and medium enterprises in agribusiness, manufacturing, and tech services by connecting them to US buyers and linking them to U.S.-aligned supply chains.”

The two governments would additionally seek to modernize Colombia’s digital, port and energy infrastructure while “positioning Colombia as a trusted nearshoring partner for supply chain diversification.”

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).
