Providing an additional jewel to Mexico’s booming tourism industry may not be — and should not be — the sole justification for nationalization; however, it is an indisputable collateral benefit. As such, the issue fits perfectly into the broader question of how a country with rising public debt can easily justify keeping such a collection at home.

An instructive look at another work of art

Last year, nearly 9 million people passed through the Louvre Museum in Paris to view the “Mona Lisa.” “Diego on My Mind” serves as its equivalent in the Western Hemisphere. Does no one realize that a museum — perhaps located in the Fourth Section of Chapultepec Park, or near the Soumaya, Jumex, Museum of Modern Art or National Museum of Anthropology — could be built around this painting by Kahlo and other iconic pieces?

Financially, this would not be the wasteful endeavor seen in other failed nationalizations, where there is never any hope of recouping the initial investment.

As with any expropriation, the Mexican Congress might need to allocate funds to cover the initial outlay; however, its role would be that of a guarantor rather than a debtor. As has been the case with other tourism ventures — such as the development of Cancún or Cabo San Lucas — Mexico would find private-sector entities (including non-profits) willing to assume the risks and reap the rewards of managing the operation. The country’s trust funds and public-private partnerships have often operated to the benefit of all stakeholders. In fact, Mexico could even choose to collaborate with the collection’s current owners in Monterrey.

The case for expropriation

Should the entire collection be seized? That matter can be addressed later.

It makes sense to seize all pieces of the Gelman Collection currently under Mexican control: specifically those housed at the government-owned Museum of Modern Art. Other works, including the 10 pieces by Kahlo and the 20 pieces classified as “historical monuments” by Diego Rivera, María Izquierdo, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros, can be handled on a case-by-case basis. It would be more advantageous for Mexico to acquire the entire package and sort out the minutiae later. This collection is scheduled to make its farewell in July. Time is running short.

… including other collections

Indeed, when observing Mexico’s detached attitude toward the Gelman Collection, the question arises: why not nationalize the SOP Collection, which was subject to the same history and legal conditions? It should be done. That collection — comprising 81 paintings, drawings and bronzes by 30 European artists — offers a glimpse into French and European culture during the early decades of the 20th century. The collection, which includes works by Bonnard, Braque, Dalí, Dubuffet, Matisse, Miró, Picasso, and Giacometti, was transferred to the Metropolitan Museum of Art from Natasha’s New York apartment in 1989; nine years later, at the time of Natasha’s death, it was designated a bequest.

Nationalization would serve another function as a kind of cleansing of governmental ineptitude or political corruption. Nationalizing would serve as a precedent, signaling to the world that Mexico’s heritage laws are real. No future concealment of collections or inaccurate tracking will be tolerated. The next time Mexico is called upon to protect its heritage, officials will not behave as if they were ignorant or complicit.

Stopping the pillage of Mexican art and culture

Of course, the nationalization of the Gelman Collection would cause entrepreneurs, art dealers and speculators at firms like Sotheby’s to raise their eyebrows, fearing a market disruption that would jeopardize their secretive business model. But this also presents a reward: an opportunity for Mexico to legitimize its stewardship of culture and send the right signals abroad to put a stop to all forms of pillage, however sophisticated they may be.

No, the history of nationalizations is not a pretty one, whether in Mexico, Venezuela, Iran or Russia. It is always concerning when leaders — vested with power and the national flag — decide that they know better than the market. Yet, there is a right moment for it. Like now.

To President Sheinbaum:

On the day you took office, you paid tribute to Frida Kahlo before your 125 million fellow citizens. Those words will ring hollow if you allow her works to be more acclaimed by others abroad than by those at home.

More recently, in Barcelona — during the so-called “Summit of Progressive Leaders” organized by the Spanish government — you stated: “I come here to acknowledge the courage of Frida Kahlo, who, even amidst physical frailty, knew how to fill the struggle for justice with color.”

It is a time for justice, not for patriotic narratives.

You may, in good faith, accept the Banco Santander Foundation’s plans to return the collection within two years. Yet let us not forget that the art world is rife with unfulfilled guarantees and broken promises. The Banco Santander Foundation assures us that any damage or degradation will be minimal; however, those within the art world know that the deterioration of quality is as certain as the law of gravity. Published financial documents suggest that Banco Santander may hold a lien on a loan that enabled the Zambrano family to acquire the collection. What happens if the Zambrano family defaults? The Spanish bank becomes the owner.

What real guarantee is there that the Gelman Collection will return? Are we to take the word of the very same people, citizens and public servants alike, who have blocked us and denied us information for at least 18 years?

Precedents for action

Use the precedent of the private Remedios Varo collection — safeguarded by the INBAL since it was donated in 2002 by a foreign couple — as a basis to affirm that your administration protects our cultural heritage and historical monuments for the benefit of the people.

Leadership entails persuading, enticing, intimidating, pressuring and appealing to every type of personality under the sun. Nationalizing this collection need not be an adversarial process. Through just a few meetings — and by leveraging your authority — you could swiftly ensure that this works for all the stakeholders involved.

No matter how one views it, the ownership of the Gelman Collection remains murky. You must declare that no private interest stands above the interest of the Nation. Tell us all, right now, that reclaiming these works is genuinely “what the People demand.”

Keith Rosenblum and Jesús Ibarra are contributors to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: El Jalapeño: FIFA allowed Mexico to host 2026 World Cup matches in exchange for Estadio Azteca’s entire revenue stream
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Representatives from world soccer’s governing body FIFA reassured Mexican fans and corporate investors this week that the 2026 World Cup was a deeply collaborative partnership, shortly after finalized financial terms confirmed that host venues were permitted to keep up to 100% of all unpaid operational cleanup costs.

The announcement comes on the heels of financial filings from Grupo Ollamani, owner of the iconic Estadio Azteca, which reported a net loss of 557.2 million pesos (US $32.2 million) during the second quarter, and a US $47 million loss on the World Cup in total. According to internal documents, the losses were directly linked to “standard tournament hosting compliance,” a procedural category that includes retrofitting stadium suites to FIFA specifications and legally surrendering the venue’s real estate and naming rights until mid-2027.

“We were immensely proud to bring the spirit of global football back to Mexico City,” said FIFA Deputy Chief of Global Commercial Extraction Eric Van Houten, speaking to local reporters. “In exchange for providing the sacred privilege of hosting five matches, FIFA asked for very little: total concessions revenue, local tax exemptions, zero corporate liability and temporary power of attorney over the municipal water grid during match days.”

When queried if local venue operators might reasonably expect to break even on their multi-million dollar capital investments, Van Houten expressed visible confusion. “Break even? The stadium received global exposure,” he noted. “When three billion people tuned in to watch a group stage match, they saw an exquisite facility that was entirely renovated to FIFA specifications. That kind of promotional opportunity is simply priceless … unless of course you’re the one paying for it. Then there is definitely a price.”

Local stadium management confirmed that while financial projections remain temporarily negative, internal morale remains high following FIFA’s official confirmation that venue employees will be permitted to keep all uncollected trash left in the upper concourses after each match.

“This is an unprecedented business model, but we are learning to appreciate the efficiency of it,” said an anonymous financial analyst familiar with the venue’s operations. “Usually, a corporate takeover takes months of hostile negotiations. FIFA managed to convince a major media holding company to pay US $47 million for the privilege of letting strangers redecorate their house and take all the furniture when they left. It is truly a lesson in how modern sports management works.”

World.title: Argentina Loses Formal Jobs as Labour Lawsuits Hit a Record
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts Record lawsuits: The Unión de Aseguradoras de Riesgos del Trabajo (UART), the workplace-risk insurers’ trade body, projects 137,800 new labour lawsuits for 2026, based on press reports. 72,525 cases were filed from January to July 2026.

The Unión de Aseguradoras de Riesgos del Trabajo (UART), the workplace-risk insurers’ trade body, projects 137,800 new labour lawsuits for 2026, based on press reports. 72,525 cases were filed from January to July 2026. Jobs lost: More than 235,000 private registered salaried jobs disappeared between November 2023 and April 2026, a 3.7% drop. Public employment fell about 73,000, for a net loss near 180,000.

More than 235,000 private registered salaried jobs disappeared between November 2023 and April 2026, a 3.7% drop. Public employment fell about 73,000, for a net loss near 180,000. Weak retention: Only 76 of every 100 private registered salaried workers are still in the same job after 12 months—the weakest level in a decade.

Only 76 of every 100 private registered salaried workers are still in the same job after 12 months—the weakest level in a decade. Informality rise: The share of informal workers hit 44.2% in the first quarter of 2026, according to INDEC, the national statistics agency. That’s a record high, meaning nearly half of workers lack formal protection.

The share of informal workers hit 44.2% in the first quarter of 2026, according to INDEC, the national statistics agency. That’s a record high, meaning nearly half of workers lack formal protection. Notifications surge: The system recorded 135,400 labour-law notifications over the last rolling 12 months, a sign of rising disputes.

The system recorded 135,400 labour-law notifications over the last rolling 12 months, a sign of rising disputes. Exchange rate: The Argentine peso closed at 1,487.75 per US dollar on 14 August 2026, so these figures translate into real economic pressure.

Formal work is thinning out, with record lawsuits and a record share of workers in the informal economy.

If you’re watching Argentina’s economy from abroad, the formal job market is sending a clear warning. Only 76 of every 100 registered private workers keep the same job a year later, and the system is bracing for a record 137,800 new labour lawsuits in 2026.

Buenos Aires at dusk. Registered private payrolls have shed more than 235,000 jobs since November 2023. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

A record wave of labour lawsuits

Argentina’s formal job market is facing a surge of legal disputes. The UART, the workplace-risk insurers’ trade body, projects 137,800 new labour lawsuits for 2026, according to press reporting from 14 August 2026. That’s a record, and it’s up from the 72,525 new cases already filed in the first seven months of the year.

The same reporting notes 135,400 labour-law notifications over the last 12 rolling months. That’s a heavy load on a system already strained by economic uncertainty.

For comparison, the peso is trading around 1,487.75 per US dollar (as of 14 August 2026), so the cost of litigation adds pressure on employers already facing high costs.

The surge is not evenly spread.That’s a regional hotspot in a national trend.

To put it in perspective, Argentina has 23 times more labour litigation than Chile, according to the same reporting. Even after labour reform, the caseload keeps climbing.

Why formal jobs are vanishing

The backdrop is a shrinking formal workforce. Between November 2023 and April 2026, more than 235,000 private registered salaried jobs disappeared, a 3.7% drop. Public employment fell about 73,000 over the same period, leaving a net loss near 180,000 jobs.

Only 76 of every 100 private registered salaried workers stay in the same job after a year—the weakest retention rate in a decade. That means more turnover, more instability, and more reasons for workers to seek legal recourse when they lose their posts.

The trend isn’t just about headlines. It reflects a slow grind: businesses cutting back, workers shifting to informal arrangements, and the state struggling to keep up.

The broader picture is stark.7% of the national workforce is in a situation of ‘labour vulnerability,’ meaning precarious employment or insufficient income, based on first-quarter 2026 data.

That aligns with the poverty data: poverty rose to 30% of the population in the first quarter of 2026, and indigence to 6.5%, according to another report.

Informality is now nearly half the workforce

Informal employment reached 44.2% of workers in the first quarter of 2026, according to INDEC, the national statistics agency. That’s the highest level in the recent series, up 2.2 percentage points from a year earlier.

This dual reality—more lawsuits among the formal, while more workers drop into the informal—suggests the system is pulling in two directions. Formal jobs become more expensive to maintain, so employers cut them, pushing workers into informal roles.

Informal workers have no registered contract, no social security contributions, and no legal protection if things go wrong. Nearly half of Argentine workers are in this situation, which means they have less income stability and less access to benefits, even as the formal sector struggles.

For investors, this fragility matters: a weaker formal workforce means lower tax revenue, less consumer stability, and a more volatile business environment.

Why the legal wave is a warning sign

The UART projection is an industry forecast, not an official government count. But the numbers are consistent with the 72,525 cases already filed in the first seven months of 2026, so the trend is credible.

A record wave of lawsuits raises the risk of higher costs for employers, which can feed into prices or job cuts. The rise in informality means more people outside the social safety net, which can hit consumption and public finances.

The system is also seeing the flip side: courts are pushing back on some claims. In one case from Resistencia, a judge dismissed a worker’s lawsuit and ordered him to pay the employer’s legal costs, calling the claim ‘manifestly unfounded.’

That suggests some legal activity may be speculative, but the sheer volume still weighs on the system.

What this means for you

If you’re living in or invested in Argentina, this isn’t abstract. A record wave of lawsuits raises the risk of higher costs for employers, which can feed into prices or job cuts. The rise in informality means more people outside the social safety net, which can hit consumption and public finances.

For those with exposure to Argentine stocks or bonds, watch the labour market. The trend is clear: formal employment is thinning, and the legal system is getting busier. That’s a signal of stress, not stability.

The data is based on UART projections via press reports, not official government statistics, so treat it as an industry view. But the direction is consistent with a broader picture of economic strain.

The peso’s slide—now at 1,487.75 per dollar—makes everything more complicated, from litigation costs to the real value of wages. Keep an eye on the next few months: if the caseload keeps climbing, expect more pressure on employers and more workers falling into the informal economy.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the UART and why does its projection matter? UART is the Unión de Aseguradoras de Riesgos del Trabajo, the trade body for workplace-risk insurers in Argentina. They track labour lawsuits because they’re responsible for insuring against workplace accidents and disputes. Their projection of 137,800 lawsuits for 2026 is based on industry data, reported by press, and signals rising formal-sector friction. How does the 44.2% informality rate affect the average worker? Informal work means no registered contract, no social security contributions, and no legal protection if things go wrong. Nearly half of Argentine workers are in this situation, which means they have less income stability and less access to benefits, even as the formal sector struggles. Is the 137,800 lawsuits figure an official government statistic? No. It’s a projection from UART, based on industry data, and reported by the press. It’s not a government or regulator figure. The number is consistent with the 72,525 cases filed from January to July 2026, but treat it as an industry forecast, not an official count. What does the 76-out-of-100 retention rate tell us? It means that for every 100 private registered salaried workers, only 76 are still in the same job after 12 months. That’s the weakest rate in a decade, showing that job stability is eroding. High turnover can lead to more lawsuits and more informality, as workers lose formal posts and move to informal ones.

World.title: Mexico’s Military Service Draw: Who the 2026 Lottery Covers
World.content:
Mexico · Explainer

Key Facts Lottery date: The Servicio Militar Nacional (SMN) draft lottery for Clase 2008 — men turning 18 in 2026 — is set for November 2026, according to SEDENA official information. The exact day hasn’t been published.

The Servicio Militar Nacional (SMN) draft lottery for Clase 2008 — men turning 18 in 2026 — is set for November 2026, according to SEDENA official information. The exact day hasn’t been published. Who is drawn: The main class is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year, plus ‘remisos’ — men who missed registering when they should have. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ (you serve) or a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’ (standby).

The main class is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year, plus ‘remisos’ — men who missed registering when they should have. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ (you serve) or a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’ (standby). 18–39 range: That age bracket exists only because the law’s obligations run to 31 December of the year a man turns 40. ‘Remisos’ — men who never registered — can be anywhere in that range. It’s not a new conscription band.

That age bracket exists only because the law’s obligations run to 31 December of the year a man turns 40. ‘Remisos’ — men who never registered — can be anywhere in that range. It’s not a new conscription band. Registration windows: The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries in the second half of the year a man turns 18. The 2026 convocatoria opens the municipal window from 2 January to 15 October 2026.

The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries in the second half of the year a man turns 18. The 2026 convocatoria opens the municipal window from 2 January to 15 October 2026. Cartilla liberation: The cartilla (military ID card) is liberated in December 2026. Those assigned ‘encuadrado’ attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027.

The cartilla (military ID card) is liberated in December 2026. Those assigned ‘encuadrado’ attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027. Voluntary for women: Women have been able to take part voluntarily since 2000 and are not subject to encuadramiento.

Women have been able to take part voluntarily since 2000 and are not subject to encuadramiento. Beyond the law: Claims that everyone aged 18 to 39 will be integrated into the Army if drawn go beyond what the law and SEDENA explicitly state. Treat them with caution.

The November draft lottery has a clear target group — and it isn’t everyone aged 18 to 39.

If you’ve seen posts claiming Mexico is about to draft everyone aged 18 to 39 into the Army, take a breath. Nothing changed this month. The claim doing the rounds is recycled coverage of SEDENA’s January 2026 convocatoria — the routine annual cycle being reported as news.

Mexico’s military service draw is held in November. No new rule was announced in August. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the lottery actually is

The SMN is Mexico’s compulsory military service. Under the Ley del Servicio Militar, the ‘service of arms’ is obligatory and of public order for Mexicans by birth or naturalization, according to press quotations. The law was originally published in 1940, with its latest reform on May 18, 2022.

The process runs in five steps: alistamiento (registration), sorteo (lottery), reclutamiento (recruitment), adiestramiento (training), and liberación (getting your cartilla freed). The lottery assigns men to ‘encuadrado’ status — meaning they must attend training — or to ‘disponibilidad’ (standby).

For 2026, the class is ‘Clase 2008’ — men born in 2008 who turn 18 this year. SEDENA officially informed that the lottery for this class will happen in November 2026. Those assigned encuadrado attend 13 Saturday sessions starting in 2027.

The 18-to-39 age range, explained

The 18-to-39 figure circulating online is real, but it doesn’t mean what the viral posts suggest. It describes ‘remisos’ — men who did not complete their SMN paperwork when they should have. These men are still under obligation to regularize their situation.

A remiso must regularize their status to obtain their cartilla. They remain under obligation until December 31 of the year they turn 40, which is why the range can span 18 to 39.

So the 18-to-39 window is about catching up on missed paperwork, not about a new draft sweeping in everyone up to middle age. The primary conscription class is still men turning 18 in 2026.

What’s compulsory, and for whom

For Mexican men, the SMN is an ‘obligación ineludible’ (unavoidable obligation), according to SEDENA communications as reported. If you’re a man who turns 18 in 2026, registration is not optional — it’s a legal duty.

If drawn encuadrado in the lottery, attendance at the 13 Saturday sessions is mandatory. Failing to present could lead to legal consequences, with up to one year of prison by court order referenced under the law.

For women, the rules are different. Participation in the SMN is strictly voluntary, and they are not subject to encuadramiento. This has been the case since 2000.

What’s actually new for 2026

The basic structure of the SMN hasn’t changed. There’s no new SEDENA notice and nothing in the official gazette for August 2026. The claim doing the rounds is the routine annual cycle being reported as news.

The 2026 convocatoria, which dates to January, opens the municipal registration window from 2 January to 15 October 2026. The Ley del Servicio Militar sets preliminaries for the second half of the year a man turns 18.

This is the same annual process. The November draw assigns a white or blue ball for ‘encuadrado’ — meaning you serve — and a black ball for ‘disponibilidad’. Cartilla liberation is in December 2026.

Why this matters for you

If you’re a Mexican man who never completed your SMN paperwork, the clock is ticking. The remiso window is real, and the November 2026 lottery for Clase 2008 is the one that applies to you most directly if you’re in that class. But even if you’re older, you still need to regularize to get your cartilla before turning 40.

For expats and investors, the practical takeaway is simpler: there’s no mass mobilization coming. The SMN is a long-standing administrative process, and the 18-to-39 scare is a misreading of the remiso rule. Your neighbor with a desk job isn’t about to be drafted.

If you have employees or family members facing this, the real deadline is paper-based: register, get your cartilla, and you’re done. The lottery is a formality for most.

Nothing in the sources suggests a shift that would affect labor markets, investment, or day-to-day life beyond the usual paperwork. The only people who need to act are those who’ve fallen behind on their SMN obligations — and they should treat this as a reminder to catch up.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is everyone aged 18 to 39 being drafted into the Mexican Army? No. The 18-to-39 range refers to ’remisos’ — men who missed registering for the SMN when they were due and must regularize their status to get their cartilla. The main conscription class for 2026 is men born in 2008, turning 18 this year. Claims about a mass draft of everyone up to 39 go beyond what the law and SEDENA state. When is the 2026 military service lottery? For Clase 2008, SEDENA officially informed that the lottery will be held in November 2026. The exact day hasn’t been published. Is military service compulsory for women in Mexico? No. Women’s participation in the SMN is strictly voluntary, and they are not subject to encuadramiento. This has been the case since 2000. What happens if I miss the registration deadline? You become a ’remiso’ — a man who didn’t complete SMN paperwork when due. You must regularize your status to obtain your cartilla, and you remain under obligation until December 31 of the year you turn 40. Legal consequences, including up to one year of prison by court order, are referenced under the law, though sources don’t clarify if this is newly enforced.

World.title: A Week On, Colombia’s Quake Toll Is Still Moving
World.content:
Colombia · Disaster

Key Facts The toll As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut: 287 dead, 4,147 injured, 194 still missing and 355 rescued.

As of the national disaster agency’s 16 August evening cut: 287 dead, 4,147 injured, 194 still missing and 355 rescued. The damage 26,392 homes destroyed and 127,608 damaged, with 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments.

26,392 homes destroyed and 127,608 damaged, with 197 buildings collapsed across 472 municipalities in 15 departments. The reach 185,996 people and 120,671 families affected, plus 3,207 schools, 304 health centres and 410 roads.

185,996 people and 120,671 families affected, plus 3,207 schools, 304 health centres and 410 roads. Numbers move both ways The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight — duplicates get removed as names are confirmed.

The count was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Falling tolls are normal in the first fortnight — duplicates get removed as names are confirmed. A private cheque David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million — about US$32 million — towards reconstruction.

David Vélez, the Colombian co-founder and chief executive of Nubank, is giving COP$100,000 million — about US$32 million — towards reconstruction. The politics A censure motion against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán was announced on 17 August over photographs of him at the beach in Santa Marta during the emergency.

Seven days after a magnitude 7.4 quake hit Chocó, the official count is still being revised in both directions — and the politics has arrived.

If you have been trying to follow Colombia’s earthquake from abroad, the hardest part is that the numbers keep changing. A week after the magnitude 7.4 quake struck on 10 August, centred five kilometres south of San José del Palmar in Chocó, the official toll has gone up and then back down. Here is where it actually stood at the last full count, and what has happened around it since.

President Abelardo De la Espriella announced the Nubank founder’s donation. A censure motion against the housing minister followed. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Where the count stands

The national disaster agency, UNGRD, publishes periodic cuts rather than a live figure. Its last full one, timed at 18:30 on 16 August, recorded 287 dead and 4,147 injured.

Another 194 people are still listed as missing, and 355 have been pulled out alive. Those two numbers are the ones to watch, because the gap between them is where the toll will move next.

The physical damage is enormous for a country this size. 26,392 homes destroyed, 127,608 damaged, 197 buildings down, and effects recorded in 472 municipalities across 15 departments.

Public infrastructure took a similar beating — 3,207 schools, 304 health centres and 410 roads are on the affected list.

Why the death toll went down

On 15 August the official figure was 294. On 16 August it was 287. A falling toll looks alarming if you have not seen it before, and it is worth explaining.

In the first days after a disaster, the same victim can be counted twice — once by a municipality, once by a hospital, once by a rescue team. As names are confirmed, duplicates come out.

The practical lesson for anyone tracking this from a distance is to timestamp every number you read. A figure without a date attached is not much use this week.

The search is over in Chocó, not nationally

This is the distinction most coverage is getting wrong. On 12 August the governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba-Curi, declared the search and rescue phase finished in her department, saying they were no longer looking for anyone under the rubble.

That applies to Chocó alone. Nationally the phase remains open, which is consistent with 194 people still unaccounted for.

So if you read that Colombia has ended the search, it is half right. The epicentre department has moved to recovery while other departments have not.

Money, tolls and a minister at the beach

David Vélez, who co-founded Nubank and runs it, is putting COP$100,000 million — roughly US$32 million — into reconstruction. He confirmed the donation himself after President Abelardo de la Espriella announced it.

The road agency ANI, under its president Ricardo Ayerbe, has waived tolls — but far more narrowly than the headlines suggest. The exemption covers vehicles carrying heavy machinery, emergency equipment and humanitarian aid, and only on a defined set of corridors.

Those include Buga–Buenaventura, the Malla Vial del Valle, Armenia–Pereira–Manizales, the Tercer Carril Bogotá–Girardot and Girardot–Ibagué–Cajamarca. Fines for overloaded vehicles are suspended so aid trucks are not penalised. If you are driving a private car, you still pay.

And the politics has landed. On 17 August a censure motion was announced against Housing Minister Jaime Andrés Beltrán, over photographs of him at the beach in Santa Marta while the emergency was running. It has been announced, not voted.

What this means if you live in or invest in the region

Housing is the number that will shape the next two years. With 26,392 homes destroyed and 127,608 damaged, this becomes a construction and public-finance story long after it stops being a rescue story.

The corridors on ANI’s exemption list are the same ones that carry freight between Buenaventura, Colombia’s main Pacific port, and the interior. Anyone moving goods through that port should be reading the ANI notices, not the general coverage.

The Vélez donation is worth noting for a different reason. US$32 million from one private individual is a meaningful share of an early reconstruction bill, and it sets a reference point other large Colombian companies will now be measured against.

And the censure motion is a reminder of how quickly disaster response becomes political here. For anyone with projects awaiting housing-ministry decisions, that is a scheduling risk worth pricing.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people died in Colombia’s earthquake? The national disaster agency UNGRD recorded 287 deaths in its cut at 18:30 on 16 August 2026, with 4,147 injured and 194 people still missing. The figure moves between cuts, so always check the date attached to it. Why did the death toll go down? It was 294 on 15 August and 287 on 16 August. Early counts often double-record the same victim through different channels, and duplicates are removed as identities are confirmed. Has the search for survivors ended? In Chocó, yes — the governor declared the search and rescue phase over on 12 August. Nationally it remains open, with 194 people still unaccounted for. Are Colombia’s toll roads free after the earthquake? Only for specific vehicles. ANI has exempted vehicles carrying heavy machinery, emergency equipment and humanitarian aid on a defined list of corridors, and suspended overload fines. Private cars still pay.

World.content:
Peru · Mining

Key Facts Investment rise — Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina.

— Peru’s mining investment grew 42.7% year-on-year to US$3.304 billion in H1 2026, per MINEM and Andina. The 74% myth — A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total.

— A widely shared figure of +74% is actually Fresnillo’s revenue increase (up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion), a Mexico-only company, not a Peru sector total. — Southern Copper’s first-half net sales were US$8.54 billion, up 38.4% (US$8,540.4m against US$6,172.9m). Weak spot — Exploration spending rose only 1.3%, to US$336.4 million, even as investment boomed.

The real story: Peru’s mining investment hit US$3.3 billion in H1 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. That 74% figure? It’s a Mexican miner’s revenue.

If you’ve seen headlines about Peru’s mining sector surging 74%, you might be forgiven for thinking the country is swimming in cash. But the actual official figure is different: mining investment rose 42.7% to US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) via state news agency Andina. The 74% bump belongs to Fresnillo, a Mexico-only miner—not Peru. Let’s clear up the confusion so you know what’s really happening on the ground.

An open-pit operation in the Peruvian Andes. Mining investment reached US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The real numbers from MINEM

Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) reported that mining investment totaled US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, a 42.7% jump from the same period last year when it was US$2.3152 billion. That’s the official, sector-wide figure, and it’s solid growth—just not the 74% some headlines suggest.

The investment leaders, according to MINEM, are Southern Peru, Shougang Hierro Peru, Las Bambas, Antamina, Buenaventura, and Cerro Verde. Southern Peru alone invested US$432.7 million, up 101.1% from a year earlier.

But there’s a weak spot: exploration spending rose only 1.3%, to US$336.4 million. Investment is booming; the search for the next deposit is not. For context, that US$3.304 billion is roughly 11.1 billion soles at the current exchange rate of 3.3647 soles per US dollar. It’s a healthy number, showing that miners are putting money into the ground—and that confidence is a big deal for a country that’s the world’s second-largest copper producer.

Where the 74% figure really comes from

The 74% figure that’s been floating around is real, but it’s not about Peru as a whole. It comes from Fresnillo, a Mexico-based mining company, which reported a 74.7% rise in first-half 2026 revenue, reaching US$3.38 billion, and net profit of US$1.46 billion, up 213%. Fresnillo has no Peru operations at all—its mines are at Saucito, Herradura, Juanicipio, Fresnillo, Cienega and San Julian. So it’s not a reflection of Peru’s mining sector.

So when you see claims about Peru’s mining profits soaring 74%, double-check the source. The official Peruvian metric is the 42.7% investment increase, and that’s the one to trust for sector health. Why does this matter? Because investment is a forward-looking indicator—it shows companies are confident enough to spend on new projects and expansion. Profits can be volatile, but investment signals long-term commitment.

The confusion likely stems from a mix of company-level results and sector-wide data being shared without clear labels. For instance, MMG’s profit surged, but that’s a single company, not the whole sector. Fresnillo’s revenue jump is impressive, but it’s a different country entirely.

Company-level wins that tell the real story

Peru-linked miners had a strong first half, even if the 74% headline is wrong. MMG, which operates the Las Bambas copper mine in Peru, reported profit after tax of US$1,366.0 million, up 89%, with profit attributable to equity holders of US$897.2 million. The 141% rise some cite is actually the increase in cash, not earnings. Las Bambas was central to that result, and MMG called it its strongest financial performance in more than a decade.

Anglo American’s Quellaveco mine in Peru generated US$2.161 billion in revenue, up from US$1.524 billion in H1 2025. That’s a 41.8% increase, driven by higher copper prices and production—even though output was slightly lower. Southern Copper, which runs major mines in Peru, posted first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%; the second quarter alone was US$4,289.0 million.

Buenaventura, a Peruvian miner, saw net income attributable of US$514.0 million on H1 revenue of US$1,153.6 million, both materially higher than the same period in 2025. Nexa Resources’ Peru subsidiary, Nexa Resources Peru S.A.A., reported US$669 million in revenue, up 45%—not the group. The Nexa group’s first-half revenue was US$1,796 million, up 34%.

Why this matters for you

If you’re invested in Latin America, these numbers matter because they show where capital is flowing. Peru is the world’s second-largest copper producer, and rising investment means more supply coming online—which could affect global copper prices and your portfolio. For instance, MMG’s record profit and Southern Copper’s revenue surge are signals that copper demand remains strong.

For expats living in Peru, a mining boom often translates into more jobs, stronger local economies in mining regions, and a firmer sol. The currency has been stable, with the exchange rate around 3.36 soles per US dollar. Mining investment also supports infrastructure and local businesses, from equipment suppliers to service providers.

But don’t get caught up in the hype. The 74% figure is a classic example of a number being taken out of context. Stick to the official MINEM data, and you’ll have a clearer picture of what’s actually happening. And if you’re watching specific stocks, remember that company-level results can vary widely—so look at each miner’s own numbers, not just the sector headline. Also, note that Peru’s energy and mines minister is Guillermo Shinno Huamani, sworn in in late July 2026 under President Keiko Fujimori—his office is the source for the official investment data.

Frequently Asked Questions

Peru’s Ministry of Energy and Mines (MINEM) reported mining investment of US$3.304 billion in the first half of 2026, up 42.7% year-on-year. Where does the 74% figure come from? The 74% figure is actually Fresnillo’s revenue growth—up 74.7% to US$3.38 billion. Fresnillo is a Mexico-only miner, not a Peru-specific metric. Which companies led mining investment in Peru? According to MINEM, the top investors include Southern Peru (US$432.7 million, up 101.1%), Shougang Hierro Peru (US$314.4 million, up 135.4%), Las Bambas (US$275.5 million, up 50.5%), Antamina (US$271.6 million, up 31.2%), Buenaventura (US$174.2 million, up 2.4%), and Cerro Verde (US$169.3 million, up 3.8%). How did Peru-linked miners perform in H1 2026? MMG’s Las Bambas contributed to a US$1,366.0 million profit after tax, up 89%. Anglo American’s Quellaveco saw US$2.161 billion in revenue. Southern Copper reported first-half net sales of US$8.54 billion, up 38.4%.

World.title: India’s KABIL Now Sees Argentine Lithium in 2030
World.content:
Argentina · Mining

Key Facts 2024 pact : In January 2024, KABIL signed an agreement with Argentina’s state-owned CAMYEN for exploration and development of five lithium blocks in Catamarca province.

: The exploration deal is worth ₹2 billion, which is about US$21 million. Block count : KABIL holds five lithium-brine blocks in Catamarca, and is evaluating seven additional greenfield blocks offered under the same arrangement.

Timeline caveat : The four-to-five-year extraction start is an expectation reported by Reuters, based on a parliamentary panel report, not a confirmed commissioning date. : The four-to-five-year extraction start is an expectation reported by Reuters, based on a parliamentary panel report, not a confirmed commissioning date. The panel says first production has slipped to December 2030. Currency check: The Argentine peso sits at 1,487.75 per US dollar (as of 14 Aug 2026), so conversion math matters for project costs.

India’s state miner expects to start pulling lithium from its five Catamarca blocks within four to five years, but that timeline is an expectation, not a done deal.

If you’re tracking Latin America’s lithium race, here’s a new player to watch: India’s state-owned miner KABIL expects to start extracting lithium in Argentina within the next four to five years. But before you bank on that date, know this — it’s an expectation from a parliamentary panel chaired by Anurag Thakur report, not a binding project schedule, and there are still feasibility studies and approvals ahead. The clearest confirmed piece of this story is the January 2024 agreement KABIL signed with Argentina’s state-owned CAMYEN for exploration and development of five lithium blocks in Catamarca province — an investment of ₹2 billion, which is about US$21 million.

Lithium evaporation ponds at Hombre Muerto in Catamarca — the province where KABIL holds its five exploration blocks. The plant pictured is not KABIL’s. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What KABIL has actually signed

In January 2024, KABIL signed an agreement with CAMYEN SE. CAMYEN SE is the mining company owned by the Catamarca provincial government.

The deal covers exploration and development of five lithium-brine blocks in Catamarca. This province in northwest Argentina is known for its salt flats and lithium production.

It was India’s first lithium exploration and development agreement anywhere in the world. It marked India’s entry into Latin America’s lithium triangle.

The five blocks include four called Cortadera and one numbered Cateo-2022-01810132. Together, they cover about 15,703 hectares.

The investment for this exploration pact is ₹2 billion, or about US$21 million. This money covers studying and developing the blocks, not building a full mine.

KABIL has reported no operating revenue for the last three years because it is still in the exploration stage. This shows the financial challenge of these overseas projects.

Catamarca has offered KABIL seven additional lithium brine blocks under the same arrangement. Greenfield means untouched land, so these are brand-new developments, not expansions.

KABIL is currently evaluating these seven blocks, according to the sources. But the commercial terms for them are not stated, so no numbers are known yet.

If KABIL accepts them, it would nearly triple its footprint in Catamarca. But evaluation means nothing is final.

Argentina’s lithium triangle includes more than Catamarca. KABIL is also in talks for two lithium projects in Jujuy, a neighboring province.

In Salta, Reuters says KABIL is working on a preliminary agreement with the Ministry of Production and Mining. That deal is not final yet.

These talks are active but lack public detail on stake sizes or investment amounts. They are less important than the 2024 CAMYEN agreement.

Reuters reports KABIL expects to start lithium extraction in Argentina in four to five years, after feasibility work. This comes from a parliamentary panel report, not a company schedule.

The same panel says first production may slip to December 2030. That is one year later than the earlier target of September 2029.

Before that, KABIL must finish feasibility studies and get later approvals. It may also need to renegotiate terms as the market changes.

In mining, timelines often slip, especially when they are expectations, not commitments. The panel also noted financial limits and execution gaps in India’s overseas mineral push, so nothing is certain yet.

The seven-block expansion in Catamarca

Beyond Catamarca: Jujuy and Salta

Why the 4-5 year timeline is soft

Why this matters for Latin America

For anyone living in or invested in Latin America, this is a signal of shifting demand. India is the world’s third-largest oil importer and a growing consumer of batteries for electric vehicles and electronics, and it’s looking to Latin America to secure lithium outside China’s supply chain. Argentina, Chile, and Bolivia form the so-called ‘lithium triangle’ that holds more than half of the world’s known lithium resources, and Argentina’s Catamarca, Jujuy, and Salta provinces are at the heart of it.

If KABIL moves from exploration to production, it would add a new buyer of Argentine lithium, potentially boosting provincial royalties and foreign investment in a country that needs both. But the project’s timeline is soft, and the financial stress of KABIL — no revenue for three years — could slow things further. For now, the five blocks are signed, the seven more are on the table, and the four-to-five-year date is a hope, not a promise.

In January 2024, KABIL signed an agreement with Argentina’s state-owned CAMYEN for exploration and development of five lithium blocks in Catamarca province, with an investment of ₹2 billion (about US$21 million). When will KABIL start producing lithium in Argentina? KABIL expects to start extracting lithium within four to five years, according to a parliamentary panel report cited by Reuters. But this is an expectation, not a binding schedule — feasibility studies and approvals are still pending. The panel says first production has slipped to December 2030. Is KABIL expanding beyond its five Catamarca blocks? Yes. Catamarca has offered KABIL seven additional greenfield lithium brine blocks, which KABIL is evaluating. Commercial terms for those blocks are not yet public. What other Argentine provinces is KABIL involved in? KABIL is in discussions for two lithium projects in Jujuy. In Salta, it is in the process of signing a preliminary agreement, but that is not yet a signed deal.

The Mexican retail giant is betting on its payments app instead of a bank license, and the numbers explain why.

If you live in Mexico, you’ve probably bought a snack or paid a bill at an OXXO. Now FEMSA, the company behind those stores, has paused its plan to turn OXXO into a full bank. Instead, it’s pushing hard on Spin, its payments app, which processed 119.1 million transactions per month in the second quarter of 2026.

An OXXO store in Mexico City. FEMSA had 24,708 OXXO stores in Mexico at the end of June. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Why FEMSA changed course

FEMSA has not given up on banking. It has just paused that plan.

On 31 March 2026, CEO Jose Antonio Fernandez Garza-Lagueera told investors the banking-licence request is on hold.

The priority is to make OXXO stores more efficient and profitable. This is part of a plan called FEMSA Forward.

On the second-quarter call on 28 July 2026, he said FEMSA will need to find funding. That could include getting a banking licence.

Look at the numbers to understand this change. Spin had 119.1 million transactions per month in Q2 2026.

That is up 61.5% from the same time last year. Active users reached 11.5 million, up 22.1%.

This is strong engagement to build on. And it happens without the heavy rules of a bank charter.

Spin by OXXO is not a bank. It never was.

It is an IFPE, which means Institucion de Fondos de Pago Electronico. Mexico’s CNBV allowed this on 7 October 2022.

In simple words, Spin can hold and move money for customers. But it cannot lend deposits like a bank does.

That difference is the main point of this story.

FEMSA is testing a small credit pilot programme. CFO Martin Arias spoke about off-balance-sheet structures as the credit book grows.

Off-balance-sheet means the debts are not shown fully on FEMSA’s main financial reports. If this business matures, FEMSA could use that funding option.

Then it might look at a banking licence again later.

So this is a ‘maybe later’, not a ‘yes now’. For now, the plan is to use the Spin system to keep customers inside the OXXO world.

That includes payments, credit, and other services.

Credit is a big part of this new phase. After years of growing users and transactions, Spin now wants to make money.

Credit is one key way to do that. The small pilot is the first step.

If it works, FEMSA could expand it without needing a bank licence right away.

There is clear proof that the credit business is growing. QED Investors has bought a strategic equity stake in FEMSA’s lending unit.

FEMSA still keeps control of that unit.

If you follow Mexican retail or fintech, this shows where growth is. FEMSA is choosing a digital-first path instead of a traditional bank model.

It is betting that millions of store visits can turn into app use.

The credit experiment

What this means for investors and expats

For anyone living in Mexico, it means Spin could become a bigger part of daily life — paying for goods, maybe taking small loans. The US dollar was trading at 17.0188 pesos, so the stakes are clear: a successful fintech play could add significant value in dollar terms.

And the market has taken notice.4% and up from 42 cents a year earlier. That earnings beat, driven partly by OXXO Mexico and Coca-Cola FEMSA, suggests the strategy is already paying off.

The pause on the banking license also reduces regulatory risk in the near term, which can be a plus for shareholders watching how FEMSA allocates capital. With the stock trading at $118.12 as of August 14, 2026, up 1.39% on the day, investors seem to be taking the news in stride.

The bigger fintech picture

FEMSA isn’t alone in chasing digital payments in Latin America. The region has seen a wave of app-based financial services, from Brazil’s Nubank to Argentina’s MercadoLibre, and Spin is FEMSA’s answer to that trend.

The key difference: OXXO’s physical footprint. With 24,708 stores in Mexico as of 30 June 2026, FEMSA has a distribution channel that pure digital players lack — a real advantage for cash-based customers making the leap to apps.

By keeping the banking license on the back burner, FEMSA can move faster and lighter, testing products like credit without the heavy compliance costs of a full bank. That flexibility is a competitive edge in a region where fintech is still evolving.

Why this matters for Latin America

This story isn’t just about one company. It’s a window into how big retailers across Latin America are choosing digital apps over traditional banking structures to reach millions of underbanked people.

For you, whether you’re a local or an expat, that means more options for everyday payments and credit, often with lower fees and faster approval times than traditional banks. And if FEMSA’s credit pilot succeeds, you could see similar moves from other retailers in the region.

FEMSA believes that small shops and big size will beat strict rules.

If Spin keeps growing this fast, you may never need a bank branch.

Just use a corner store and a smartphone.

Debt ask: Quito wants better terms on its Chinese debt, which was about $2.2 billion as of August 2025. That debt is down from $9.6 billion in 2016, but no renegotiation is confirmed.

Hydropower deal: A possible PowerChina contract at Coca Codo Sinclair is reported at up to about $1.5 billion over 25 years. This is for operation and maintenance, but it is reported, not signed.

No new package yet: No agreement, memorandum, or dollar figure has been announced from the August meetings. The Belt and Road framework and free trade agreement existed before this trip.

Ecuador’s president heads to Beijing with a wish list: mining cash, relief for 14 suspended shrimp exporters, and softer terms on roughly $2.2 billion in Chinese debt.

If you have money in Latin American commodities or trade, this is a trip worth watching. Ecuador’s President Daniel Noboa is in China from 16 to 23 August on a state visit at Xi Jinping’s invitation, carrying an agenda that covers energy and mining investment, a lifeline for 14 shrimp exporters, and easier repayment terms on Chinese debt. The trip is the first leg of a broader Asia tour that runs until 28 August and includes Singapore and Vietnam, where Noboa is also scheduled to meet both countries’ prime ministers.

Noboa and Xi Jinping at an earlier meeting. The August state visit runs 16 to 23 August. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What Noboa wants from Beijing

Noboa’s agenda is a shopping list of Latin America’s classic asks: investment, trade access, and debt relief. He is scheduled to meet Xi Jinping, Premier Li Qiang, and NPC Standing Committee Chairman Zhao Leji — all confirmed in their posts. The meetings are the core of the state visit, and the stated purpose is to deepen bilateral ties and attract investment.

Ecuador wants Chinese money in energy and mining, to strengthen exports, and to sort out the shrimp suspension that hit 14 companies. There is also the matter of the Coca Codo Sinclair hydroelectric plant, where the government wants PowerChina to handle operation and maintenance. The shrimp issue is especially urgent for a sector that employs tens of thousands of people, and any delay in lifting the suspensions hits export revenues.

The numbers behind the trip

Trade is the headline. Bilateral trade hit $17.33 billion in 2025, up 24% year on year, with Ecuadorian exports to China at $9.55 billion and a $1.77 billion surplus. That surplus gives Quito some leverage in talks, though China’s sheer market size means the leverage cuts both ways.

On debt, Ecuador’s total to China is about $2.2 billion as of August 2025, down from $9.6 billion in 2016. Better terms on that would free up fiscal room for a government juggling security spending and a tough economic outlook. Debt is on the pending list, but no renegotiation has been confirmed.

On the shrimp front, China suspended imports from 14 Ecuadorian companies in October 2025 over sodium metabisulfite residues and white spot virus. Getting those lifted matters for a sector that is a major employer and export earner. Ecuador’s shrimp exports to China were worth billions of dollars annually, and the suspension has already disrupted supply chains.

The Coca Codo Sinclair angle

Coca Codo Sinclair is a 1,500 megawatt hydroelectric plant, built by Sinohydro, and transferred to Ecuadorian control in April 2026. It’s a key piece of Ecuador’s energy grid, and its operation and maintenance are on the table. The possible PowerChina deal is reported at up to about $1.5 billion over 25 years — that’s reported, not signed.

The plant, built with Chinese financing, has faced operational issues in recent years. A new contract would ensure its continued operation while transferring technical expertise. The plant’s output is critical for Ecuador’s electricity supply, and any disruption would have ripple effects across the economy.

Why it matters for Latin America

This isn’t just about Ecuador. China is the top trading partner for several Latin American countries, and the terms of its deals in Ecuador — whether on debt, mining, or infrastructure — set precedents that ripple across the region. If Ecuador gets softer debt terms, other indebted nations like Argentina, Bolivia, or Venezuela will be watching closely.

For investors, the outcome of the shrimp talks is a bellwether for how China handles trade disputes with smaller partners. For mining, any new Chinese investment in Ecuador’s copper or gold projects could shift the regional balance of extraction rights and export routes.

Ecuador joined the Belt and Road in 2018, and Xi and Noboa signed a cooperation plan in June 2025. The free trade agreement has been in force since May 2024. Ecuador’s experience — combining trade, debt, and infrastructure — is a microcosm of the complex relationship.

What is not yet agreed

The reporting is strong on the planned agenda and the existing trade framework, but as of 17 August no agreement, memorandum, or dollar figure has been announced from these meetings. The outcome of the Xi meeting has not been reported. The Belt and Road cooperation document and the free trade agreement were signed and in force before this trip, so they are not new from these meetings.

Treat the trip as a negotiation, not a done deal. If you are an investor, watch for concrete numbers on mining concessions or debt restructuring terms in the days after the visit. The absence of a signed package so far suggests the talks are still fluid, and any announcements will likely come in the form of joint statements or press releases from Quito or Beijing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does Noboa’s China visit matter for investors? Because Ecuador is a major exporter of shrimp, oil, and minerals, and China is its top trading partner. Any deal on mining investment or debt relief could move the country’s risk premium and the outlook for its exports. What is the status of the shrimp export suspensions? China suspended imports from 14 Ecuadorian shrimp companies in October 2025 over sodium metabisulfite residues and white spot virus. Noboa wants those restrictions lifted, but no agreement has been reported from the August meetings yet. How much debt does Ecuador owe to Chinese banks? Ecuador’s debt to China is about $2.2 billion as of August 2025, down from $9.6 billion in 2016. Quito is seeking better repayment terms, but no renegotiation is confirmed. What is the Belt and Road document mentioned in the reporting? It is a cooperation framework under China’s Belt and Road Initiative. Ecuador joined in 2018, and Xi and Noboa signed a cooperation plan in June 2025. It is not new from the August meetings.

World.title: Kast’s Security Reform Hits a Wall on His Own Side
World.content:
Chile · Politics

Key Facts The reform Eleven changes to Chile’s constitution, aimed at organised crime and terrorism. It enters through the Senate, with formal presentation on Tuesday 18 August.

Eleven changes to Chile’s constitution, aimed at organised crime and terrorism. It enters through the Senate, with formal presentation on Tuesday 18 August. The rejection Guillermo Ramírez, who leads the UDI, said that as things stand his party cannot back the reform because it damages the country’s institutions — and he said it before the final text had even arrived.

Guillermo Ramírez, who leads the UDI, said that as things stand his party cannot back the reform because it damages the country’s institutions — and he said it before the final text had even arrived. Kast’s answer The president did not argue the merits. He called it premature to declare the reform short of votes when the text has not been formally presented.

The president did not argue the merits. He called it premature to declare the reform short of votes when the text has not been formally presented. RN’s position Andrea Balladares, the senator who in March became the first woman to lead Renovación Nacional, backs the security agenda but not the route — she says the constitution should not become a catalogue of measures.

Andrea Balladares, the senator who in March became the first woman to lead Renovación Nacional, backs the security agenda but not the route — she says the constitution should not become a catalogue of measures. The opposition Raúl Soto, a PPD deputy who also runs the party, calls the draft a Trojan horse and says it carries the seed of an illiberal government.

Raúl Soto, a PPD deputy who also runs the party, calls the draft a Trojan horse and says it carries the seed of an illiberal government. The maths It needs four-sevenths of both chambers — 89 of 155 deputies and 29 of 50 senators. That is a high bar without the UDI.

Chile’s president wants eleven changes to the constitution to fight organised crime — and the first party to say no was one of his own.

If you follow Chilean politics for a living, this is the week the government’s security plan stopped being a question about the opposition. President José Antonio Kast, sworn in on 11 March 2026 for a four-year term, is trying to put eleven changes into the constitution — and the first firm rejection came from the UDI, a party on his own side of the aisle.

Carabineros on duty in Santiago. The reform would write public security into the constitution as a duty of the state. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the reform actually does

The package is called ACOT, the Agenda Against Organised Crime and Terrorism. It is one constitutional reform plus roughly thirty separate bills, and the government has asked for fast-track handling.

The constitutional piece makes eleven changes. It writes public security into the constitution as a duty of the state, creates an official list of criminal organisations, and sets up separate prison regimes for people convicted of organised crime.

The most contested part is a new state of exception. It would be triggered by a serious disturbance of public security, run for thirty days, and be renewable.

None of this is law. The text enters through the Senate and is formally presented on Tuesday 18 August, which is exactly why the timing of the row matters.

The UDI said no before reading it

Guillermo Ramírez, the UDI’s president, put it plainly: as things currently stand, the party cannot support the constitutional security reforms, because in his view they damage the country’s institutions.

He said that before the final text reached Congress. That sequence — a rejection ahead of the document — is the part that irritated the government.

Kast did not defend the substance in response. He said it was premature to declare that the reform lacks the votes when it has not yet been formally presented.

Senator Iván Moreira, also of the UDI, made the same narrow point from inside the party. His argument was simply that the definitive text of the reform is not yet known.

RN backs the goal and questions the method

Renovación Nacional, the other large party on the government’s side, did not follow the UDI into outright rejection. Its president is Andrea Balladares, a senator who was elected on 28 March 2026 and is the first woman to lead the party.

She said RN strongly backs the government’s security agenda. That is support, not a break.

Her objection is to the vehicle. The constitution, she argued, cannot be turned into a catalogue of measures, or rewritten every time the country runs into a problem.

Her summary of the disagreement is the cleanest line anyone has offered: on security, what is needed is effectiveness, not maximalism.

The opposition goes harder

Raúl Soto is a deputy for the PPD and the party’s president, and he sits with the opposition. He went well past procedural complaints.

He said the draft carries the seed of an illiberal, autocratic or authoritarian government. He also described it as a possible Trojan horse inside the ACOT package.

That language tells you what the fight will be about once the text is public. Not whether Chile should confront organised crime, but how much permanent power the state should take to do it.

What happens from Tuesday

The government has asked for fast-track treatment of the whole ACOT package, which is one constitutional reform plus around thirty ordinary bills. The ordinary bills need simple majorities. The constitutional one does not.

The government can push the thirty bills while the constitution fight continues. It can claim security progress without winning the argument.

The UDI’s stance is not a final vote. Ramírez said it is the party’s position for now, so it can change once the text is public.

Watch one narrow thing: will the government trade away the new state of exception to save the rest? Or keep it and risk the whole reform?

Why this matters if you live in or invest in Latin America

Chile is the benchmark for investors in the region who want predictable rules. That is the real asset at risk, not any single crime number.

The math is harsh. A four-sevenths majority means 89 of 155 deputies and 29 of 50 senators, and the government cannot reach that if a coalition party is openly against it.

So the likely results are a narrower, negotiated reform or a standstill. Either way, the signal is that constitutional change still needs broad approval, which is the reassuring part of a messy week.

Watch the Senate from Tuesday. The key question is not if the UDI is angry, but if the state-of-exception clause survives in a chamber the government does not control.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Chile’s security reform passed? No. It is a constitutional reform that enters through the Senate, with formal presentation on Tuesday 18 August 2026. It has not been debated or voted. Why is Kast’s own coalition resisting? The UDI’s president, Guillermo Ramírez, says that as things stand the reforms damage Chile’s institutions. RN’s president, Andrea Balladares, supports the security agenda but objects to changing the constitution to deliver it. What did Kast actually say? He called it premature to say the reform does not have the votes, on the grounds that the final text had not yet been formally presented. He did not argue the substance. What majority does it need? Four-sevenths of both chambers — 89 of 155 deputies and 29 of 50 senators. That is why losing the UDI matters so much.

World.title: Fernández Tours Flooded Limón as Pressure Builds for an Emergency Declaration
World.content:
President Laura Fernández spent this morning touring flood-damaged communities in Limón province, as pressure built on her government to issue a formal emergency declaration for the Caribbean coast. Casa Presidencial released the itinerary last night and circulated an updated version at this morning

The schedule ran from a shelter visit in Valle La Estrella through damaged areas in Limón, Matina and Guácimo, closing at a shelter in Guácimo in the late afternoon, and included a meeting with agency heads and the mayor of Limón. Its been reported the tour was to begin at 8:45 a.m., while the agenda circulated Monday morning listed the first stop at 9:20 a.m.

The call for a declaration came yestarday afternoon from Mangell Mc Lean, a legislator with the opposition Partido Liberación Nacional who represents Limón. He said he had travelled through the province and described it as facing “a critical situation, with destroyed roads and isolated communities,” adding that he had contacted local authorities before formally asking the president to consider a declaration for the Costa Rican Caribbean.

Article 29 of the National Emergency and Risk Prevention Law, allows the executive branch to declare a state of emergency anywhere in the country by decree. This effect is financial since a declaration lifts the ordinary budget constraints imposed by Article 180 of the Constitution, which lets the government move money quickly and contract reconstruction work under an exception regime instead of standard public procurement timelines.

Once a decree is signed, the Comisión Nacional de Emergencias must produce a General Emergency Plan setting out the causes of the disaster, an estimate of damage and losses, and the works required to address it. Public institutions then have 30 days to submit documented damage reports, with a further 30 days available, and the commission verifies that the damage was actually caused by the event before any project enters the plan. The money runs through the National Emergency Fund.

The same stretch of coast has been through the process before. In 2021, an executive decree placed Limón, Matina, Pococí, Guácimo, Siquirres and Talamanca under a state of emergency, alongside Turrialba, Jiménez, Sarapiquí and five cantons in Alajuela, after a Caribbean storm system.

The damage that prompted Mc Lean’s request accumulated across the weekend as tropical wave No. 32 crossed. The Comisión Nacional de Emergencias reported 495 people in shelters nationwide as of its 5 p.m. Sunday count, distributed across 11 sites. Its earlier count, taken at 4:25 p.m. Sunday, logged 154 people sheltered in the Caribbean, with 11 at the Matina community hall, 67 at Escuela La Plástica in Valle La Estrella and 76 at Escuela Pandora Oeste. La Nación, also citing the commission, reported 134 people sheltered in Limón province.

The Costa Rican Red Cross evacuated 65 people across the Limón area, with 16 in Matina, 15 in Cariari de Pococí, 14 in Río Jiménez de Guácimo, 16 in Talamanca and four in Valle La Estrella. More than 100 others were evacuated in Sarapiquí. The Cuerpo de Bomberos reported responding to more than 33 flood incidents and rescuing roughly 150 people.

Rising flow on the Río Sixaola has left the communities of Gandoca and Sixaola without road access. In Turrialba, mayor Carlos Hidalgo Flores reported seven homes as total losses, among them a house destroyed by a falling tree in Verbena Norte, in the Santa Rosa district. The Ministerio de Educación Pública cancelled Monday classes across the Limón and Sulá regional directorates.

The commission, headed by Alejandro Picado, is holding an orange alert over the Northern Zone, the entire Caribbean slope and the canton of Turrialba, with a yellow alert across the Central Valley, Central Pacific and South Pacific. Only the North Pacific sits outside the alert system altogether.

The flooding is the first large natural disaster to test the Fernández administration, which took office on May 8 and holds 31 of the 57 seats in the Legislative Assembly. Whether it signs a declaration will determine how quickly damaged roads, bridges and drainage systems along the Caribbean are rebuilt, and how much of that work is paid for outside ordinary budget channels.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Corcovado Faces Ranger Shortage and Environmental Crime
World.content:
Concerns are growing over Costa Rica’s ability to protect Corcovado National Park as park rangers contend with illegal gold mining, poaching, logging, illegal fishing and incursions into protected land while working with limited personnel and resources. The latest warning comes from environmental advocates who say environmental crimes are increasing inside and around the park on the Osa Peninsula.

Bernardo Aguilar, president of the Civic Environmental Parliament, has called for more personnel dedicated to surveillance, protection and maintenance. The staffing numbers show the challenge. SINAC data released this summer indicated that Corcovado had 48 park rangers as of June 17.

But Enrique Obando, a ranger working in Corcovado, said only about 15 were assigned primarily to control and protection duties, while the others were needed for tourism and other park operations. He estimated that each protection ranger is effectively responsible for roughly 3,000 hectares of difficult tropical forest terrain.

Corcovado protects 42,570 hectares of land and another 5,375 hectares of marine territory. Its forests, beaches, wetlands and coastal waters provide habitat for some of Costa Rica’s best-known wildlife, including jaguars, tapirs, pumas and peccaries. The dangers facing those charged with protecting the park became particularly clear earlier this year.

Four men were detained in January after rangers discovered an alleged illegal gold-mining operation along the Sirena River. Investigators said the group had equipment including GPS devices, water pumps and a generator. One suspect escaped, while several of those detained allegedly threatened park rangers during the operation. The case is under investigation by environmental prosecutors.

Rangers have also encountered increasingly organized mining operations in remote parts of Corcovado. During another operation in March, eight rangers walked approximately 10 kilometers from the Los Patos station to reach an illegal mining camp. Three men were detained and mining equipment was seized. Rangers involved in the operation described working with limited communications and relying partly on outside conservation groups for food, equipment and other logistical support.

Illegal gold mining has long been a problem on the Osa Peninsula, but recent investigations have raised concerns that some operations are becoming better financed and equipped. Rangers have reported finding miners with metal detectors and satellite phones, making enforcement in Corcovado’s remote interior increasingly difficult. The staffing pressure extends beyond Corcovado.

A University of Costa Rica report published in June found that SINAC had 137 employees throughout the entire Osa Conservation Area, which includes Corcovado, Piedras Blancas and Marino Ballena national parks along with several other protected areas. The same report cited the 2025 State of the Nation report showing that SINAC’s overall budget had fallen by about 40% after several consecutive years of reductions.

The problem is not limited to land. Illegal fishing and removal of marine resources have also been identified as threats in areas associated with Corcovado, adding a large stretch of coastline and ocean to the territory authorities must monitor. For Costa Rica, the stakes extend beyond conservation.

Corcovado is one of our most important nature-tourism destinations and a centerpiece of tourism on the Osa Peninsula. Thousands of travelers visit the region each year specifically for its rainforest and wildlife, making effective protection of the park important both environmentally and economically.

Costa Rica has long promoted its national parks and protected areas as central to its international reputation. In Corcovado, however, rangers are being asked to protect a vast and difficult landscape while simultaneously managing visitors, responding to environmental crimes and confronting operations that can be increasingly organized and dangerous.

The latest warnings are renewing a familiar question: whether the resources assigned to protect one of Costa Rica’s most valuable wild areas are keeping pace with the threats inside it.

World.title: Family Demands Answers on Missing Political Prisoners in Nicaragua
World.content:
Relatives of a retired military officer and his wife, who were detained a year ago in Nicaragua, demanded Saturday that the government of Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo provide information about their whereabouts and health amid fears they could die in prison. Retired Colonel Carlos Brenes, 71, and his wife, Salvadora Martínez, 68, were detained last August, during police raids in the cities of Carazo and Masaya, in which several other people were also arrested, Thelma Brenes, the retired officer’s daughter, said.

“They have a duty to tell us where they are, how they are doing and to return them to us alive,” Brenes said from exile. Human rights organizations and relatives of detainees who maintain a search mechanism say that as of the end of July, there were 60 political prisoners in Nicaragua, 23 of whom were considered victims of enforced disappearance.

They warn that 15 are older adults, including Brenes and Martínez. Brenes’ daughter said the family fears a repeat of the case of leader Brooklyn Rivera, who died in May while in state custody after nearly three years without any information about his whereabouts.

She said her father, who was imprisoned between 2018 and 2019 and released under an amnesty, suffers from diabetes, high blood pressure and mobility problems. She also said Nicaragua’s prison system does not provide political prisoners with the medical care they need.

She also denounced what she described as a pattern of “detention by association” in Nicaragua, in which relatives of government opponents are also arrested, as she said happened with Martínez, her stepmother. Ortega and his wife Murillo, who holds the title of co-president, tightened their control over Nicaraguan society following the 2018 protests, whose repression left more than 300 people dead, according to the United Nations.

Opposition figures say Murillo is carrying out an internal purge across state institutions in preparation for the possible death of Ortega, who suffers from lupus and kidney failure. The government’s offensive against its opponents has also included a constitutional reform aimed at excluding opposition parties from elections. It is scheduled to be put to a vote in early September.

World.title: General Cañas Highway Lane Closures Begin Monday in Costa Rica
World.content:
Drivers using the General Cañas Highway between Alajuela and San José should prepare for additional congestion beginning Monday as crews carry out eight days of work along one of Costa Rica’s busiest roads. Partial closures will affect the inside lane in the Alajuela-to-San José direction from August 17 through August 24. The restrictions will be in place each day between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m.

The work could be particularly important for travelers arriving at Juan Santamaría International Airport and continuing toward San José, since the airport connects directly with the General Cañas corridor. Drivers heading from San José toward the airport will be traveling in the opposite direction from the scheduled lane closure, although congestion along the highway can affect traffic more broadly.

The National Power and Light Company(CNFL), will use the closures to put in 90 patriotic light displays ahead of Costa Rica’s Independence Day celebrations on September 15. The decorations will include representations of the Torch of Freedom and people dressed in traditional clothing using Costa Rica’s red, white and blue national colors.

Two crews, two cranes and 10 CNFL technicians will work along the highway. Safety cones will be placed around the work areas to alert approaching motorists. CNFL will also take advantage of the road work to carry out preventive maintenance, including inspections of wiring, photocells and control panels connected to the lighting system.

The work has been coordinated with the Ministry of Public Works and Transportation. Eric Esquivel, CNFL’s director of Distribution, urged motorists to reduce their speed and use additional caution while workers and cranes are positioned along the highway. The timing avoids the heaviest part of the morning rush hour, but the General Cañas routinely experiences significant congestion, and reducing available road space between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m. could create delays.
