Anyone arriving at the San Jose airport during the affected hours should allow additional time for ground transportation to San José and surrounding communities. Residents traveling from Alajuela toward the capital may also want to consider alternate routes when possible.

The closures begin tomorrow August 17 and are scheduled to continue through August 24.

World.title: Costa Rica Heavy Rains Cause Flooding and Travel Disruptions
World.content:
Heavy rains from Tropical Wave No. 32 left flooding, overflowing rivers, landslides and road problems across several parts of Costa Rica, while forecasters warned that unstable conditions would continue Sunday. The Caribbean and Northern Zone are expected to receive the heaviest rainfall, with moderate to strong showers possible through the morning. Rain and thunderstorms are also forecast for parts of the Pacific and Central Valley later in the day.

The weekend weather has already caused problems in Cartago, Limón and Alajuela. Turrialba was among the hardest-hit areas Saturday after heavy rainfall caused the Turrialba River to rise sharply. One house fell into the river, while other homes were affected and residents in the immediate area were warned not to return because of unstable conditions.

A landslide was also reported in San Rafael de Santa Cruz de Turrialba, affecting elderly residents. Authorities closed the Las Monjas bridge in central Turrialba as a precaution after the river current apparently damaged part of its foundation. Elsewhere in Cartago province, a landslide blocked National Route 10 in the Quebrada Honda area near Juan Viñas, while flooding affected roads in Santa Teresita de Turrialba and Río Bajo de Abarca in Alvarado.

Those heading through mountainous parts of Cartago should check road conditions before leaving, particularly on routes toward Turrialba and Irazú Volcano.Along Route 219 toward Irazú Volcano National Park, rain caused additional road damage and difficult driving conditions.

The weather also caused trouble on Route 32, the main highway between San José and Limón. A landslide closed the highway for approximately four hours Saturday before crews removed debris and reopened the road. In Matina, Limón province, flooding was reported in the Davao area. An emergency shelter was prepared in the nearby community of Larga Distancia as a precaution, although no residents had been moved there at the time of the latest report.

Farther north, overflowing rivers affected San Juan and Pataste in Guatuso, Alajuela. Police officers were sent through affected communities to determine whether families needed assistance. The risk has not ended with the passage of the tropical wave. Costa Rica remains under the influence of the Intertropical Convergence Zone, while strong trade winds continue to bring moisture from the Caribbean. Those conditions are expected to keep the atmosphere unstable Sunday.

The Caribbean and Northern Zone face the greatest risk this morning, with recurring moderate to heavy rainfall possible. The Pacific Central and South are expected to see scattered afternoon downpours and thunderstorms, while the Central Valley could experience periods of rain and isolated showers.

Strong winds are yet another concern. Gusts could reach 40 to 60 km/h (25 to 37 mph) in lower areas and 70 to 90 km/h (43 to 56 mph) in mountainous locations. The combination of additional rainfall and already saturated ground increases the possibility of new landslides, flash flooding and rising rivers. Soil saturation in mountainous Caribbean watersheds is estimated at between 70% and 100%, while areas around the Golfo Dulce in southern Costa Rica are above 90%.

The Northern Zone and Caribbean remain under a yellow weather alert, while the Central Valley and the Central and South Pacific are under a lower-level green alert. Residents and visitors traveling Sunday are advised to use additional caution around rivers, steep slopes and roads with a history of landslides. Conditions can change quickly during heavy rain, particularly on mountain highways.

Anyone driving today should also confirm road conditions before heading toward Limón, Turrialba or other areas affected by yesterday’s storms.

World.title: Minister of Education Attends 2026 Taiwan Scholarship Orientation
World.content:
Minister of Education Attends 2026 Taiwan Scholarship Orientation

By Zoila Palma: Today, Hon. Francis Fonseca, Minister of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, attended the 2026 Taiwan Scholarship Orientation along with H.E. Dame Froyla Tzalam, Governor-General of Belize, and H.E. Amino Chi, Ambassador of the Republic of China (Taiwan).

Minister Fonseca encouraged the scholarship recipients to capitalize on this valuable opportunity and serve as Belize’s ambassadors in Taiwan.

Fonseca also emphasized the importance of recipients returning home to Belize and putting into action what they learn through this opportunity.

Fonseca expressed appreciation to the Government and people of Taiwan for their “continued generosity and commitment to Belize’s development,” particularly through investments in education and opportunities for Belizean students.

World.title: Maclovio Ack emerges as PUP’s Punta Gorda mayoral candidate
World.content:
Maclovio Ack emerges as PUP’s Punta Gorda mayoral candidate

By Zoila Palma: On August 16, 2026, the People’s United Party (PUP) held its municipal convention in Punta Gorda Town (PG) to select its mayoral candidate and six councilor candidates for the 2027 Municipal Elections. The convention took place at the Toledo Community College from 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

According to the PUP, 1,233 ballots were cast, with the party describing the turnout as the “largest municipal convention recorded in the history of PG.”

Following the close of polls and the counting of ballots, Maclovio Ack emerged victorious as the PUP’s mayoral candidate for the 2027 Municipal Elections in Punta Gorda Town.

The PUP also congratulated the six successful councilor candidates, namely Gloria Avila, Anthony Fuentes, Kerlin Moreira, Olivia Sho, Indira Coleman and Roberto Virez. Avila topped the polls among the councilor candidates.

The party also extended appreciation to the mayoral and councilor candidates who were unsuccessful at the PG convention, commending them for their participation and contribution to the party’s democratic process.

World.title: Hell Hath No Fury: Barefooted woman in black ransacks nail tech’s house; Stabs up couch, mattress, cuts up clothes and empties acetone, nail polish, BBQ sauce, soda over everything
World.content:
Hell Hath No Fury: Barefooted woman in black ransacks nail tech’s house; Stabs up couch, mattress, cuts up clothes and empties acetone, nail polish, BBQ sauce, soda over everything

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 45-year-old Belize City woman has been charged with burglary and aggravated assault following a bizarre incident in which a nail technician reported that her home and business equipment were extensively damaged, with furniture allegedly stabbed repeatedly and several items covered in sauces, cosmetics and other liquids.

Police say the 23-year-old homeowner reported that at around 7:49 p.m. on Friday, August 14, she was at a mechanic shop when she received a telephone call from a friend informing her that a woman dressed entirely in black and barefooted had been seen inside her home.

The woman immediately sought police assistance and returned to the residence with officers, where she allegedly discovered extensive damage.

According to the police report, two small sofas and a mattress had been stabbed approximately 25 times and smeared or soaked with substances including barbecue sauce, hair jam, nail polish, acetone, soap water, coconut oil and red Fanta.

Ten pillows had reportedly been ripped open, while a table used by the woman for her nail business was damaged with acetone and powder. Nail polish, nail buffers and cosmetic powders were also allegedly destroyed.

The woman additionally reported that a number of her clothing valued at approximately $2,500 had been cut and soaked with acetone, while several bottles of vitamins and tonic had been emptied.

A bottle of Chanel perfume valued at $290, a Samsung S7 cellphone and Social Security and bank cards were also reported missing. The woman estimated the total value of the damaged and missing property at approximately $6,007.

Police subsequently detained 45-year-old housekeeper Roumayne Veleen Andrews. On Sunday, August 16, Andrews was formally arrested and charged with burglary and aggravated assault.

World.title: Gunman bursts shot in the air after robbing Bella Vista store of $800, escapes on waiting motorcycle
World.content:
Gunman bursts shot in the air after robbing Bella Vista store of $800, escapes on waiting motorcycle

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an armed robbery at Jazlin Store in the Farm 4 area of Bella Vista Village, where a gunman reportedly stole $800 before firing a shot and escaping on a waiting motorcycle.

The robbery occurred at around 7:50 p.m. on Sunday, August 16.

According to police, a cashier reported that a man wearing a red shirt, a mask and a black motorcycle helmet entered the establishment armed with a handgun.

The robber allegedly demanded money and took approximately $800 in Belize currency from the cash register.

Police say that as the gunman was leaving the store, he fired a single shot into the floor before escaping on a motorcycle being operated by another person waiting outside.

Officers canvassed the scene and obtained surveillance footage from the store owner as part of the investigation. No arrests have been reported.

World.title: Belize, Guatemala and Mexico mark first Anniversary of Calakmul Declaration
World.content:
Belize, Guatemala and Mexico mark first Anniversary of Calakmul Declaration

By Zoila Palma: Belize, Guatemala and Mexico have marked the first anniversary of the Calakmul Declaration, a regional commitment to safeguard the Great Selva Maya and strengthen cooperation on biodiversity and conservation.

The milestone was commemorated at the Caracol Archaeological Reserve, where the Institute of Archaeology joined wildlife and natural resource conservation organizations.

The European Union in Belize also joined regional partners to recognize the anniversary, with EU Ambassador Dr. Erja Askola and EU Ambassador to Guatemala Johanna Karanko participating alongside government representatives, civil society organizations and other stakeholders.

The EU described the declaration as an important milestone for biodiversity protection and conservation efforts across the region.

The Selva Maya is considered one of the most critical ecosystems in the Americas, covering approximately 5.7 million hectares of forest across Belize, Guatemala and Mexico.

Regional cooperation is considered essential to protecting the forest while promoting sustainable development and supporting communities and local economies in the three countries.

The European Union said it has provided significant financial support through various programmes aimed at preserving and protecting the Selva Maya.

World.title: Armed men tie up Northern Fisherman security guard during early-morning burglary
World.content:
Armed men tie up Northern Fisherman security guard during early-morning burglary

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating an aggravated burglary at the Northern Fisherman Cooperative in Belize City where a security guard was allegedly held at gunpoint and tied up by a group of masked men early Saturday morning.

According to police, a security guard reported that at around 2:00 a.m. on August 15, he was performing security duties at Northern Fisheries when approximately four masked men, each reportedly armed with a firearm, approached him.

The gunmen allegedly pointed their weapons at him and ordered him not to move before tying him up and placing him on the ground.

The guard told investigators that about 20 minutes later, he heard the intruders say they had found a chest inside one of the offices. He then reportedly heard what sounded like a metal object being dragged from the building before hearing a vehicle speed away.

Police visited and processed the scene and observed surveillance cameras mounted around the building. Investigators are reportedly still working to determine exactly what was stolen.

No arrests have been reported and the investigation continues.

World.title: Canadian man who ran from police for drinking in public busted with 6.78 grams of cocaine; charged with drug trafficking
World.content:
Canadian man who ran from police for drinking in public busted with 6.78 grams of cocaine; charged with drug trafficking

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Canadian businessman living in Placencia has been charged with two counts of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply after police allegedly found a total of 6.78 grams of suspected cocaine in his possession on Sunday evening.

Police say that at about 6:45 p.m. on August 16, officers were conducting mobile patrol on the Placencia Main Road when their attention was drawn to 52-year-old Grant Arthur Stowell, who was allegedly drinking from a Belikin beer bottle in public.

According to police, when officers approached and asked Stowell to desist from public drinking, he became agitated and eventually ran into a nearby store. An officer pursued him and allegedly saw Stowell remove an item from his pocket and place it on a store shelf.

Police retrieved a piece of tissue paper which allegedly contained a small transparent plastic bag with a white powdery substance suspected to be cocaine. The substance was later weighed at 5.60 grams.

Police say a subsequent search of Stowell’s wallet led to the discovery of another small plastic bag containing suspected cocaine weighing 1.18 grams.

Stowell, described by police as a Canadian business owner residing in Placencia, was formally arrested and charged with two counts of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply. He reportedly exercised his right to remain silent after being cautioned.

World.title: Belize advances Regional Environmental action with new strategies and partnerships
World.content:
Belize advances Regional Environmental action with new strategies and partnerships

By Zoila Palma: Belize has marked several important milestones in regional environmental action with the launch of major initiatives aimed at protecting natural resources, strengthening climate resilience and promoting sustainable development.

The initiatives were launched by the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management in collaboration with the Central American Commission on Environment and Development (CCAD) during Belize’s Pro Tempore Presidency.

Among the key developments is the updated CCAD Regional Environmental Framework Strategy (ERAM) 2026–2035, which will serve as a shared environmental strategy for the SICA region.

The framework seeks to promote an environmentally sustainable, resilient and inclusive future through action on environmental quality, seas and biodiversity, integrated water-resource management, forests and sustainable landscapes, and climate change.

Belize also joined the launch of the new “Great Forests of Central America and the Dominican Republic” brand, known as Green Heritage or “Patrimonio Verde.”

The communication strategy aims to strengthen regional storytelling by highlighting measurable results, environmental impacts, data-driven decision-making and the network of partners working across Central America and the Dominican Republic.

Another major initiative is the regional CAM Project, implemented in partnership with the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), which will invest US$20 million to improve watershed management and protect marine ecosystems.

Belize’s Belize River, New River and Rio Hondo watersheds have been identified as priority areas.

Chief Environmental Officer Anthony Mai said the project will strengthen governance, promote integrated watershed and coastal-zone management, support nature-based solutions and sustainable financing, and build regional technical capacity.

Belize also formalized a new Memorandum of Understanding with The Nature Conservancy to strengthen cooperation on freshwater conservation and aquatic ecosystem management.

The partnership will support ecosystem restoration, monitoring and data systems, freshwater biodiversity conservation, climate adaptation, public awareness and transboundary water cooperation.

The initiatives were supported by Minister Orlando Habet, CEO Milagro Matus and technical leaders from the Ministry and regional partners, as Belize continues efforts toward a more resilient and sustainable future.

World.title: Defend truth, liberty
World.content:
Reverend Astor Carlyle (right) shakes hands with Governor General Sir Patrick Allen as Lady Allen (second right) and Chief of Defence Staff Vice Admiral Antonette Wemyss Gorman (left) look on at the end of Sunday’s church service commemorating 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension, Up Park Camp in St Andrew. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Jamaicans have been urged to summon the courage of a previous generation and stand firm in defence of truth and liberty just as men and women from this region answered the call to serve when World War II plunged the world into geopolitical turmoil and economic uncertainty.



Reverend Captain Astor Carlyle made the appeal on Sunday in his sermon during the service celebrating the 80th anniversary of the Royal Air Forces Association (RAFA) Jamaica 580 Branch at Garrison Church of the Ascension inside the Jamaica Defence Force’s Up Park Camp headquarters in St Andrew.

According to RAFA, the service, held under the theme ‘80 years of service, sacrifice, and unity’, marks the commencement of a year of celebrations to mark its founding.

Referencing the first lesson — Isaiah 6:1-8, which tells of the prophet Isaiah seeing a vision of God, realising he is sinful, gets cleansed by a burning coal, and volunteers to serve God by saying, ‘Here am I. Send me!’ — Rev Carlyle said that in the time of Isaiah, Judah needed someone to shoulder the responsibility of being God’s representative during great confusion.

“Throughout the Bible, God asks questions, but there is one question from the lips of God that is very relevant for a day like this when we celebrate 80 years of the Royal Air Forces Association; it is a question that we heard in the first scripture reading today: Whom shall I send? Who will go for us? And this was a question asked of the prophet Isaiah in a time that needed a Godly voice and a Godly presence to bring calm and consciousness to a nation in crisis,” Carlyle told the congregation of mostly ex-servicemen and women.

“This was a time of chaos, a time of complexity, a time of corruption, and when the young Isaiah stood in the presence of God and considered the grave need, he responded with five words, ‘Here am I, send me.’ Isaiah saw what was at stake, and without concern for himself, he answered in the affirmative,” Carlyle said.

“This is a picture of the kind of spirit with which our Caribbean service members engaged the desperate call from the allied forces in 1939. It was a time of geopolitical and economic instability. Dictators were emerging in Europe and Asia, threatening the fragile peace that the Treaty of Versailles sought to ensure. The Great Depression and the subsequent invasion of Poland required the allied forces to sound the rallying call, and with a spirit of duty and a sense of mission our Caribbean servicemen said ‘Here am I, send me.’ Some trained as pilots, some trained as navigators, some were ground crew under the British Commonwealth air training plan.

“They served in Europe, they served in North Africa, they served in the Mediterranean, they served in Asia. Many Jamaicans served with the Royal Air Force bomber command and fighter command, defending Britain during air raids and helping push back the Axis forces. These young men of the Caribbean faced grave danger, but not for fame or reward, they believed in freedom that was worth defending and they paid the ultimate sacrifice. That is why we celebrate their gallantry today,” Carlyle said.

He stated that the service Jamaicans gave during the war stands as a reminder that the call to duty is for the willing, and encouraged citizens to demonstrate a willingness to serve, just as the war veterans did.

“Isaiah displayed that spirit when God asked ‘Whom shall I send?’ He didn’t give excuses, he didn’t say I am not qualified enough or I have too many responsibilities, or I am too young or I am too old. He simply said, ‘Here I am, send me.’ That is the heart of a willing servant. God expects the same of you and me, He’s asking us that same question today. As our world shows signs of economic shocks and geopolitical uncertainty God is asking who is willing, who will stand for truth, who will serve?” Carlyle told the congregation.

Earlier, in her welcome, RAFA President Major (Retired) Johanna Lewin shared that the founding members of the organisation, formed on August 16, 1946, were a band of merry men who served in the Royal Air Force during World Ward II and did so with a deep sense of pride.

RAFA, she said, initially was for those who served in the war and returned home to Jamaica “to continue their camaraderie and visit the proverbial river — the bar”.

“They wanted to ensure that all was not forgotten and that the comradeship and shared sense of duty that they developed during the war years were persevered. How many of you are familiar with Colonel Reggie Chin, who was commanding officer of the Third Battalion for many years and who served with RAF during the war? How many of you are familiar with Michael Manley, former [Jamaica] prime minister, who served with the Royal Canadian Air Force during World War II? We could be here all day. It’s a long story and cannot be given justice here,” Lewin said.

She shared that RAFA started under a hut at one end of the airfield at the JDF Air Wing in Up Park Camp.

“We were offered three prime camp locations, but the one selected was what we know as Curphey Place in Swallowfield, the home of RAFA and the Jamaica Legion. The land was eventually given in perpetuity for the benefit of veterans. RAFA evolved and became more than just a means for these sassy World War II veterans to visit the ever-present river and chat and reminisce and sing about their experiences in Britain,” Lewin said.

“One of the early and major philanthropic works took place when the British charity… established Cheshire Homes, what we would term a hospice. RAFA was the first local entity to pledge $10,000, a tidy sum in those days, to build one of the units. Cheshire Homes is what we now know as the Mona Rehab. We were able to fund the original columbarium in Briggs Park and now the extension. RAFA has continued its tradition of raising funds and giving,” Lewin said.

World.title: First hurdle cleared
World.content:
KOZYCKI... campaign focused on fighting corruption, working to rebuild trust in Government; tackling affordability, lowering the costs for working families; and expanding access to affordable and quality health care

NEW YORK, USA — The Georgia-based attorney who says he was inspired to run for a seat in the United States Congress to help deportees like Jamaican Godfrey Wade has cleared the first hurdle, winning the Democratic Party’s primary in the state’s 7th Congressional District.

Tony Kozycki, an immigration lawyer, said he was disgusted by the system when he represented Jamaican-born US veteran Godfrey Wade and discovered how difficult it was to get him his day in court for a repaid bounced cheque and an unproven assault charge 12 years ago.

Wade, who lived legally in the US for 50 years, served overseas in the military and was honourably discharged. After being flagged for the offences he was deported to Jamaica earlier this year. Kozycki has since been fighting the case, with little success. He never became a US citizen.

Asked for an update on the case, the attorney told the Jamaica Observer, which carried the deportation story, that there had not been any major new legal developments or petitions filed on Wade’s behalf.

“However, we have not given up, as I still believe Godfrey deserves the opportunity to return to the United States and have his case heard fairly. We continue to advocate for him and remain committed to seeing him receive the process he deserves,” said Kozycki.

“Wade’s case did more than expose a broken immigration system, it exposed a failure of representation by Rich McCormick,” Kozycki added.

McCormick is the Republican attorney, an incumbent whom Kozycki will face in the midterm elections for the Georgia 7th Congressional District, after snagging the Democratic Party nomination by polling 19,742 or 40 per cent of the votes against nearest rival Case Norton’s 11,036 or 22.3 per cent.

The other two contestants polled a combined 36,000 votes in the May 2026 primary. Kozycki returned to defeat filmmaker Norton in the run-off, after garnering 11,667 to Norton’s 5,561 votes.

Kozycki accused McCormick of failing to provide adequate representation for Wade.

Both he and Wade have consistently maintained that notices for the Jamaican to attend a hearing were never received, due to problems with an address used by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), which they say courts records show.

Moreover, restitution of the bounced cheque and all applicable fees were made in full, according to Wade’s family. His attorney noted that no physical violence was ever alleged in the assault charge.

“All we are asking is for the case to be reopened and Mr Wade to have his day in court. There is no need to trust me or Godfrey, just look at the documents and the evidence. All we want is one day before a judge and I know we will win this case,” Kozycki told the Observer during an interview in March this year.

As for his campaign priorities, Kozycki said they centre on three issues: “Fighting corruption and working to rebuild trust in Government, tackling affordability and lowering the costs for working families, and expanding access to affordable and quality health care.”

There are significant Jamaican and other Caribbean communities in the metro Atlanta area which forms part of Georgia’s 7th Congressional District, something which has not been lost on Kozykic and his campaign.

Noting that Wade’s deportation has left many in the Jamaican community here disappointed over how he was treated, the attorney said: “I certainly welcome the support of the Jamaican-Americans in the district and all who believe in our campaign’s message of public service and bringing people together.”

As the nominations for candidates in the November midterm elections wind down, in the meantime, Jamaicans in Broward County, South Florida, are keeping a close watch on the contest in the state’s 20th Congressional District where one of their own, Dale Holness, is making a third bid for Congress, against four other candidates.

The 20th Congressional District is predominantly black and heavily favours the Democratic party. Were Holness to win the primary, due this Tuesday, August 18, and the November 2026 General Election, he would become the first Jamaican-born politician to enter the United States Congress.

Another Florida candidate, Republican Byron Donalds, who is running to be the state’s next governor, could add to the number of elected officials in the US with a Jamaican connection. Donalds’ mother was born in Jamaica, as was the mother of Maryland Governor Wes Moore, who is seeking a second term in the post.

Congresswoman Yvette D Clarke, who represents New York’s 9th Congressional District and leads the Congressional Black Caucus, is the highest-ranking representative with a Jamaican connection in Congress, as her parents are Jamaican-born.

World.title: Observer story forces KSAMC response
World.content:
A drone shot shows the location of the proposed development on Broadway Close in Kingston 8. The grassy area to the left is where the multi-family development is expected to be erected.

Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) City Engineer Xavier Chevannes has sought to allay concerns among Manor Park residents who accuse the local authority of evading questions about a proposed multi-family development at 2 Broadway Close, Kingston 8, to which they object.

Chevannes was responding to a Jamaica Observer report on the dispute last Friday highlighting the residents’ objection to any plans for a multi-family development in the area and their complaint that they have tried, without success, to get information from the city managers on the development.

Repeated attempts by the Observer, before publication, to get a comment from the KSAMC had also been unsuccessful.

In a letter, which they shared with the Observer, the residents claim that people who live on Broadway Close, Broadway Road, Harrow Drive, and Waterworks Road are worried about the proposed development.

“The developers posted a notice of intention to build at 2 Broadway Close on July 6, 2026. Within 48 hours the Broadway Mews Association formally requested the plans. The developer responded that the plans were in progress and would be provided once completed. Since then, there has been no further correspondence,” the residents said in the letter.

“Despite multiple requests, the community has been left in the dark. The developers were aware of the community’s interest within 48 hours of the notice going up. Yet they have chosen to ignore all subsequent requests for information,” the residents added.

They claimed that when the community submitted a formal request for plans under the Access to Information Act, they were told it could take up to 60 days to receive them.

“The Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation informed residents they had only 35 days to file an objection. This creates an impossible situation where residents are being asked to object to a developer whose plans they have not seen, may not receive before the deadline, and which the developer has refused to share,” the residents claimed in the letter.

According to the residents, unofficial sources have indicated that a five-storey building is planned for the area, but efforts to get the authorities to either confirm or deny this had failed.

But, according to Chevannes, there are no such plans.

He told the Observer last Friday that at the time of the request from residents, no application for a building permit was made by any developer in relation to 2 Broadway Close. He said that what was posted on the fence of the property was a standard notice of intention to build.

Chevannes said that the application for a permit officially reached his desk on Friday and that the necessary meetings and consultation with residents will take place at the appropriate time.

“It’s a small development, less than 15 units, which is a mixture of town houses and apartments. Without saying much, the town houses are two-storey and the apartments are three-storey. The maximum floor height that is proposed is three floors,” Chevannes said.

“Residents are concerned about this, but this is what we now have before us and we are considering whatever it is that we need to consider,” he said.

Chevannes said the KSAMC received a letter outlining the residents’ objection to the proposed multi-family development on Tuesday, August 11.

“We reached out to the applicant today, the 14th of August, indicating that we are in receipt of an application and we are in the process of setting up an objection meeting. The law requires an intent notice be placed on-site in a conspicuous position and also at the nearest police station or post office, which the applicant did. So we reached out to the applicants and the objectors and we intend to schedule that meeting as soon as possible,” the city engineer said.

“Under the Building Act, the decision that the committee makes in processing the application has to take into consideration the objection. Not to say that an objection automatically means an approval will be denied, but it must take into consideration the implications in accordance with the Building Act. We have to deal with the objections and provide any clarity an objector might require,” he explained.

He added that those objections would be shared with the KSAMC’s attorneys as well as a representative from Jamaicans For Justice — “Someone from an objective perspective, just to weigh in on the discussion with the objectors. Basically, what is obtained in an objection meeting is clarity that the applicant or the developer would have failed to provide to the residents.”

In a letter to residents, Richard Spence, the developer, urged them not to see the project as any inconvenience to the community.

“This is to clarify and hopefully dispense with rumours emanating from a recent article in the Jamaica Observer. Our proposed development is a modest two-storey mix of town houses and apartments with adequate underground parking. This information was shared with Mr Desmond Mair, president of Broadway Mews Association, as I responded to a letter from the association regarding our potential development,” Spence wrote.

He pointed to an extract from his letter to the association, dated February 11, 2026.

Spence also said he could not understand from where the rumour of a five-storey building came.

“Under the law, we may well be allowed a five-storey building, but it is, and was never our intent, and it is not what we submitted to the relevant authorities as our proposed development. Our application and submissions for approval are still in progress, and as we communicated to the president of the association, Mr Mair, on July 8, 2026, we await the response from relevant authorities to share further detail. Please be assured that having lived here for over 50 years, and intending to continue living here, we are very sensitive to our neighbours and surroundings. We hope that this puts an end to the recent misinformation being shared,” Spence wrote.

However, some residents are still sceptical of the planned development.

“To me, they put up a notice; if nobody objects, then fine. If you object, there are no plans for you to see. People feel they can’t object until they see the plan. You hear that it will take 60 days to see the plan and then the time just blows off and you can’t object again. By that time they would have put in anything they want,” one resident argued on Saturday.

“Based on our objection letter, some people in another upscale community got a hold of it and they want to do their own objection because they were in the same position where they think they had to see a plan and couldn’t get no plan either. A whole lot of people want to talk,” the resident said.

Another resident, who said most of the people who live on Broadway Close have been there for 40 years, cited possible health risks to the elderly.

“Don’t forget the construction for two or three years and the traffic. To add 25 units we are talking about 50-plus cars. This little road can’t manage that. We have concerns about even just going outside. These people are old and all that construction dust would kill them. It is not that we don’t want the developer to build, but build a house. Why you have to build town houses and apartments and all that? They are crowding up the place,” the resident argued.

World.title: Undeniably Clive Hunt
World.content:
.

At 74 years old, legendary music producer, arranger, multi-instrumentalist and artiste Clive Hunt is showing no signs of slowing down. After more than five decades helping to shape the sound of Jamaican music and working with some of the biggest names locally and internationally, the visually impaired music veteran is stepping from behind the console and into the spotlight with his new album, Undeniably Clive Hunt aka Lizzard.

Released August 14, and available across major streaming platforms, the 11-track project presents another side of the acclaimed veteran.

While Hunt is internationally recognised for his work as a producer, arranger and musician, singing is not entirely new territory for him.

He recalls recording several songs earlier in his career with some performing well in the UK and the US New York Tri-State area. Despite being encouraged over the years to record more of his own music, Hunt largely remained behind the scenes, creating for others.

“I have a lot of music unreleased and unfinished, but I did these songs in recent years,” Hunt said. “I make a lot of music in my spare time, and these were the latest collection of music I did, and I decided to put them out,” he shared.

Hunt describes the album as a roots reggae album with a twist.

He wrote or co-wrote the material on the project, with the exception of Waves of War, his interpretation of the work of influential Jamaican singer and songwriter Joe Higgs — someone whom Hunt said he emulated and who taught legends like Bob Marley, Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer.

For Hunt, however, the album is about considerably more than rhythm.

“I think these are the type of content that people need to hear and be aware of. Reggae is more than a beat, it’s the message,” he said of the drop which includes Earth Run Dry, Jamaican Party, Di Valley, Good To Be There, No Peace, Victory, Satta I, and Mango Walk.

Already attracting international attention, Hunt said renowned British reggae broadcaster David Rodigan has been playing tracks on the BBC Radio in the UK.

The album comes during another productive period in Hunt’s extraordinary career. Among his recent work include Fields of Gold: A Reggae Tribute to Sting, which received Grammy consideration for the 2026 Grammy Awards. Hunt has also been recognised with Recording Academy-sanctioned Grammy certificates for his contributions to several projects.

Born in Linstead, St Catherine, in 1952, Hunt began recording professionally in 1972. His credits stretch across generations and genres, with work involving names including Dennis Brown, Grace Jones, Chaka Khan, Alpha Blondy, The Skatalites, Maxi Priest, Etana, Jah9, Chronixx, Popcaan, Samory I, and many others.

His influence can be heard on landmark Jamaican recordings, including work associated with The Abyssinians’ Satta Massagana, Jimmy Cliff’s I Can See Clearly Now, Beres Hammond’s Putting Up a Resistance, and Dawn Penn’s You Don’t Love Me (No, No, No).”

Late reggae icon Dennis Brown dubbed Hunt “the Jamaican Quincy Jones”, a reflection of the breadth of his musicianship, arranging, and production work.

Despite being visually impaired, Hunt continues to create, record, produce and perform internationally. He recently performed some of the new songs on the album in Cologne, Germany, and said another trip is already ahead for a music tour.

Undeniably Clive Hunt aka Lizzard is produced by Clive Hunt, with Rowen Johnson as co-producer, and released through Iconic Azul/Love Injection Production.

Musician credits are also attributed to guitarists Lamont “Monty” Savory, Nico Groskopf, Mitchum Khan; basses Val Douglass, Jason Welch; drummer Kirk Bennett; keyboardist Robbie Lyn; horns Oshane Love, Okeil McIntyre. Acknowedements to engineers Mikey Williamson, Roland McDermott, Hasani “Snysh” Williams, and Nigel Burrell.

World.title: TO THE RESCUE!
World.content:
Jamaica Kingsmen batsman Kirk Mckenzie goes big during his knock of 69 against Trinbago Knight Riders in the Caribbean Premier League Twenty20 match at Sabina Park in Kingston on August 15, 2026. Photo: Naphtali Junior

JAMAICA Kingsmen all-rounder Andre Russell says the blazing powerplay from openers Kirk McKenzie and Reeza Hendricks gave his team a “high per cent chance” of winning, as the franchise kick-started its Caribbean Premier League (CPL) campaign with a five-wicket win over Trinbago Knight Riders at a near-packed Sabina Park on Saturday.

Sent in to bat, the Knight Riders posted 182-6 from 20 overs. Captain Nicholas Pooran and Kieron Pollard each hit 44. Pooran fired four sixes and one four off 32 balls, while the veteran Pollard hammered four sixes and three fours off only 22 deliveries. Alex Hales made 29 and Colin Munro added 16.

For the Kingsmen, Russell and Hunain Shah took two wickets each. Russell conceded 34 from four overs, while Shah gave away 31 from his full allotment.

In reply, the Kingsmen raced to 183-5 in 18.4 overs behind a career-best, 25-ball 69 from opener Kirk McKenzie. He hit six fours and six sixes and shared a 93-run opening stand with Hendricks, who made 37.

The wheels wobbled briefly when Usman Tariq removed McKenzie on the last ball of the seventh over, then bowled Shayan Jahangir for two and had Hendricks caught next over.

Pollard had Keacy Carty caught for 11 to leave the Kingsmen at 126-4 in the 14th over but Captain Rovman Powell and Russell steadied things with a 48-run stand. Russell smashed a quick 27 off 15 balls to leave the Kingsmen 174-4 in the 18th over.

Powell finished 29 not out and Hasan Khan was three not out as the Kingsmen got home with eight balls to spare. Tarig finished with three for 21 from four overs.

“Kirk McKenzie and Reeza Hendricks batting in the power play, it was tremendous. When you get a start like that you’re basically 80-90 per cent chance of winning the game,” Russell said in a post-match interview.

The veteran also said he plans to have a word with McKenzie about shot selection, after the youngster was bowled by Tariq trying an aggressive shot.

“I think the way he got out, I need to have a chat with him because it caused us to lose two wickets in quick succession. And I think T20 is such a funny game. The ball is round, and when you have good, quality spinners like what the Trinbago Knight Riders have we can’t take anything for granted.

“He was set, Reeza was set at the crease. That ball wasn’t there to hit.

“But I’m happy for him tonight. He batted out of his skin. He played some excellent shots and took on the bowling attack and so I’m happy for this win,” Russell noted.

Russell, a former Knight Rider, said he used his knowledge of their tactics to help plan. He even asked the groundsmen at Sabina Park — Jamaica’s premier cricket ground — for the middle pitch on the batting square to counter TKR’s “wide ball” plans to exploit short boundaries.

“I know… they like to bowl the ball for you to hit to one side of the ground. And, you know, it starts from the groundsmen. I told the groundsman, ‘Let us play in the middle.’ And it’s our home. We should use the advantage to the best of our ability.

“And if one side was bigger than one side, then they would have maybe out played us in the bowling department, but I think [given the] mind games that I know they play, I kind of counteract[ed] that tonight,” he explained.

Russell emphasised the importance of winning at home in Jamaica, crediting the energetic crowd for pushing the team to victory.

“It means a lot to our full house tonight. I think we have to give the fans credit because that really helped to push us and to give us this victory tonight, so it means a lot to the team and the franchise, and also for Jamaica and the cricket lovers in Jamaica.”

Russell highlighted the significance of the CPL returning to Jamaica for the first time since 2019. He noted the high attendance — surpassing recent West Indies international matches — and hopes the Government’s renewed support and the team’s exciting play will sustain local interest.

“It means a lot. Not just to us as players, but I think for this, for this lovely island, that cricket is such a big sport in this [country]. When you talk about sports you’re talking about football, track and field, cricket — and we are happy to have the Government back on our side and, you know, we getting the energy that we need.

“And as you can see tonight, I haven’t seen this at Sabina Park for a while. And even when West Indies come out to play here, we don’t see this type of crowd. So I think this will motivate all these fans that came out tonight, and they might try to make an effort to come back Tuesday night, even though it’s a work week,” he said.

World.title: Cut in half
World.content:
Roger Clarke High School in Balaclava, St ElizabethPhotos: Garfield Robinson

BALACLAVA, St Elizabeth — The drastic decline in student enrolment at Roger Clarke High School here to just under half its previous population of 700 has Principal George Lewis worried that some students won’t return at the start of new academic year in September.

Lewis is calling on parents and guardians to ensure their children return to the classroom next month.

“Parents need to be held accountable that their child must be in school because education is guaranteed under the Child Care and Protection Act, and there are so many other Acts that demand that students be in school. Enforcement is important but too many children are on the road during school time. And it is not that [they are on] shift; they are just not coming to school,” he said.

The decline in the school’s population has been compounded by existing structural damage, particularly leaking roofs and blown-out windows, which shuttered the school for just over two weeks last October following the passage of Hurricane Melissa and placed it in the Ministry of Education’s tier two for restoration.

“[The drop] in our enrolment [started] from the advent of COVID-19 and it has continued. Hurricane Beryl [in July 2024] caused further decline in our enrolment and Hurricane Melissa has caused us to lose some students in the middle of the school year. Students who were previously here in October didn’t return when we reopened on the 18th of November,” Lewis told the

Jamaica Observer last Wednesday.

He said although guidance counsellors have located students, some are reluctant to return to school and have instead opted to work at establishments including bars.

“We visited them and met with their parents. Whether it is that they moved out because their homes were destroyed or they become engaged in income-earning activities, some opted not to come back to formal school. Whatever the reason, that contributed to the continued decline and, of course, [there are also] the [students] who we get from the Ministry [of Education],” Lewis explained.

He said that getting those students back in school will require a collective effort.

“… If you drive around St Elizabeth during the school day — and not many schools are on shift — you will see an unacceptably high number of students on the road during school time. Who is it that is ensuring that these students are not on the road idling?” he asked.

“Whether they are at a garage working, or they are at a bar working, or just on the corner or gone to a river. [They are] doing things other than coming to school. It has affected Roger Clarke High School, but it is not just [here],” added Lewis.

In January, school leaders at Maggotty High, Black River High, and Newell High said they were seeing a fluctuation in the turnout of students. They attributed it to teenagers having taken jobs, including construction, while others have relocated to other parishes.

Lewis said in June the school had a graduating class of just 26 students, and efforts have been doubled by teachers and students to do well in external exams, including the Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC).

“Our math CSEC passes were exceptionally high. We moved from 14 per cent in the school year 2023/2024 to 60 per cent in 2024/2025. We were particularly proud of that… Hurricane Melissa brought us down but we are expectant and hopeful that the results this year will continue on that trajectory. We have approximately 320 students, given that we just graduated 26 in June, and then we have received 45 students via PEP for this coming school year,” he said while explaining that only 30 of the 45 students have registered for the upcoming academic year, while the school has also accepted transfer students.

Despite no remedial work to the school plant Lewis said he is prepared to accommodate students in September.

“Nothing has been done in terms of the roof except just to put tarpaulin there, but if it rains and it is windy then those tarpaulins will lift. In terms of preparation for school, we are well under way there. One of the benefits to my school is that we do not have a shortage of furniture for students; because of the reduction in the numbers I have enough to seat all students… Any shortage of furniture is for teachers,” he explained.

But a lack of reliable water supply and spotty Internet service are among the woes facing the school.

“Water remains a problem in Balaclava so we had occasions when there was no water in the area and so we had to close school midday… We have a lot of rainfall and we do have catchment tanks but then, if we have no water from [the National Water Commission] in excess of three days then our storage capacity will be depleted and [we will] have to close school. We call NWC and they will respond to us, but sometimes it is not fast enough,” he said while pointing out that three times in the last academic year the school was shuttered due to water issues.

“We don’t have reliable Internet access here so we have to invest in two Starlink [devices],” he added.

The school, which was originally Balaclava High until it was renamed in honour of late former agriculture minister and St Elizabeth North Eastern Member of Parliament Roger Clarke in 2015, also suffered significant damage to its poultry and greenhouse programmes.

Lewis is however determined to rebuild those programmes and have the school expand into fish farming for its 50th anniversary.

“One of the things that we want to engage in for the new school year as our legacy project is aquaculture… and solar to help build our resilience. After the hurricane we were without electricity for a long time, so we became a generator city,” he said while thanking the American Friends of Jamaica for starting a solar system project at the school.

— Jonn Stewart

World.title: A woman with a purpose
World.content:
SOME revolutions begin with a protest. Others begin with a business plan. For Shelly Heaven, the possibility of changing Jamaica began much closer to home: at the family table, with her two young sons learning that the food they ate was not simply something that filled them, but could shape the lives they lived.

Long before FarmLinkr became a growing agricultural business, Heaven had developed a conviction that what Jamaica eats matters, and that the country’s relationship with food could have profound consequences for its health, its farmers and its future.

It was this conviction that eventually led her into agriculture. Not because she had always planned to become an agricultural entrepreneur, but because she began to see the connections between problems that were often treated separately. Jamaican farmers were producing food but did not always have reliable access to markets. Consumers wanted fresh, nourishing produce but could struggle to find it consistently. At the same time, Jamaica was blessed with fertile land and an abundance of agricultural products while facing a growing burden of non-communicable diseases. To Heaven, these were not isolated challenges. They were pieces of the same puzzle.

She began asking what could happen if the relationship between the people growing Jamaica’s food and the people buying it could be made simpler, stronger and more efficient. That question became the foundation for FarmLinkr.

When Heaven first envisioned the business, she was not thinking about warehouses, branded products or islandwide delivery. Her original idea was an online, location-agnostic marketplace that would allow farmers to showcase what they had available and give buyers an easier way to find what they needed. It was a relatively simple solution to a very real problem: connecting supply with demand.

But entrepreneurship rarely unfolds exactly as planned.

As Heaven listened to the market and responded to what consumers and farmers actually needed, the business evolved. FarmLinkr moved beyond simply connecting buyers and sellers and became a business that sells and delivers products islandwide, while also developing branded products that have made their way into supermarkets. The evolution was not a departure from the original vision, but an extension of it. Heaven recognised that if the goal was to make local food more accessible, FarmLinkr had to be willing to meet consumers where they were.

That willingness to adapt has become one of the defining characteristics of her entrepreneurial journey. Technology remains an important part of FarmLinkr, but Heaven has never treated technology as the end goal. The platform is a means of creating connections, while the larger ambition is to make it easier for consumers to discover, access and choose wholesome, locally grown food and, in doing so, create stronger opportunities for the farmers producing it.

Her journey has also given her a wider view of what Jamaican agriculture could become.

Heaven points to the Netherlands as an example of what is possible when agriculture is treated not simply as traditional farming, but as a sophisticated, technology-driven industry. For Jamaica, she sees opportunities in climate-controlled and protected agriculture, precision farming, artificial intelligence, data-driven farming, drones, sensors and robotics. For a country operating within the hurricane belt, these technologies could help farmers become more resilient while improving consistency, productivity and efficiency.

More importantly, Heaven believes this transformation could change who sees themselves in agriculture.

For young Jamaicans, agriculture does not have to mean only planting, harvesting and working the soil by hand. It can mean engineering, technology, logistics, data, marketing, artificial intelligence and entrepreneurship. It can create careers for young people who may never have imagined that agriculture had a place for their skills.

But Heaven knows that vision alone cannot transform a sector. Investment is necessary, and she has become an advocate for what she calls “patient capital” for agricultural businesses. Rather than viewing agriculture simply as an industry too risky to invest in, she believes the right technology, infrastructure and systems can help manage those risks and create businesses capable of producing sustainable returns.

It is this belief that sits behind Heaven’s description of Jamaican agriculture as a “sleeping gold mine”.

The phrase is not simply about the value of Jamaica’s land. The opportunity lies in everything that could be created from it: stronger local food systems, greater market access for farmers, reduced dependence on imported food, new businesses, new technologies, new careers and greater economic value from what the country already has. Jamaica has the land, the climate, the agricultural knowledge and the people. What Heaven sees is an industry that has enormous wealth within it, but has not yet been fully developed, modernised or mined for its potential.

For her, the answer is not to abandon traditional agriculture, but to build on it intelligently.

“Agriculture is a sleeping gold mine; let’s start mining smartly and wake up this sleeping treasure chest for our country.”

Today, Heaven, founder and chief executive officer of FarmLinkr, has been ranked #71 on Businessuite’s Women Power 100, recognising Jamaica’s most powerful and influential businesswomen. The recognition adds another milestone to an entrepreneurial journey that began with a personal concern and grew into a much larger purpose. But perhaps the most significant part of her story is not the recognition itself. It is what her journey reveals about starting before everything is figured out.

For younger women trying to build something of their own, Heaven’s experience offers an important lesson. A purpose does not always arrive as a fully formed business idea. Sometimes it begins with noticing a problem, asking a difficult question and being willing to follow the answer. Her journey shows that the first version of an idea does not have to be the final one. Businesses evolve when entrepreneurs listen, learn, adapt and remain committed to the problem they set out to solve.

There is also something particularly powerful in the fact that Heaven did not enter agriculture because it was the obvious path for her. She entered because she saw an opportunity to make a difference. That distinction matters for women still finding their footing in business. The journey does not always begin with certainty, capital or a perfect roadmap. Sometimes it begins with conviction and the courage to build from there.

For Heaven, that journey has now grown beyond building a company. She wants FarmLinkr to play a role in transforming Jamaican agriculture, strengthening the relationship between farmers and consumers, opening new markets, encouraging innovation and making local food more accessible. She wants to see a generation of Jamaicans view agriculture differently, not as an industry stuck in the past, but as one capable of driving the country’s future.

What began with a mother thinking about the food on her family’s table became a business built around connecting farmers with consumers, and that business has grown into a vision for what Jamaica’s food system could become.

The farmer remains an essential part of that journey. The consumer is the one who ultimately chooses what reaches the plate. FarmLinkr exists in the space between them, building the connections that make those choices easier and creating greater opportunities along the way.

Heaven’s vision is bold, but its starting point is remarkably simple: Jamaica already has something valuable. The opportunity now is to recognise it, invest in it and build it smarter.

The sleeping gold mine is here. Shelly Heaven believes it is time for Jamaica to start mining.

World.title: Ahhh Ras Natango rules the world
World.content:
Tamika Williams (left) with her husband Ian (centre) and their adult son, Ayale in an undated photo. The family are the owners and operators of Ahhh Ras Natango Gallery and Garden in St James.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Tamika Williams was moved to tears on learning that her family-run Ahhh Ras Natango Gallery and Garden in St James has been ranked the world’s top attraction by travellers in an AAA Club Alliance analysis of TripAdvisor reviews.

“For Jamaica to make that list, and when you look at the calibre of countries and the calibre of attractions, and then this being a small business, a community tourism business, it just floored me. Never expected it,” Williams told the Jamaica Observer.

The ranking, published in July by AAA Club Alliance, was based on an analysis by ChicksX of TripAdvisor reviews, examining the frequency of positive and negative keywords visitors consistently described as “memorable”, “breathtaking”, and “better than expected”.

AAA Club Alliance explained that the study distinguished these attractions from those more commonly characterised as overrated.

Ahhh Ras Natango was ranked ahead of more well-known attractions, including the Irish National Stud & Gardens in Ireland; Al Noor Island in the United Arab Emirates; Canada’s Cabot Trail, Stone Hall Castle, and Capilano Suspension Bridge; Florida’s Stetson Mansion; Kiambethu Tea Farm in Kenya; Australia’s New Castle Memorial Walk and SkyPoint Climb; and The Rooms in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Williams said that when she received news of the results, “Mi just cry, just sat down and cry”.

That emotion was fuelled by her appreciation for the recognition, given that the attraction is still recovering from the ravages of Hurricane Melissa which devastated sections of Jamaica last October.

Four buildings, including gazebos, a restroom, and meeting area, were destroyed. The kitchen and the work area used by her husband, Ian — an artist known professionally as Ras Natango — remain out of operation, while much of the vegetation was badly damaged.

“We are operational, but we’re not fully open. We’re doing our best. We are staying the course and trying to figure out where to go, and then just out of nowhere, this came in,” Williams told the

Observer.

She described the international recognition as “an adrenaline shot” that renewed her determination to rebuild.

“I said, ‘No man, you can’t give up. No, don’t give up,’ ” she related.

Williams hopes the exposure will bring more visitors, increase awareness, and help the family restore the property. She also hopes the story will encourage others facing adversity to persevere.

“Just keep on doing what you love, because people on the outside are watching,” she said.

Opened in 2008, Ahhh Ras Natango has built its reputation largely on visitor reviews and word of mouth recommendation. Williams said the attraction has consistently held the number one position on TripAdvisor’s things to do list in Montego Bay.

She believes the attraction’s appeal lies in its story and its connection to Jamaican culture.

Williams, Ian, and their adult son, Ayale, are equal owners and have managed the business largely on their own through the COVID-19 pandemic, Hurricane Beryl in 2024, and now Hurricane Melissa.

Williams attributes their success to passion and an uncompromising commitment to every visitor.

“Our athletes do well in everything, whether it is football, whether it is especially athletics. There is a hunger in our belly when people feel marginalised and they have a dream,” she said.

“When they go on the track they leave everything there. So when every guest comes through our gate, we leave everything there,” she added.

That personal connection, she said, often leaves visitors feeling they have experienced more than a conventional tourist attraction.

“Every single guest that leaves here…they hug us up and say, ‘I feel like I just went home to my family. I feel like I had a family meeting’,” Williams told the

Observer.

Located about 2,000 feet above sea level in Camrose, the property offers panoramic views from Montego Bay towards Falmouth. Its botanical garden was created by terracing a solid rock cliff and includes an art gallery and gift shop featuring Jamaican art as well as products made on the property.

“It’s just an experience. That is what it is. It is not an attraction, it is an experience,” Williams said.

Visitors typically spend about two hours exploring the garden while learning about Jamaica’s history, culture, music, flora, and fauna.

The property is also a community resource, supporting school field trips and community activities. Williams said Camrose has also been developed as an international City of Peace.

Ecotourism remains central to the operation, with composting, rainwater harvesting, terracing, and conservation incorporated into the property.

Birds have become an even more important part of the experience since Melissa destroyed much of the vegetation. With many fruit- and seed-producing trees gone, the family has begun supplementing food for hummingbirds and other species.

“We realised that even though all the trees were gone, and the birds eat fruits and seeds, and there are no fruits and seeds, we had to supplement feeding them,” she said.

The family expects it could take five to 10 years for the larger trees to return, but Williams insists the garden remains alive.

For her, the international ranking is more than an accolade.

“It is a way for me to remember that even in the darkest hour there is light,” she said.

“…the most beautiful sunrises and sunsets is just that moment before darkness gives way to light,” Williams said.

World.title: UK defense secretary’s phone number found online after Burnham hit by texting scam
World.content:
All three ministers declined to comment on the record. The reference to Streeting’s number online has since been deleted, and officials are working to remove the other two.

Ministers are given secure government devices to conduct business for their briefs, in particular for high-risk roles like defense, and are expected to use those for non-personal comms.

A government spokesperson said: “The government has robust procedures in place to ensure the security of sensitive information.”

But Prerana Joshi, research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) think tank, said that having direct numbers for Cabinet ministers in the public domain is a risk, warning that numbers could be spoofed and used to call others at a time when the U.K. is “in a high threat situation” globally.

“In any civil space, if your number is exposed, a whole host of malign, nefarious or even opportunistic cyber criminals or cyber actors could get hold of it, and they have tactics,” Joshi said.

‘No significance’

Downing Street would not comment on the revelation that Burnham exchanged messages with the impersonator, citing “national security.”

World.title: Ukraine urges EU sanctions on Rosatom over allegations of nuclear safety violations
World.content:
POLITICO's investigation revealed warnings from Egyptian authorities and internal assessments by Rosatom regarding the construction of the El Dabaa nuclear plant. The documents obtained by POLITICO raised concerns ranging from the quality of concrete work to delays and management problems, while an Egyptian agency alleged “deliberate negligence” and violations of “nuclear safety culture.” Nuclear material has yet to be introduced at the site.

Rosatom previously defended its safety record at El Dabaa and pointed to regular scrutiny of the project by Egyptian, Russian and International Atomic Energy Agency officials. None of the allegations contained presented to Rosatom by POLITICO, have been “confirmed within the contractual, technical and oversight procedures envisaged by the project," the company said in a statement.

It did not respond to a request for comment on Sybiha’s remarks on Monday.

Sybiha’s call puts renewed pressure on EU governments that continue to cooperate with Rosatom despite Russia’s war in Ukraine. In Hungary, the company is building two new reactors at the Paks II nuclear plant using the same VVER-1200 technology planned for El Dabaa.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar last week challenged Rosatom’s claim that construction for the reactors remained on schedule, saying his government was carrying out a full review of the project.

World.title: Russia cancels major Red Square military jamboree amid drone attacks
World.content:
A Russian National Guard serviceman stands in front of St. Basil's Cathedral in Moscow on April 1, 2026. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images

“The event has been postponed until 2027 due to circumstances beyond the organizers’ control,” said festival bosses.

A major military music festival in Moscow has been canceled four days before it was due to start, the organizers said on Telegram.

The lavish parade, known as the Spasskaya Tower International Military Music Festival, attracts thousands of visitors and brings together dozens of military bands in the heart of Moscow on Red Square near the Kremlin.

The event, which began in 2007 at President Vladimir Putin’s orders, is one of Russia’s most prominent military-themed events, alongside the May 9 Victory Day parade in Moscow and the Navy Day show in St. Petersburg. Spasskaya “Tower was only canceled once before — in 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

World.title: Latvia wants €7B from EU to cope with fallout from Russia’s war
World.content:
The demand comes at a sensitive moment. Latvia has been one of Europe’s staunchest supporters of Ukraine, sharply increasing defense spending since Moscow's full-scale invasion, even as sanctions and the collapse of bilateral trade have cut deeply into economic links that once ran eastward. But ahead of an Oct. 3 national election, parties arguing that Riga should demand more in return for sanctions and military support are gaining ground.

The European Commission has proposed substantially increasing EU-level defense funding in the 2028-2034 budget, including a €125.2 billion security, defense industry and space pot in the European Competitiveness Fund. That money is designed to finance projects across the bloc rather than provide Latvia with a pre-agreed €7 billion allocation, and the entire budget remains subject to negotiations between EU governments and the European Parliament.

Kulbergs argues that Latvia deserves special consideration because it is borrowing to provide security for countries much farther from the front line. “We are getting our budget deficit to the maximum […] and from that debt we're paying […] the defense of the whole [of] Europe,” the prime minister said at the government chancellery.

Much of Latvia’s military spending ultimately flows back to richer Western European economies, Kulbergs added, pointing to arms purchases from Germany, France, Spain, Sweden and the Netherlands. “We fuel their economies,” he added.

Election pressure

A sharper version of the same argument is emerging on the campaign trail.

Ainārs Šlesers, a veteran populist businessman whose party sits with the far-right Patriots for Europe group in Brussels, says Latvia should demand compensation when it backs EU sanctions on Russia. Šlesers condemns Moscow’s invasion and says support for Ukraine should continue, but argues that Latvia cannot absorb the costs indefinitely.

World.title: Czech PM Babiš apologizes for picking flowers in national park
World.content:
Andrej Babiš arrives at the Elysée Palace in Paris on July 13, 2026. | Magali Cohen/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

“I will definitely pay a fine if necessary, of course,” he said.

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš apologized Sunday for picking flowers in a protected area on Lysá hora, a mountain in eastern Czechia, saying he would pay a fine if necessary.

Babiš said in a Facebook video that he plucked the flowers while remembering a late colleague from his ANO movement with whom he had previously climbed the mountain.

“Maybe I broke some law, for which I apologize and I will definitely pay a fine if necessary, of course,” he said.

World.title: Burnham exchanged messages with impersonator of top Trump aide
World.content:
The British embassy in Washington was so concerned about the incident that it raised it with the White House, two of the officials said. Like others in this article, they were granted anonymity to discuss a matter of national security.

Inside the U.K. government, there were fears that Wiles’ phone had been hacked again.

A White House official said: “This incident had nothing to do with the Chief of Staff’s devices being hacked.”

Last year, the White House and the FBI launched an investigation after senators, governors and U.S. business executives received texts and phone calls from someone claiming to be Trump’s chief of staff.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Wiles told associates her cellphone contacts had been hacked.

What was discussed in the exchange with Burnham — and when the messages were sent — is unclear, with the erroneous contact kept a closely-guarded secret.

Burnham became PM on July 20, but it was clear he was on course to succeed Keir Starmer from the moment he won the Makerfield by-election on June 18.

This story has been updated to include a comment from a White House official.

World.title: Germany rethinks law protecting politicians from insults
World.content:
Moritz Oppelt, the CDU justice minister of Germany’s southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg echoed the sentiment, arguing the law should serve only its original intent of protecting local politicians, who are often subject to particular vitriol.

“Top politicians can and must be able to withstand tough criticism,” he said. “It is fundamental to our democracy, and part of our understanding of democracy in Germany, that people are free to discuss political decisions at the federal and state levels and criticize them very harshly. That does not mean that insults in the political sphere should become normalized. There are, of course, limits.”

Variations of this view find consensus across Germany’s fractured political spectrum. The far-left Left Party and far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party want the law abolished outright, while the CDU, Greens and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) all support revising it.

“Politicians like Friedrich Merz insult ordinary people in this country every day by calling them lazy or malingerers,” said Luke Hoss, a Left lawmaker, referring to the chancellor’s remarks that Germans should work more to boost economic growth. “The provision creates a special criminal offense that applies only to politicians and should be abolished.”

Tobias Peterka, an AfD lawmaker, said tough criticism comes with the job. “Anyone who voluntarily enters politics and exercises public authority must — as Germany’s Federal Constitutional Court has repeatedly emphasized — tolerate harsher criticism than private citizens, not less,” he argued.

While a version of the law giving special protection to politicians, Section 188 of the criminal code, has existed since 1951, former Chancellor Angela Merkel’s government in 2021 strengthened the legislation as part of broader efforts to combat right-wing extremism and hate speech.

World.title: ‘Deliberate negligence’: Russian nuclear power company with EU operations accused of violating safety standards
World.content:
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 prompted Europe to impose sweeping sanctions on the country, Rosatom has tried to convince European governments that it remains a reliable and competent supplier in the nuclear power market. But the accusations of safety breaches could add to existing concerns over the Kremlin-controlled company’s operations in the EU.

In an emailed statement to POLITICO, Rosatom said it upholds the highest levels of nuclear safety and had done so throughout the construction of El Dabaa. The company declined to comment on whether it had received the letter or the complaints from Egypt's Nuclear Power Plants Authority, which did not respond to multiple requests for comment about its communications with Rosatom.

“The high standard of work organisation, the quality management system and the safety culture are affirmed by the sustained attention paid to the project by the political leadership of the Russian Federation and the Arab Republic of Egypt, as well as by the leadership of the International Atomic Energy Agency, whose representatives regularly attend key project milestones,” said the company by email, adding that a recent ceremony for one of El Dabaa’s reactor units was attended by Russian, Egyptian and IAEA officials.

Egypt's El Dabaa is located on the Mediterranean Sea coast, some 300 km northwest of Cairo. | Alexander Ryumin/TASS via Belga

None of the allegations contained in the letter, presented to Rosatom by POLITICO, have been “confirmed within the contractual, technical and oversight procedures envisaged by the project," read the company’s statement.

Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said in July he expected the construction of all four El Dabaa reactors to finish by 2030, with the first reactor unit set to begin producing power by 2028. No nuclear fuel has yet been introduced to the site. Rosatom's Egyptian plant will use the same technology at the heart of Hungary's Paks II project, the Kremlin-backed nuclear expansion that has repeatedly raised tensions between Budapest and the European Commission.

The Commission told POLITICO it was not aware of the confidential documents and allegations they contain. “For the EU, nuclear safety is a key priority,” said a Commission spokesperson.

World.title: Mount Etna lightning strike kills hiker from the US
World.content:
A 29-year-old American tourist has died after being hit by lightning while hiking on Mount Etna in Sicily.

 

The man was struck on Sunday as a severe thunderstorm swept across the volcano.

He was rushed to a hospital in Catania by a firefighter helicopter but was pronounced dead. His identity has not yet been made public.

An emergency call came in shortly before 8 pm. He had been in the isolated Rocca Capra area of the active volcano, in the Valle del Bove, around 1,400 metres above sea level.

According to preliminary information from authorities, the man is believed to have been on his own and may have been in an area closed to the public or otherwise subject to restrictions because of Etna's recent activity. An investigation into the incident is ongoing.

The rescue operation

An Italian firefighter Drago 142 helicopter was dispatched to the scene, where rescuers attempted to resuscitate the man. He was then winched aboard and flown to Catania's Cannizzaro hospital, where he arrived in cardiac arrest.

Doctors continued resuscitation efforts, but he was later pronounced dead, at around 9:30 pm. His body has been transferred to the hospital morgue.

Police are investigating but, according to agency reports, no family members have yet been traced.

Etna remains highly active

Etna has continued to show highly eruptive activity in recent hours.

The National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology's (INGV) Etna Observatory reported the opening of a new lava vent in the Valle del Bove area after part of the eastern flank of the Rittmann summit cone collapsed.

The new vent, according to data released by the INGV, lies at around 2,350 metres above sea level and has produced a lava flow of about 500 metres, which has now come to a halt and cooled.

Another vent at around 1,900 metres remains active, with lava continuing to flow down to about 1,600 metres.

At the same time, explosive activity continues at Voragine, one of Etna's summit craters.

The eruption plume has risen to around 6,000 metres above sea level, drifting south-east.

Volcanic tremors also remain at high, steady levels, confirming that the volcano is still in an active phase. The INGV is monitoring the situation closely.

The lava flows descending the slopes of the volcano, seen from Serracozzo near Catania AP Photo

Volcanic ash disrupts flights at Catania

Etna's activity continues to affect air traffic to and from Sicily.

The presence of ash in the atmosphere has led authorities to extend the closure of sector B1 of the airspace and restrict arrivals at Catania-Fontanarossa airport.

Until noon on Tuesday, there will be no more than 10 flights arriving per hour, while there are currently no restrictions on departures.

Passengers are nevertheless being advised to check the status of their flight with the airline before travelling to the airport.

This is not the first time Etna's activity has caused severe disruption at Catania airport. In recent days, ash emissions had already led to cancellations.

Thunderstorms pose significant risk in mountains

The American tourist's death came as a 42-year-old man also died on Piz Starlex in South Tyrol, after apparently being struck by lightning during his descent.

His body was located late in the evening by a drone at an altitude of around 2,600 metres.

Mountain rescue teams warn that thunderstorms are among the most serious dangers for people hiking in the mountains.

Ridges, peaks, and rocky zones are particularly exposed, and hikers are advised to leave high ground and seek shelter as quickly as possible should they see lightning or hear thunder.
