World.title: FACT CHECK: No plans to merge Araling Panlipunan and MAPEH – DepEd
World.content:
In a statement on August 8, the Department of Education clarified that the post circulating online is based on an outdated report

Claim: The Department of Education (DepEd) plans to merge the subjects Araling Panlipunan (Social Studies) and Music, Arts, PE, and Health (MAPEH).

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A graphic bearing the claim was posted on August 7 by Carl Balita, an educator and media personality with 3.1 million Facebook followers.

The post featured the official DepEd logo alongside text reading, “DepEd, planong pag-isahin na lang ang Araling Panlipunan at MAPEH (DepEd plans to merge Araling Panlipunan and MAPEH).”

The same graphic was also shared on August 8 by the Facebook page “Hugot pa Teacher,” which has 568,000 followers.

The facts: The posts are based on an outdated report. On August 8, DepEd clarified that the posts were based on an April 2023 PTV News report regarding a proposed merger of the two subjects into one — Sibika, Sining at Kultura, Kasaysayan, at Kagalingang Pangkatawan (SIKAP) — for students from Kindergarten to Grade 3.

While that plan did exist in 2023, DepEd stated that the news item “reflects outdated discussions from 2023 and does not represent current policy.” According to the education department, “Makabansa” serves as a distinct learning area for Grades 1 to 3 under the revised K to 10 curriculum, while Araling Panlipunan and MAPEH will continue to be taught as separate subjects starting in Grade 4.

“We urge the public to practice critical thinking, check context, and verify release dates before sharing content online,” the statement added.

AP and MAPEH: According to a 2013 DepEd curriculum guide, Araling Panlipunan or Social Studies aims to shape critical, reflective, responsible, productive, and patriotic citizens, as well as equip them with an appreciation for historical and social issues.

The subject MAPEH, meanwhile, covers lessons in music, arts, physical education, and health to “culturally enrich students and help them enjoy and learn new things.”

In 2023, DepEd launched its “Matatag” revised K-10 curriculum, which reduces the number of learning areas for students to focus on foundational skills.

Edited caption: Around five hours after DepEd debunked the misleading post on August 8, the “Hugot pa Teacher” page edited its caption.

As of writing, the post now includes a disclaimer stating that the report was based on a 2023 draft proposal. However, the original publication material remains up and continues to circulate online.

Meanwhile, Balita’s post also remains up without any DepEd clarification.

Debunked: Rappler has previously debunked false claims related to DepEd and its curriculum and programs.

– Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com

Lyndee Buenagua is a senior student journalist and an alumna of Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: From Illicit Wealth to Public Services: Where Kazakhstan’s Recovered Assets Are Going
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has returned 1.154 trillion tenge (US$2.5 billion) in assets to state ownership since launching its asset-recovery program in September 2023. The central question now is how effectively these funds can be converted into long-term public benefits, particularly in regions facing infrastructure shortages.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has repeatedly stressed that the asset-recovery process should serve a broader public purpose.

“The restoration of social justice through the return of illegally acquired assets is not a matter of political expediency or a PR campaign, but a principled position of the state,” Tokayev said in a Jan. 5 interview with the Turkistan newspaper.

The funds are channeled through the Special State Fund, created to finance social and infrastructure projects. According to the General Prosecutor’s Office, 617.6 billion tenge (US$1.3 billion) has been allocated to 466 projects, with water supply, healthcare and education accounting for the largest share. The scale and geographic distribution of this spending indicate that asset recovery is becoming not only a legal and fiscal process, but also a mechanism for addressing regional infrastructure gaps.

From recovered assets to public infrastructure

Of the 1.154 trillion tenge returned, 1.044 trillion tenge (US$2.3 billion) is in cash, while the remainder consists of real estate, company shares, land and other assets. Annual returns increased sharply from 302.5 billion tenge (US$653.9 million) in 2024 to 773.7 billion tenge (US$1.67 billion) in 2025. The fund returned a further 77.7 billion tenge (US$167.9 million) this year.

The Special State Fund has allocated financing for 235 water-supply projects, 190 healthcare facilities, 17 education projects, 11 infrastructure projects, seven transport facilities and six sports facilities, reported Kazinform on Aug. 17.

Implementation has already moved beyond the allocation stage. More than 253 billion tenge (US$546.9 million) has been spent on 364 projects, of which 349 have been commissioned. Completed projects include 188 water-supply facilities, 163 healthcare facilities, seven education facilities, three sports facilities, one transport facility and two infrastructure projects.

The figures show that the program is producing physical assets, but they also highlight an important implementation issue: the impact of returned funds will depend on whether projects address persistent local infrastructure deficits and remain operational over the long term.

Where the money is going

Eastern Kazakhstan received the largest allocation at 78.9 billion tenge (US$170.5 million), followed by North Kazakhstan with 69.4 billion tenge (US$150 million) and Astana with 64.7 billion tenge (US$139.8 million). The lowest allocations went to Shymkent, the Atyrau Region and the Mangystau Region.

These differences do not necessarily reflect a region’s size or economic importance. According to the General Prosecutor’s Office, allocations depend on the number of applications submitted by local authorities, the availability of completed design and cost documentation, project priorities and the severity of infrastructure shortages.

This makes project preparation an important factor in determining access to financing. Regions with clearly prepared projects and pressing infrastructure needs are better positioned to receive funding.

The National Budget Commission decides how funds are distributed. Once financing is approved, projects are implemented under Kazakhstan’s budget legislation and subject to financial control, state audit and treasury procedures.

What to watch next

The program’s success will depend not only on the amount recovered, but on how well the money is used. Key measures will be completed projects, better infrastructure and improved access to essential services.

The long-term goal is to ensure that recovered funds reach regions with the greatest needs and improve people’s quality of life.

World.title: Kazakhstan Deepens University Ties with Japan and South Korea
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding academic and scientific cooperation with leading universities and research institutions in Japan and South Korea. The country seeks to strengthen higher education, research and artificial intelligence (AI) development.

During visits to Seoul and Tokyo in August, Science and Higher Education Minister Sayasat Nurbek met with university leaders and government officials to discuss academic partnerships, joint research, faculty and student exchanges, and workforce development.

Strengthening ties with Japan

In Tokyo, Nurbek held talks with the leadership of Tokyo Metropolitan University and the United Nations University (UNU).

During a meeting with Tokyo Metropolitan University President Takaya Ohashi, the two sides discussed expanding university partnerships, increasing academic mobility and launching joint educational and research projects. Nurbek also invited Ohashi to attend the Strategic Partners Forum, scheduled for November in Astana.

Cooperation with the UNU was another focus of the visit. During talks with the university’s Rector and U.N. Under-Secretary-General Tshilidzi Marwala, the officials discussed expanding collaboration in science, higher education, research and sustainable development.

The two sides also explored ways to expand the university’s presence in Kazakhstan, in line with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to strengthen international academic partnerships. Marwala accepted an invitation to attend the Strategic Partners Forum in Astana.

The visit builds on growing educational cooperation between Kazakhstan and Japan following Tokayev’s official visit to Tokyo for the inaugural Central Asia-Japan Summit in December 2025. During the summit, Tokayev described human capital as “the main engine of development” and invited Japanese universities to establish branches and educational centers in Kazakhstan.

In an earlier interview with The Astana Times, Japan’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan Yasumasa Iijima said that educational cooperation has become an increasingly important pillar of bilateral relations alongside trade and investment.

Kazakhstan’s efforts to expand international academic partnerships come as the country strengthens its position as Central Asia’s leading higher education hub. In July, Almaty reached its highest-ever position in the QS Best Student Cities 2027 ranking, while the country recorded another year of growth in international student enrollment.

AI partnership with South Korea

In Seoul, Nurbek met South Korea’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Science and ICT Bae Kyung-hoon.

The discussions focused on expanding cooperation in science, higher education and AI, including technology transfer, joint research and the training of highly qualified specialists.

One of the key topics was the planned opening of a branch campus of the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) in Kazakhstan.

Nurbek also met with KAIST Vice President Jaemin Jung to discuss academic exchanges, joint research projects and cooperation in AI and digital technologies.

Separate meetings with the leadership of Seoul National University and Korea University focused on expanding collaboration in medicine, engineering, information technology and other priority fields. Both universities maintain partnerships with Kazakh higher education institutions.

Educational cooperation between Kazakhstan and South Korea is also expanding through dual-degree programs.

Seoul Cyber University currently partners with Q University, Almaty Humanitarian and Economic University, and Maqsut Narikbayev University (MNU). The expanding partnerships reflect Kazakhstan’s ambition to become a regional hub for AI and digital innovation.

The visits come as Kazakhstan and South Korea deepen broader strategic ties. Earlier this month, Tokayev accepted an invitation to visit Seoul during talks with South Korean Presidential Chief of Staff Kang Hoon-sik.

South Korea has also become an increasingly popular study destination for Kazakh students. According to the Korean Educational Development Institute, 1,516 Kazakh students were enrolled at South Korean universities as of April 1, 2024.

The trend reflects broader educational cooperation between the two countries. Earlier this year, Woosong University opened a branch campus in Turkistan, while exchange partnerships continue to expand across multiple institutions.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Parliamentary Campaign Enters Final Week With Focus on Rule of Law
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Kurultai election campaign entered its final stretch, with nationally televised debates dominating the campaign. The debates offered voters an opportunity to compare the platforms of the seven competing political parties.

The campaign featured the first-ever team debates involving representatives of all seven parties, broadcast on the Jibek Joly television channel. The week also included a series of one-on-one debates between individual parties.

The debates marked the only occasion during the campaign when parties appeared as full teams rather than individual candidates. The format tested each party’s ability to present a unified position while responding to questions from opponents and viewers. The public could also vote in real time through QR-code polling.

Political observers said the debates signaled the gradual emergence of a more interactive political culture in Kazakhstan, where candidates are expected not only to present policy proposals but also to defend them under public scrutiny.

That growing emphasis on policy differences was also reflected at an Aug. 14 meeting of the Sarap Expert Club in Astana. Experts said voters are increasingly looking beyond broad campaign promises and focusing instead on how parties propose to address issues such as healthcare, education and social protection, including how their policies would be financed and measured.

Rule of law takes center stage

The main theme of the team debate was law and order, focusing on public safety, judicial reform, equality before the law and public trust in state institutions.

The discussion drew public attention as voters looked beyond campaign slogans for concrete proposals to strengthen the country’s legal system.

“The third round of the election debates was particularly intense. Law and order is a topic that concerns everyone. Kazakhstan has accumulated extensive experience in legal reform, and that process continues to evolve. Much has been achieved, but there is always room for improvement,” Kazakh political scientist and historian Daniyar Ashimbayev wrote on his Telegram channel.

The debate also tested the parties’ ability to move beyond technical proposals and discuss broader values shaping the country’s political and legal system.

The televised debate consisted of four rounds.

Representatives explained why voters should support their parties before evaluating their rivals’ election platforms. They then answered live questions from viewers and concluded by making one specific campaign pledge they committed to fulfilling if elected.

The exchanges were often confrontational, with parties challenging each other’s proposals while defending their own policy priorities.

Among political commentators, Ashimbayev singled out the performance of the Adilet Party, represented by prosecutor Aizhan Aimaganova and lawyer Madi Myrzagarayev, chairman of the National Bar Association.

During the debate, Aimaganova stressed that the rule of law rests on three principles: an independent judiciary and law enforcement system, an open and accountable government, and effective protection of citizens.

“The law must apply equally to everyone,” she said, adding that the state should act proactively rather than simply respond to violations.

Ashimbayev described the pair as a “surprisingly effective tandem of experienced legal practitioners.”

Among the party’s proposals, Ashimbayev highlighted measures to reduce crime through better urban infrastructure, expanded digital services for law enforcement agencies and stronger institutions to protect citizens’ rights. He also pointed to the proposal to establish a unified forecasting and analytical center to identify emerging public security risks before they escalate.

Competing for voters

During the debates, Aq Jol Democratic Party and Respublica continued to compete for entrepreneurs and economically liberal voters, with both parties emphasizing business development and market-oriented reforms.

The Auyl Party remained focused on agricultural development and rural communities, reinforcing its traditional electoral base.

Meanwhile, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (NSDP) and the People’s Party of Kazakhstan concentrated on social policy. While the Baytaq Green Party distinguished itself by emphasizing environmental protection and sustainable development.

The debate attracted a record level of public participation.

According to Jibek Joly, 165,153 viewers cast votes through the broadcast’s QR-code polling system.

The Adilet party received the highest level of public support with 60.6% of the vote, followed by Auyl with 15.1% and Respublica with 10.2%. NSDP received 3.9%, Aq Jol 3.5%, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan 3.3%, and Baytaq 2.7%. Another 0.7% of respondents selected the option “no one.”

The week also featured head-to-head debates between Aq Jol and Respublica, as well as between the NSDP and the People’s Party of Kazakhstan.

According to political analysts and reactions on social media, Aq Jol’s representative adopted a more confrontational style, relying heavily on factual arguments, while Respublica emphasized political renewal and generational change.

The debate between NSDP and the People’s Party focused primarily on ideological differences, social policy and competing approaches to economic development.

As of Aug. 17, three nationally televised debates had taken place, with a fourth and final debate scheduled for Aug. 19 on 24KZ TV channel.

Elections to Kurultai are scheduled for Aug. 23.

On Aug. 12, the Central Election Commission accredited an additional 405 observers, bringing the total number of accredited election observers to 656.

World.title: Caspian Seal Conservation Faces New Challenges as Sea Changes
World.content:
ASTANA – The Caspian Sea is home to the Caspian seal, the world’s only seal species found exclusively in the Caspian Sea. The species spends most of its life in the water and travels considerable distances in search of food, while the northern Caspian’s winter ice fields provide critical breeding grounds.

The main conservation challenge is no longer simply protecting known seal habitats, but adapting protection to a changing Caspian Sea. Declining water levels and warmer winters are affecting traditional breeding and haul-out areas, while pollution, fishing nets and other human activities add to the pressure.

In Kazakhstan, the Caspian seal is listed in the Red Book and is protected by law. Scientists are increasingly focused on how environmental changes affect the species and where new protection measures may be needed, according to the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.

A habitat in transition

A documentary by the Institute of Hydrobiology and Ecology, “On the Shoals of the Caspian Sea, the Call of the Seals”, highlights the work of Kazakh researchers. Scientists conduct aerial surveys, locate seal rookeries and analyze population and habitat data.

Assel Baimukanova, a researcher at the institute, said the retreating sea is changing the distribution of suitable habitats.

“As the sea regresses, seals lose their traditional habitats. However, new islands are forming, and it is crucial that they remain safe for the seals,” she said.

This means conservation can no longer focus only on historically known sites. Newly formed islands and shoals may become important resting and breeding areas and require timely protection.

Climate and human pressure

Climate change is adding to existing human-related risks. Caspian seals breed on ice in the northern Caspian during winter, but warmer winters can reduce the availability of suitable ice. Pollution, fishing, shipping, oil activities, tourism and poaching pose additional threats.

“Seals breed on the ice of the northern Caspian, but with warmer winters becoming more frequent, we are facing a critical question: can the species adapt to these changes and survive?” Baimukanova said.

Fishing gear remains a particular concern. Researchers and partner organizations have removed several tonnes of discarded fishing nets and plastic waste from seal habitats during previous conservation campaigns, reducing direct risks to the animals.

From monitoring to regional action

The Caspian seal is also an important indicator of the wider health of the Caspian ecosystem. The sea is home to more than 300 endemic invertebrates, 76 fish species and globally significant populations of migratory birds. As a top predator that moves across the basin, the seal can reflect changes throughout the food chain.

Researchers monitor seal mortality, population structure, habitat and food sources. Satellite imagery identifies new islands and sandbanks that may serve as haul-out sites, while field teams collect water, soil and biological samples.

The problem extends beyond Kazakhstan’s borders. All five Caspian states have ratified regional agreements on marine environmental protection and aquatic biological resources. Kazakhstan established the Caspian Seal State Nature Reserve in 2024, according to Baimukanova, but researchers argue that coordinated transboundary protection will also be needed as habitats shift.

Dr Simon Goodman of the University of Leeds said some decline in the Caspian Sea level is likely to continue even with efforts to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions. Conservation planning should therefore begin early enough to balance biodiversity protection with human interests and wellbeing, he said.

For Kazakhstan, the next challenge is to turn scientific evidence into coordinated conservation measures. Their effectiveness will depend on protecting existing seal habitats, identifying and securing new areas as the Caspian ecosystem evolves, and reducing human pressures from fishing, shipping, pollution and other activities.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Exploration Drive Supports Shift Toward Higher-Value Mining
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is expanding geological and geophysical exploration to strengthen its mineral-resource base and support a strategic shift toward deeper processing and higher-value production.

By the end of this year, exploration is expected to cover 2.2 million square kilometers, with work completed at 25 sites. A key priority is the transition from regional 1:200,000-scale surveys to more detailed 1:50,000 geological mapping (GS-50).

This year, 20 GS-50 projects were launched to identify prospective areas for gold, copper, polymetals, rare earth elements, lithium, tungsten, molybdenum and other strategic minerals, reported the Ministry of Industry and Construction on Aug. 17.

The government has allocated 40.7 billion tenge (US$88 million) for geological surveys and seismic exploration in 2026-2028. Of this, 32.7 billion tenge (US$70.7 million) is allocated to GS-50 projects and 8 billion tenge (US$17.3 million) to seismic exploration. The program also plans six 2D seismic projects in the North Torgai and Shu-Sarysu sedimentary basins.

The program combines airborne geophysics, geochemical and laboratory studies, remote-sensing analysis, drilling and geophysical well logging. Its strategic value is to reduce geological uncertainty and improve the investment case for future mining projects.

From exploration to processing

The exploration program supports Kazakhstan’s strategic objective of moving beyond a predominantly raw-material economy.

At the Astana Mining & Metallurgy Congress 2026 on June 11, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said the country aims to develop deeper processing and competitive value-added production. Over the past two years, more than US$1 billion worth of higher-value mining and metallurgical facilities have been launched.

The approach places greater importance on geological data. David Fogel, assistant secretary of Commerce and Director General of the U.S. and Foreign Commercial Service, said at the congress that mapping and surveying are fundamental to reducing uncertainty and attracting investment.

“If you don’t map the resources and the geography properly, then you’re not going to be very efficient and you’re not going to be able to attract large-scale investment,” Fogel said, adding that artificial intelligence is already transforming geological analysis and surveying.

His remarks underline a key point for Kazakhstan: exploration is not only about identifying deposits, but also about producing the reliable data needed to mobilize large-scale capital.

Tungsten as a test case

The Northern Katpar and Upper Kairakty tungsten project illustrates this strategy.

The venture between U.S.-based Cove Capital and Kazakhstan’s Tau-Ken Samruk envisages a full production cycle covering mining, beneficiation and metallurgical processing in Kazakhstan. Cove Capital expects total investment requirements of at least US$1.1 billion, subject to completion of the definitive feasibility study and a final investment decision.

The planned output includes ammonium paratungstate (APT), a higher-value intermediate used to produce tungsten powders, tungsten carbide and other specialized materials.

Existing studies indicate potential combined production of around 12,000 tons of tungsten annually, although final capacity and project economics remain under assessment.

The project demonstrates the distinction between geological potential and commercial production. Kazakhstan’s ability to move projects from exploration and feasibility to financing and operations will determine whether its strategy generates sustained economic value.

International relevance

At AMM 2026, U.S. officials highlighted geological mapping as a way to reduce investment risks, while Saudi Arabia stressed the importance of integrated chains covering mining, processing, logistics and technology.

For Kazakhstan, exploration is therefore becoming the first stage of a wider industrial strategy.

The key indicators ahead will be commercially significant discoveries, progress toward feasibility studies and financing, and the development of processing capacity and supporting infrastructure.

The strategy’s success will ultimately depend not on the amount of territory surveyed, but on how effectively new discoveries are converted into mines, processing facilities and competitive products for global markets.

World.title: China’s Bid for an AI World Order: What’s Behind WAICO
World.content:
Trump locks Europe out of AI models; China presents the counter-proposal — a global AI platform, and everyone’s invited. What Beijing wants and why Europe remains skeptical.

By founding the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), China has created its own international framework for governing artificial intelligence — without the players that have traditionally shaped technology policy. For now.

The founding treaty was signed on July 16, in Shanghai by representatives from 29 countries, with UN Secretary-General António Guterres in attendance. The organization is headquartered in Shanghai. Founding members include Russia, Brazil, Indonesia, Pakistan, Malaysia, Kazakhstan, Kenya, South Africa, Serbia, Belarus, Cuba, Venezuela, and Zambia, among others. The United States, E.U. member states, and India are not participating.

In Chinese diplomatic circles, WAICO is described as a “major step” through which the People’s Republic is answering the Global South’s call for greater participation in AI development. The organization is meant to serve two purposes: spreading AI applications across the Global South and organizing training and seminar programs. The goal, Beijing says, is to use AI “for good.”

Four principles — and a jab at Washington

The conceptual framework rests on four principles that China’s leadership laid out at the first World AI Conference in Shanghai: openness and win-win cooperation, risk awareness, inclusivity, and solidarity in global governance.

Under win-win, Beijing groups scenario-based applications such as AI plus industry and AI plus health — in other words, integrating AI with existing economic sectors. AI must remain safe, reliable, and controllable, the argument goes. China says it is working on technical oversight, early-warning and emergency-response mechanisms, as well as laws, standards, and ethical guidelines. Misuse is to be prevented and AI kept under human control.

China rejects what it calls the overextension of national security — the principle of placing one country’s security above the interests of others. The target is clearly export controls and access restrictions.

Asked whether this language should be read as a response to the short-notice blocking of leading American models for European users, Beijing pointed out that Chinese models are open-source, rendering any accusation of bloc-building moot.

The fourth principle aims at multilateralism. Governance rules and technical standards should be coordinated internationally, and Global South countries should receive support in building their own capacities — to avoid, in China’s phrasing, new historical injustices.

What China is concretely offering

Over the next five years, China intends to provide 5,000 AI training slots for participants from Global South countries. Whether these are degree programs, scholarships, or short-term courses remains unclear. Plans also include AI cooperation centers with organizations such as ASEAN, the African Union, the Arab League, BRICS, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization. A flagship project is an AI-powered early-warning system that, according to Chinese sources, forecasts typhoons and other extreme weather events in more than 30 countries.

How China translates technological cooperation into concrete projects — across blocs and without exclusive commitments — is currently on display in Kazakhstan. In June, the Central Asian country agreed with the American firm Firebird on investments of up to ten billion dollars in a computing cluster with up to 100,000 Nvidia GPUs in the coal-mining city of Ekibastuz. A month later, on the sidelines of the AI summit in Shanghai, more than 70 contracts with Chinese partners worth a combined total of over $15 billion were signed. The cross-sector package includes, among other things, a partnership with Huawei, the acquisition of Huawei technology, and further expansion of the data-center site in cooperation with the Hengtong Group.

Open to all — including Europe?

From Beijing’s perspective, an upgrade to an official UN body is not ruled out; the organization is still in its early stages, they say. Nor is EU membership excluded. The organization is in principle open to all and is not aimed exclusively at the Global South.

Beijing dismisses the accusation that the aim is to carve out new spheres of influence. It is not building blocs, the argument goes; the basis of cooperation is consultation and mutual benefit.

Still, the connection to the Digital Silk Road is hard to miss. When it comes to overlaps with the digital component of the Belt and Road Initiative — in areas like digital services, health, and education — the answers remain vague. WAICO programs are described more as a complement to existing relationships.

The European Reading

Sources in Brussels security circles say WAICO is read less as a development initiative than as a strategic instrument. What matters is not the announced training slots or cooperation centers but the question of who will shape infrastructure, technical standards, and digital ecosystems in the years ahead. Countries that adopt Chinese models, networks, and processes early on could find themselves increasingly tied to providers and decision-making centers in Beijing or Shanghai over the long term.

Kazakhstan, however, shows that such cooperation does not necessarily lead to exclusive dependency. Astana is working simultaneously with American and Chinese partners, deploying Nvidia processors while also integrating Huawei and other Chinese providers into the expansion of its digital infrastructure. The government is deliberately keeping multiple technological pathways open rather than fully aligning with either of the two major blocs.

That is precisely what makes the example strategically significant: for many Global South countries, the issue is less about making a geopolitical statement than about accessing capital, computing power, and rapid implementation. The contract goes to whoever most convincingly bundles financing, technology, and infrastructure. For Europe, this is nonetheless a warning: future dependencies will not be determined solely by where systems originate, but above all by who delivers them first and operates them over the long haul.

The EU has been working since 2025 on implementing its concept for AI gigafactories — facilities each housing more than 100,000 advanced AI processors. For now, however, the focus in government offices is mainly on sites, financing, and procurement.

What stands out is the speed at which contracts are being signed and capacities built up elsewhere. Kazakhstan is simultaneously engaging American and Chinese technology companies, while Europe is still translating its own sovereign model into practice. The question is whether the planned pace will be fast enough to keep up with international developments.

In Brussels, digital sovereignty is thus moving to center stage. Europe wants to build its own computing capacity while avoiding long-term dependence on individual foreign providers for critical infrastructure.

Arindrajit Basu of the Carnegie Endowment describes WAICO as a state-centric model that primarily serves Chinese interests. Other Western analyses characterize WAICO as a counterpart to the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative. Participants or countries that have expressed interest in the American format include EU member states, Japan, Australia, and India.

Beijing courts Washington

Notably, Beijing is said to be open to cooperation with the United States. The two countries should extend their hands to each other, diplomatic circles say. AI is a global field, and its development must ultimately work for everyone.

When confronted with the objection that the U.S. administration does not currently appear inclined to cooperate, the response is puzzlement at Washington’s course — along with a reference to jointly supported UN resolutions. In Chinese publications, the line is stated more plainly: it is in the greatest shared interest of both nations that AI serve all of humanity. Following government consultations, a bilateral AI dialogue has also been agreed upon.

Beijing’s multilateral foundation is a UN General Assembly resolution on international AI capacity-building, adopted unanimously on July 1, 2024, which China had introduced. It calls for human-centered, inclusive, and sustainable AI development and special support for developing countries.

Building on that, China points to its own programs: the Global AI Governance Initiative of 2023, a 13-point action plan for global AI governance from 2025, and an AI Capacity-Building Action Plan for Good and for All.

The five-year plan as engine

Domestically, the push coincides with the launch of the 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026–2030. According to Chinese sources, an intelligent economic system is to be built; the core AI industry, diplomatic circles say, has already reached a volume of more than 1.2 trillion yuan.

AI is no longer anything special in China, the narrative goes — it is already widespread, from smart manufacturing to consumer devices. At the same time, laws, regulations, application guidelines, and ethical principles are being continuously developed to keep AI safe and controllable.

China also sees itself as a provider of international public goods, including through the release of open-source models.

Export controls, energy, exchange rates

One sore point in Europe that stands in the way of closer cooperation is China’s export controls on critical minerals needed for semiconductors, batteries, and other key technologies. Beijing rejects the claim that these have caused lasting supply problems, pointing to expedited approval procedures and general licenses for companies. The additional controls, however, are suspended only until No. 10. Whether the relaxations will be extended or stricter licensing requirements will resume afterward remains an open question.

Beijing also pushes back against the recent accusation by Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz that China is keeping the renminbi artificially low. Against the euro, the Chinese currency has in fact risen from around 8.27 to roughly 7.71 yuan per euro since late October — an appreciation of a good seven percent.

The latest currency report from the U.S. Treasury Department, dated July 23, also does not classify China as a currency manipulator. Due to a lack of transparency in its exchange-rate policy, however, the country remains on the U.S. monitoring list. Europe’s criticism of China’s trade surpluses, subsidies, and state-led industrial policy is far from settled.

Despite Merz’s sweeping announcements about resuming German-Chinese government consultations, no date has been set so far. The chancellor had indicated a meeting would take place this year, or early 2027 at the latest. There is, as they say, plenty to discuss.

The author is Alexander Dergay, the founder and managing partner of Orbis Nova, a research and analysis firm. Dergay is also cooperating with geopolitical foresight agency Nightingale Int. He worked for several years as an adviser and analyst specializing in geostrategic risk before serving as an foreign policy editor at the Berliner Zeitung and the Ostdeutsche Allgemeine Zeitung, Germany.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Scholars Call for Broader View of Golden Horde’s Legacy
World.content:
ASTANA – Three historians from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and the Republic of Tatarstan in Russia explored how the Golden Horde continues to shape the historical narratives and identities of their countries during a podcast organized by Kazakh historian and Golden Horde researcher Zhaksylyk Sabitov.

The discussion highlighted both the shared historical legacy of the medieval empire and the distinct national perspectives that have emerged across Central Asia and the Volga Region.

According to Damir Iskhakov, an ethnologist and researcher of Tatar ethnogenesis at the Marjani Institute of History in Kazan, perceptions of the Golden Horde have changed significantly in recent decades.

“There was a time when many Kazakhs believed their origins lay primarily with the Kipchaks or other earlier peoples rather than the Golden Horde. Today, historical evidence and the composition of Kazakh clans clearly demonstrate a direct connection with the Golden Horde,” he said.

He added that growing scholarly interest has strengthened understanding of the Golden Horde’s contribution to the formation of the Kazakh nation.

Gaibulla Babayarov, a specialist in ancient Turkic epigraphy and numismatics at the Institute of Oriental Studies in Tashkent, noted that bringing together experts from different countries enriches understanding of the Golden Horde.

“Each country has its own unique perspective, which makes discussions like this especially valuable,” Babayarov said.

Babayarov highlighted that the Golden Horde is often mistakenly viewed as unrelated to Uzbekistan’s history.

“In reality, the Golden Horde period played an important role in the ethnogenesis of the Uzbek people,” he said.

While most of present-day Uzbekistan belonged to the Chagatai Ulus, the country’s northwestern territories, particularly Northern Khorezm, were part of the Golden Horde. Many Uzbek clans originated in the Dasht-i Kipchak, with Babayarov estimating that nearly half of traditional Uzbek tribal groups trace their roots to that region.

“For this reason, the histories of the Golden Horde and the Chagatai Ulus should be studied together rather than separately. They share common roots and represent a shared historical heritage,” he said.

Clan system united Turkic peoples

The discussion also focused on the Golden Horde’s clan structure.

Iskhakov described the subject as one of the least studied areas of medieval history because of the limited number of surviving historical sources.

“One of our main tasks today is to trace how a relatively small number of original clans, perhaps 12 or 14, eventually evolved into the much larger clan system described in the Edige epic, which refers to the ‘Ninety-Clan Horde.’ What is remarkable is that many of these clans can still be traced among various Turkic peoples,” Iskhakov said.

He also noted that the Golden Horde was organized through a strict hierarchy of clans. The ruling dynasty was closely connected through marriage alliances with the leading emir families that helped govern the state.

Babayarov added that Soviet-era scholarship often overlooked clan history in Uzbekistan because Uzbeks were portrayed primarily as a settled people rather than a society with strong tribal traditions.

He noted that ethnonyms and clan names remain preserved in village names across much of Uzbekistan, particularly in the Samarkand, Kashkadarya and Surkhandarya regions.

Balancing genetics and history

Sabitov urged caution when interpreting genetic research in historical studies.

“Genetics is an important research tool, but it should not be used to determine who is or is not a ‘real’ representative of an ethnic group,” he said.

He noted that genetic studies often produce various conclusions depending on the questions researchers ask.

“If you search for similarities among Turkic peoples, you will find similarities. If you search for differences, you will find differences. Ethnicity cannot be reduced to DNA,” he said.

Iskhakov agreed, saying genetics is useful for tracing family relationships over several centuries but becomes much less reliable when applied to medieval populations.

“Ethnic identity is shaped primarily by shared historical memory, language and culture. Genetics represents only one small part of that much larger picture,” Iskhakov said.

Revisiting Tatar history

Iskhakov also recalled how Soviet historiography largely excluded the Golden Horde from the history of the Tatars.

He said that during the Stalin era, official scholarship promoted the theory that modern Tatars descended exclusively from the Volga Bulgars. While the Golden Horde was portrayed as unrelated to Tatar history.

Only after the collapse of the Soviet Union did historians begin integrating the Golden Horde into mainstream interpretations of Tatar ethnogenesis.

“Today, the Golden Horde occupies its rightful place in the multi-volume history of the Tatar people. We now recognize the contributions of the ancient Turks, the Bulgar period, the Kipchaks and the Golden Horde as equally important stages in our shared history,” Iskhakov said.

World.title: Archaeological Discoveries Across Kazakhstan Shed New Light on Medieval Life
World.content:
ASTANA – A series of recent archaeological discoveries across Kazakhstan is offering new insights into the history, culture and everyday life of communities that lived on the Great Steppe centuries ago.

Findings from archaeological sites in the Zhambyl, Turkistan and Pavlodar regions include medieval buildings, a mosque and paved streets, valuable artefacts and a remarkably preserved mobile dwelling associated with the Kimak-Kipchak period (9th-10th centuries). Together, the discoveries highlight the diversity of life in the medieval steppe and the region’s links with neighbouring civilisations.

Archaeologists working at the Akzhar settlement in Zhambyl Region have uncovered remains of structures dating to the 11th–12th centuries. The medieval settlement is located west of the Kurenbel village in the Zhualy district, between tributaries of the Akzhar River.

The excavations revealed structures made of mud brick, along with fragments of ceramics, iron and glass objects, stone tools and bones of domestic animals, reported the region’s Culture and Language Development Department. Researchers say the findings can help reconstruct the daily life of the people who inhabited the settlement during different periods.

The animal remains are of particular interest to researchers, as their study could provide information about the diet, economy and lifestyle of the settlement’s residents.

The excavations are being carried out as part of a scientific program studying the Syr Darya and Karatau regions in antiquity and the Middle Ages. Researchers expect the findings to help clarify Akzhar’s role in the development of medieval urban culture in the Karatau region.

Further south, archaeological work at the Otyrar settlement in the Turkistan Region has revealed several layers of historical development dating 13th-18th centuries.

Researchers identified five construction horizons containing residential and household areas, brick-paved streets and kilns used for firing bricks. One of the most notable discoveries was a collective burial site, known as a dakhma, identified for the first time at Otyrar.

At the lowest, fifth construction horizon, archaeologists uncovered the remains of a mosque dating to the Golden Horde period. A street paved with large stones led to the building and connected to a staircase made of fired bricks. According to the researchers, a paved street of this scale had not previously been documented at Otyrar.

The excavations also revealed painted window grilles, parts of inkpots, door or gate fittings, Chinese-style ceramic fragments, Chinese coins and coins minted in the names of rulers of the Golden Horde, a powerful state that dominated much of the Eurasian steppe from the 13th to 15th centuries.

One particularly notable discovery was a ring bearing an inscription, which researchers believe may have served as a seal in the medieval period.

The archaeological evidence points to Otyrar’s extensive connections with other parts of the region. Similar materials have been found at sites associated with Sogdiana, Tashkent, Fergana and Zhetysu, while imported objects and coins indicate the city’s participation in wider trade and cultural networks.

Researchers also believe the newly uncovered street could help reconstruct the layout of medieval Otyrar and identify commercial and public spaces that once stood along it. The excavations at the Otyrar settlement were conducted by a team led by Mukhtar Kozha, a professor and chief researcher at the Institute of Archaeology of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi International Kazakh-Turkish University.

In the Pavlodar Region, archaeologists have uncovered what researchers describe as an exceptionally rare example of a mobile dwelling from the Kimak-Kipchak period, reported the region’s press office.

The discovery was made at the Baidala burial ground in the Kenzhekol rural district of Pavlodar. The site is considered one of the significant archaeological monuments associated with the era of the Kimak Khaganate. According to researchers, the area may correspond to Imakia, described as a political center of the Kimak Khaganate, a medieval state or tribal confederation that existed roughly from the 9th to the early 11th century in what is now northeastern and central Kazakhstan and parts of western Siberia.

The most significant discovery is a fully preserved mobile dwelling consisting of a wooden wheeled structure with a tent-like covering. Archaeologists said its construction is similar to that of the traditional Kazakh yurt and that the discovery appears to be unprecedented in the archaeological record of the Eurasian steppe.

The dwelling was accompanied by a wooden saddle, stirrups, a bit, weapons, jewellery, silk textiles and other artefacts. These objects provide additional evidence about the material culture and everyday life of medieval nomadic communities. Before the discovery, knowledge about similar mobile dwellings largely came from written sources and schematic depictions.

Archaeological research at Baidala has been conducted for more than two decades led by archaeologist Timur Smagulov. Further excavations, conservation and restoration of the finds are planned, along with proposals to turn the complex into a museum site and develop it as an important historical and cultural heritage attraction.

The remains of buildings and streets reveal the organization of settled communities and their urban infrastructure, while the mobile dwelling offers a rare physical representation of nomadic life. Artefacts from Otyrar, meanwhile, point to the movement of goods, technologies and cultural influences across Central Asia and beyond.

For archaeologists, such discoveries are more than isolated objects or structures. They provide pieces of evidence that can be combined to reconstruct how people lived, travelled, traded and interacted across the Great Steppe.

While excavations and conservation work continue, researchers expect further discoveries to contribute to a more detailed understanding of Kazakhstan’s medieval heritage and its place in the broader history of Eurasia.

World.title: Former Georgian PM Irakli Garibashvili accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail
World.content:
Former PM accuses Ivanishvili of blackmail

Jailed former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili has accused Georgian Dream honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili and the current government of blackmail.

In a statement released from prison on 17 August 2026, the former prime minister claimed he was being pressured to plead guilty to new corruption charges and permanently withdraw from politics at Ivanishvili’s demand. It is the first time that a former close ally of Ivanishvili has openly spoken out against the founder of the ruling party.

Plea deal ultimatum and plan to quit politics

A photograph of a printed letter dated 17 August was posted on the Facebook pages of Garibashvili and his wife, Nunuka Tamazashvili. Only four paragraphs of the letter were made public. It is unclear who wrote the letter or how it was delivered.

According to the published document, the government is offering the former prime minister a compromise. Under the proposed terms, Garibashvili would have to plead guilty to a new corruption-related charge.

The letter sets out the proposal in detail:

“They are offering me the option of pleading guilty in one case, where everything would be arranged by agreement, including a confession, witness signatures and so on. They are offering a plea bargain while retaining the same five-year sentence: that is, as it has been explained to me, the sentences would be combined, but the final term would remain five years.”

According to the document, a corruption conviction would serve as a form of “insurance” for the government, aimed at preventing the former prime minister from returning to politics in the future.

Two options and a political condition

The published letter refers to investigations into several cases. Its author suggests that these could result in corruption charges.

The text outlines two possible courses of action for Garibashvili. The first would involve continuing to contest the case in court.

“Let’s discuss this seriously and see it through to the end,” the document says.

The second option is presented as a compromise. According to the letter, Garibashvili would plead guilty in one of the cases, with the details agreed in advance:

“Let’s plead guilty in one case, where everything will be arranged by agreement: a confession, witness signatures and so on.”

The document also says that a new plea deal would not increase the five-year prison sentence already imposed on Garibashvili. The sentences would be combined, leaving the overall term unchanged at five years.

However, the proposal comes with a political condition.

“After leaving, you cannot engage in politics. If it is decided to ‘renege on the agreements’, then the corruption charges that will be brought will serve as an insurance mechanism, preventing even the thought of returning to politics,” the document says.

The authenticity of the letter has not been independently verified, and its author remains unknown. There is also no confirmation that new cases are in fact being prepared against Garibashvili.

Garibashvili’s first open confrontation with Ivanishvili

This marks Irakli Garibashvili’s first public confrontation with Bidzina Ivanishvili. For many years, Garibashvili was regarded as one of his most loyal political allies.

He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister, first from 2013 to 2015 and again from 2021 to 2024.

Garibashvili was sentenced under a plea agreement reached on 12 January 2026. He was given a five-year prison term and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated from him.

The case concerned the laundering of illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. Garibashvili is currently serving his sentence in a prison in Rustavi.

The new statement means that the former prime minister himself is now linking possible further legal action against him to demands that he stay out of politics. However, the material made public so far presents only Garibashvili’s version of events.

Response from MP Irma Inashvili, named in letter

The letter published by Garibashvili mentions MP Irma Inashvili and Dito Chubinidze. According to the text, they — along with “supporters like them” and campaigns on social media — have raised suspicions.

“Supporters such as Dito Chubinidze and Irma Inashvili, as well as campaigns organised on social media, have raised very serious suspicions and caused us tangible harm,” the document says.

Inashvili denied any involvement in organised campaigns. She said Irakli Garibashvili was her friend, but that she expressed her views publicly and independently.

“I have never planned or conducted any campaigns on social media; I don’t need such campaigns — I already express my views openly in my own name!” Inashvili wrote.

She said Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze was the main target of her criticism.

“I expose Kobakhidze and fight against him,” Inashvili said.

Opposition says Garibashvili being politically neutralised

Opposition figures have described Garibashvili’s letter as a sign of an internal conflict within the government. Their comments amount to political assessments and do not independently corroborate the circumstances described in the letter.

Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change, said the contents of the letter pointed to a political motive behind Garibashvili’s imprisonment.

“Ivanishvili’s bargaining with Garibashvili — ‘I will punish you even more severely unless you give me guarantees that you will leave politics for good’ — confirms that the motive for his arrest is neither to punish a corrupt official nor to fight corruption in general, nor does it serve any public or state interest. It serves Bidzina’s personal political interests,” Gvaramia wrote.

He also qualified his comments by noting that the authenticity of the letter had not been established. Gvaramia particularly highlighted what he described as an attempt to politically neutralise Garibashvili.

Levan Samushia, a member of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, linked the statement to the country’s current system of governance. He said any potential threat against Garibashvili’s family warranted a legal response.

“It is clear that Garibashvili is speaking about a possible, alleged threat to his family. This is an issue that requires particular attention and, naturally, provides grounds for launching an investigation,” Samushia said.

Berdia Sichinava, a representative of the Gakharia for Georgia party, said he preferred to wait for further information before reaching a definitive conclusion. Nevertheless, he linked the developments to an internal conflict within Georgian Dream.

“The situation appears alarming because it concerns his family, and at this point clarity is the best means of protecting him and his loved ones,” Sichinava said.

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the United National Movement, described Garibashvili’s case as a warning to current government figures.

“Garibashvili’s case should be learnt by heart by Ivanishvili’s current servants, officials and representatives of the financial sector who justify the government,” Dekanoidze wrote.

Government silent as questions remain unanswered

At the time of writing, reports about Garibashvili’s allegations had not appeared on the websites or Facebook pages of the pro-government Imedi and Rustavi 2 television channels.

Government representatives have yet to respond publicly to the central allegation. They have not said whether Bidzina Ivanishvili had any involvement in sending the letter to Garibashvili. It also remains unclear whether any new investigations into the former prime minister are under way.

Background: From alliance to prison

For many years, Irakli Garibashvili was regarded as one of Bidzina Ivanishvili’s closest political allies. He served twice as Georgia’s prime minister.

On 24 October 2025, Garibashvili was charged with laundering illicit proceeds on an especially large scale. A plea agreement was reached on 12 January 2026, under which the former prime minister was sentenced to five years in prison and fined one million lari. Two cars and $6.5m were also confiscated. He has since been serving his sentence at a penitentiary facility in Rustavi.

Legal proceedings against former senior figures in the ruling team were preceded by internal party disagreements and arrests of officials from various state agencies. There have also been reports of investigative measures involving members of Garibashvili’s family.

The developments suggest that the power struggle within Georgian Dream has entered an increasingly acute phase.

World.title: Georgia does not join EU’s updated sanctions against Iran
World.content:
Georgia did not join EU sanctions against Iran

Georgia did not join the EU partner countries that backed the bloc’s updated sanctions against Iran. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the measures involve three decisions imposing restrictions on Iran.

What are the decisions?

The EU has amended its sanctions regime against Iran. It removed and added several individuals and updated information on one organisation. All other restrictions remain in force.

The EU also adopted a decision on Iran’s military support for armed groups operating in Russia, the Middle East and the Red Sea region. The EU extended the existing sanctions and removed four individuals from the list.

In another decision, the EU added six individuals to its sanctions list over human rights violations in Iran.

The countries of the European Economic Area — Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway — joined the EU measures. So did EU candidate countries Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Ukraine.

Georgia did not join them.

Georgian Dream’s position

Georgian Dream MP Tengiz Sharmanashvili said Georgia only joins international decisions when they serve the country’s interests.

“The question of whether Georgia joins a resolution or takes steps in international affairs is determined by one criterion alone: whether it serves the country’s interests at that particular moment,” he said.

Sharmanashvili noted that two other EU candidate countries, Turkey and Serbia, had also not joined the sanctions against Iran.

“If it goes against Georgia’s interests, we do not care whose interests it serves,” the MP stressed.

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry has not yet responded to a request from Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty to explain why the country did not join the EU sanctions.

The EU’s enlargement reports have already noted Georgia’s limited alignment with the bloc’s foreign policy. According to the 2025 report, Georgia’s alignment with the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy had fallen to 40% by October 2025, down from 53% in 2024.

Georgia did not join EU sanctions against Iran

World.title: Geostat: Foreign investment in Georgia reached $1.9bn in 2025
World.content:
Foreign investment in Georgia

Foreign direct investment in Georgia reached $1.9 billion in 2025, up 19.3% from the previous year, the National Statistics Office of Georgia said.

Geostat revised last year’s figures and recalculated foreign direct investment data from 2021 onwards. According to the revised figures, reinvestment accounted for most of the increase in 2025, making up 82.5% of total investment.

The UK became the largest investor in Georgia’s economy, investing $426.6 million during the year. Azerbaijan and Turkey followed.

The three countries accounted for more than 44% of total foreign direct investment.

Financial and insurance activities attracted the largest share of investment, with more than $633 million invested in the sector. Real estate and trade followed.

According to Geostat, these sectors together accounted for more than half of all foreign direct investment in Georgia in 2025.

World.title: Peaceful return of Abkhazia: opposition leader Nika Gvaramia’s vision for Georgia’s policy
World.content:
Peaceful return of Abkhazia to Georgia

The Abkhaz conflict could be resolved not through war or discussions about the past, but through Georgia‘s European integration, economic development and shared security interests. Opposition politician Nika Gvaramia made the remarks in an interview with Formula television.

Gvaramia believes Georgia must overcome the trauma left by the war. At the same time, the country should become an attractive political and economic space for Abkhaz people.

He identifies EU membership, the development of the Anaklia port and a stronger Georgian role in the “Middle Corridor” as key elements of this strategy.

Gvaramia’s interview has already sparked public debate. Many viewers believe the politician moved beyond traditional rhetoric and proposed a rational and pragmatic approach to resolving the conflict, something rarely seen in Georgia’s political arena.

Personal memories of Sukhumi and Abkhazia’s strategic importance

Nika Gvaramia was 16 when he left Sukhumi. In an interview, he said he had lived in Tbilisi twice as long as he had lived in Sukhumi. Nevertheless, he still considers Sukhumi his home city.

For him, Abkhazia is both his homeland and a territory of particular strategic importance to Georgia. Gvaramia does not view the issue solely from the perspective of a displaced person.

He says Abkhazia’s geographical location, access to the Black Sea and economic potential distinguish this conflict from other conflicts in the post-Soviet space.

At the same time, he believes the 2008 war also demonstrated the strategic importance of the Tskhinvali region. The blockade of the country’s main transport route from that territory split Georgia in two and threatened links between the country’s eastern and western regions.

Nika Gvaramia

Gvaramia says that his experiences during the war and forced displacement made it difficult for him to look at the Abkhaz issue without emotion for a long time. He also recalls evidence of crimes committed in Abkhazia that he encountered while working at the prosecutor’s office.

However, he says that in recent years he has concluded that an approach based solely on trauma makes finding a solution impossible:

“Trauma is very important, it is part of historical memory… But traumatic memories are dangerous: they carry a threat, they act like a noose — they prevent us from moving forward and block development.”

Trauma, fear of war and government rhetoric

According to Gvaramia, Georgian Dream has turned the public trauma of war into a constant source of fear. As a result, the goal of restoring territorial integrity has given way to the attitude of “as long as there is no war”.

He said that for many years he himself approached the Abkhaz issue from a position of anger and intransigence. He considered dialogue with Abkhaz people impossible and saw the use of force as the solution. Later, he concluded that this approach was harmful to the country.

“Unfortunately, the actions of Georgian Dream have not led to the position that ‘this is my country, and I will fight to the end’. Instead, they have created the attitude: ‘I do not want war; there must be no war.'”

Gvaramia considers the desire to avoid war natural. People in Georgia have direct experience of the 2008 conflict: they watched the bombing of cities, the deaths of people and bombs falling on their country on live television.

However, he believes the problem arises when the government uses this experience as a tool of political control. Constant reminders of the threat of another war push people towards inaction instead of encouraging them to seek a solution to the problem.

In his view, Georgian society wants Abkhazia back, but not at the cost of war. Gvaramia believes politicians should take both sentiments into account at the same time.

“If we want to work with these people and consider ourselves politicians, we must understand that they also care about Abkhazia’s future, but they do not want war.”

According to Gvaramia, a military solution is unacceptable today not only because of public opinion. Georgia does not have the resources needed for such an approach, so statements about war that lack a realistic assessment of the country’s capabilities cannot form the basis of a responsible political plan.

He notes that the younger generation is gradually losing its emotional connection with Abkhazia and calls this one of the main challenges:

“Essentially, if we lose Abkhazia from our memory, that will also mean a real loss of the territory.”

In his view, over time, memories of the past alone will not be enough to preserve the idea of territorial integrity.

Pashinyan’s example and overcoming trauma

Gvaramia cites Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan as an example of a leader who managed to overcome the burden of traumatic historical memory. In his view, Pashinyan tried to separate the state’s future from historical and territorial claims.

In this context, Gvaramia discusses Armenia’s changing approach to issues related to Mount Ararat and Karabakh.

He believes the aim of this policy was to free Armenia from Russian influence and create new economic opportunities for the country:

“Such changes take decades, but Pashinyan achieved them in a very short time. He removed the image of Ararat from the official seal and said that it is part of our history, but not part of our geography.

If we want problems with Turkey, then yes, let’s continue depicting Ararat, but then we will remain poor and dependent on Russia. If we do not want that, then let’s reach an agreement and remove Ararat from the seal, because it is not actually in our territory.

Then our relations with both Turkey and Azerbaijan will improve. We will have more money, gain the prospect of moving towards the European Union and no longer be tied to Russia.”

At the same time, Gvaramia stresses the legal difference between Abkhazia and Karabakh. He notes that the international community recognises Abkhazia as Georgian territory, while Karabakh was not recognised as part of Armenia.

But for him, the main issue is not the status of these territories, but the political influence of traumatic memories and the possibility of breaking free from their grip.

The European Union as a magnet for Abkhazia

According to Gvaramia, the first step towards rapprochement with Abkhaz people should rest on mutual needs rather than rhetoric about mutual love. He believes such appeals do not reflect the reality that has emerged since the war, and that the truth is that Abkhaz and Georgian people do not feel affection for each other today:

“We are lying when we say that we are brothers… We do not love each other now; we cannot love people who kill our neighbours. But we should think about the fact that, at this moment, we need each other from a pragmatic point of view.”

At the same time, Gvaramia stresses that Abkhaz people do not have warm feelings towards Russians either:

“Abkhaz people are not a nation that loves Russians, and they never have been. There is a perfectly rational reason for that. Russians consider them second-class people, while Georgians do not — and Abkhaz people feel this very clearly.”

Gvaramia envisions a Georgia that has joined the EU as an attractive country for Abkhaz people. Such a state would offer access to European passports, freedom of movement, a developed economy and institutional guarantees protecting minority rights.

In his view, EU involvement would also create financial opportunities for rebuilding Abkhazia. Security guarantees, meanwhile, would come not from a Russian military presence but from international and European institutions.

Under this model, Abkhaz people should not become second-class citizens of Georgia. They should have full political and civil rights:

“We are offering Abkhaz people a good life — and is there any Abkhaz person who would refuse a good life? But we are not offering it at the cost of turning them into second-class people. No, they must be full citizens of Georgia.”

Gvaramia believes Georgians and Abkhaz people will need several decades to become accustomed to each other again. At the initial stage, mutually beneficial economic cooperation could form the basis of their relations.

Anaklia and the Middle Corridor

A key element of Gvaramia’s strategy is the deep-water port of Anaklia. He sees Anaklia as a potential economic “magnet” for Abkhazia.

Under his plan, Georgia should become an important link in the Middle Corridor, connecting Central Asia with the Black Sea. The route would connect Europe with the markets and resources of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and other countries in the region.

Gvaramia places particular emphasis on rare earth metals and lithium. In his view, the importance of these resources is growing, while Central Asian countries need an alternative route to Western markets because existing routes depend on Russia, China or Iran.

“The main thing for me is EU membership and developing the Middle Corridor. I use this word deliberately — development. We need to develop this route.”

In his view, Georgia should build the Anaklia port with Western capital, while American, British and European organisations should take part in its management. In that case, the port would become more than just an economic asset and could provide an additional security guarantee for Georgia:

“Nothing receives stronger protection from the Western world than property: not international treaties, not security commitments, not the charters of any alliances. No, property enjoys the greatest protection in any Western society.”

Gvaramia also believes Anaklia needs a democratic system of governance to develop. A major international investor will not pursue a long-term project in conditions of corruption and a lack of transparency.

That is why, in his view, a Western investor sees the port’s construction, European integration, democratisation and restoration of territorial integrity as parts of a single strategy.

Gvaramia believes the port of Ochamchire could also become part of this economic space in the future. This would make cooperation with Georgia serve Abkhazia’s economic interests.

Limits of compromise and a governance model

In the interview, Gvaramia says resolving the conflict will require concessions from both sides. However, he does not propose a specific model for future political governance.

The discussion touched on the experiences of Lebanon, Bosnia, Northern Ireland and Cyprus. Some of these examples show that allocating government positions and powers along ethnic lines can make state institutions ineffective.

Gvaramia does not rule out an agreement covering Abkhazia’s special legal status, the distribution of political powers, the return of displaced people and property issues:

“Reconciliation is impossible without concessions.”

At the same time, he noted that Georgia is a state recognised under international law. Therefore, creating a new state “from scratch” should not become a necessary condition for resolving the conflict.

Gvaramia sees the European Union as the key foundation for a possible agreement. In his view, the EU accession process could provide security guarantees for Abkhaz people while preserving the principle of Georgia’s territorial integrity.

Enguri HPP: cryptocurrency mining and corruption allegations

In the final part of the interview, Gvaramia discussed electricity supplies and cryptocurrency mining in Abkhazia. He made serious corruption allegations against the government and Bidzina Ivanishvili personally.

According to Gvaramia, a significant share of the electricity generated by the Enguri HPP goes to Abkhazia free of charge. However, he says a substantial portion of this resource goes not to meet people’s needs but to power cryptocurrency mining farms:

“They supply them with twice as much electricity as they need, yet they still face shortages. It is astonishing. Why? Because this electricity goes to crypto farms — to the ability to make money literally out of thin air.”

He alleges that this scheme benefits groups operating in Abkhazia’s de facto authorities, Russian interests and people linked to the Georgian government.

He also criticised possible fuel supplies to Abkhazia from Georgian-controlled territory. According to Gvaramia, it remains unclear how such shipments are documented, who pays for them and where exactly the fuel goes.

In his assessment, there is a risk that the fuel could serve the needs of Russian military infrastructure in Abkhazia. Gvaramia also considers the issue in the context of Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Tamta Mikeladze’s assessment: an important vision and unanswered questions

Tamta Mikeladze, head of the Centre for Social Justice, described the interview as an expression of a rational and pragmatic political vision. She said Gvaramia had moved beyond established political rhetoric on Abkhazia and linked the issue of territorial integrity to the country’s development strategy.

Mikeladze particularly highlights his comments on overcoming traumatic memories, rejecting the false choice between war and capitulation, the European Union’s appeal and the possible role of the Anaklia port in strengthening security.

In her view, an important part of the interview is the challenge it sets for the opposition: alongside criticising the government, it should offer the country a comprehensive alternative project.

Tamta Mikeladze

However, Mikeladze sees several problems with Gvaramia’s approach. The first is the possible overemphasis on economic interests.

She notes that in ethno-political conflicts, economic benefits do not always outweigh fears of losing one’s identity, nationalist narratives and the idea of independence.

Therefore, Tbilisi should offer solutions on protecting Abkhaz identity, language and political autonomy. A promise of prosperity alone will not be enough.

The second issue is the Russian factor. According to Mikeladze, Gvaramia’s model relies heavily on a weakening of Russia.

It remains unclear what would happen if Moscow maintained its influence and military bases in the region. Under such circumstances, economic appeal cannot replace alternative security guarantees.

The third issue concerns efforts to overcome trauma. Mikeladze notes that Pashinyan’s approach has caused serious divisions within Armenia.

Some sections of society see his policies not as overcoming trauma but as a national defeat. Such changes therefore require long-term democratic, social and cultural work with communities affected by the conflict.

The fourth issue concerns the model for sharing power. According to Mikeladze, this aspect has often undermined previous peacebuilding efforts. The political status of Abkhazia, its representation and the distribution of powers are therefore far from secondary details.

Despite these questions, Mikeladze considers the interview an important basis for public debate. She believes other politicians should also offer democratic, future-oriented alternatives rather than build their positions around the traumas and confrontation of the past.

She also calls on the media to exercise caution. According to Mikeladze, if Georgian Dream uses territorial integrity to justify political or economic interests, the opposition should provide a well-grounded response.

Mikeladze’s main message is that the debate on Abkhazia should no longer focus solely on memories of war, mutual accusations and general calls for reconciliation.

Public policy should answer difficult questions: how will Abkhaz identity be protected, who will guarantee security, how will power be shared, and under what conditions can a common political space be created?

Peaceful return of Abkhazia to Georgia

World.title: The future of Abkhazia: from preserving the language to building a civic nation. View from Abkhazia, video discussion
World.content:
Abkhaz language and civic nation

The editor of the newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, Inal Khashig, and political scientist Astamur Tania discuss the challenges and state policy regarding the Abkhazian language, the shift in historical narratives surrounding the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, as well as the necessity of building an inclusive civic nation for the sustainable future of Abkhazia.

Main theses and arguments:

Preservation and Development of the Abkhaz Language — The language issue is viewed as the foundation of national identity, requiring not merely electoral campaigns, but a long-term state program encompassing education, ideology, and administrative measures. Overcoming Formalism in Language Policy — Existing legislative initiatives and laws (such as the 2007 law) face implementation problems; there is a risk that successive delays and amendments will boil down to a formalistic approach without real results. Balance Between the State Language and Interethnic Harmony — Grace periods for non-Abkhaz citizens to master the Abkhazian language are aimed at preventing discrimination and fostering a unified civic platform under conditions of inevitable bilingualism (Abkhaz and Russian). Countering Historical Revisionism — Attempts to rewrite the history of the conflict are observed in the Georgian information space (including the promotion of the pseudoscientific “Ingorokva theory” and the interpretation of the 1992 war exclusively as Russian aggression), which relieves Georgia of responsibility and hinders a peaceful settlement. Abkhazia’s Agency and the Reduction of Hate Speech — Abkhazia emphasizes its status as an established nation and an active subject of relations; both sides acknowledge the destructiveness of “hate speech” in the media, as a resumption of the conflict would be catastrophic for everyone. Formation of a Civic Nation and the Rule of Law — The key challenge is the transition from ethnic self-awareness to an inclusive civic nation that unites all ethnic groups in Abkhazia on the basis of shared values, legal order, security, and consensus.

Inal Khashig: Hello, Chegemskaya Pravda is on the air. Today, we are going to speak again about the very same topics that concern our Abkhaz society. This prolonged discussion regarding the Abkhaz language, the standards of proficiency in this language, the state language for members of parliament. At the parliamentary hearings, the parliamentary committee rejected – that is, did not recommend – the draft constitutional amendments proposed by the president.
