Australia, meanwhile, has only just begun its descent. Sydney and Melbourne have been in decline for several months, while, at a national level, the trend has turned negative as growth in even the tearaway cities like Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide has evaporated.

Rolling 28-day change in dwelling values, as at August 10, 2026. (Supplied: Cotality)

Research group Cotality argues that the sustained growth we've experienced over the past five years has left Australian households with enough reserves to weather a storm.

But what made Australia different to its Pacific neighbours?

The obvious contrast was in interest rate policy.

New Zealand's housing market, including Auckland, is experiencing a prolonged downturn. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Both New Zealand and Canada hiked interest rates far more dramatically than Australia, curbing demand for housing finance from 2022 onwards. Unemployment was also far higher than here.

Immigration also played a major role. Australia has maintained levels of arrivals that far outweighed dwelling construction ever since the pandemic — ensuring shortages — while Canada imposed heavy restrictions to limit arrivals, including students.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

In New Zealand, net migration came to a standstill as the country's high unemployment rate prompted an exodus of Kiwi workers across the Tasman to take advantage of a more buoyant economy.

Meanwhile in Canberra, the immigration debate is only just beginning.

It is playing out as buyers have already begun a retreat from Australian real estate, sparked by interest rate hikes and a fundamental shift in tax policy as incentives for investors have been wound back.

Diverging paths

Australian housing may be among the world's most expensive, but New Zealand and Canada did their best trying to catch up after the global financial crisis.

From 2010 onwards, New Zealand real estate surged an incredible 164 per cent until it peaked in early 2022.

New Zealand's real estate marked peaked in early 2022. (Reuters: Lucy Craymer)

That's after accounting for inflation. In nominal terms, the price movements were even more extreme but, when comparing different countries, stripping out inflation provides a more accurate reflection.

Residential property prices for New Zealand. (Supplied: Federal Reserve St Louis, Bank for International Settlements)

Canada experienced a similar surge, up about 150 per cent.

Will the RBA blink on inflation? Deflating a property bubble takes some skill, something that has escaped almost every government or central bank that has ever attempted it.

On this side of the ditch, our property prices, while coming off a higher base, rose just 40 per cent after inflation over the same period.

But after the invasion of Ukraine, our paths diverged quite radically. Canada and New Zealand began a long slide into property losses.

Canadian housing prices have shed about 20 per cent since then, while the Kiwis have dropped close to 30 per cent once inflation is included, in one of the longest property market downturns in its history.

Buyers have already begun a retreat from Australian real estate. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Australian real estate, on the other hand, began a gentle U-turn in 2023, even as interest rates were being pushed higher, accelerating back towards record levels as rates were cut last year.

But that is about to change.

Loading

Why the difference?

Interest rates played a major role.

The New Zealand Reserve Bank set a blistering pace in its quest to kill inflation, sending the official cash rate to 5.5 per cent, way above its Australian counterpart, which restrained interest rate hikes with a 4.35 per cent peak.

The Bank of Canada pushed interest rates far higher than Australia's too, pushing its official rate to 5 per cent.

And that played through into the broader economy.

Canada's economy has been hit hard by US tariffs, adding to its woes. (Reuters: Carlos Osorio)

New Zealand retreated into recession several times as the rate hikes stifled growth. Unemployment, meanwhile, only avoided surging to embarrassing levels because of the number of Kiwis who fled the country.

While the country's population has grown since 2022, a large number of residents, many of whom are younger and highly educated, left for higher-paid positions in Australia.

That has helped take pressure off the housing market.

Australia's housing supply hasn't kept pace with demand. (ABC News: Liana Walker)

Meanwhile in Canada, the unemployment rate climbed to 7 per cent in 2023 and since then the economy has been hit hard by the imposition of US tariffs under the Trump administration.

In some cities, including Toronto, unemployment has surged to 9 per cent, dampening demand for housing and accelerating declines.

Negative wealth and population

In New Zealand and Canada, the housing downturn is beginning to ricochet through the broader economy, highlighting the challenges the RBA and the federal government may face in the near future.

Household spending is restrained, and retailers are struggling in both countries, hindering efforts to revive economic growth.

Australia's economy is already sluggish, with growth expected to come in at less than 2 per cent this year, giving the RBA little wriggle room to use interest rates to keep inflation in check.

Michele Bullock never raised interest rates as high as in New Zealand or Canada. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

A string of retailers has shut in the past 12 months, and even market darlings like JB Hi-Fi have been under fire from investors as difficult trading conditions are expected to weigh on performance.

Given the extent to which property is ingrained into the Australian psyche, the political blowback from an extended downturn is likely to gather pace.

The RBA believes it's done If the Reserve Bank's economic forecasts are right, then the governor says it is done raising interest rates.

Australian households are among the world's richest, coming in third behind Luxembourg and Belgium, according to a UBS study.

That's down to our booming property market. And while that incredible rise in wealth has driven consumption on the way up, a prolonged or steep drop in housing values is likely to undermine demand across the broader economy.

Canada, which embraced immigration curbs two years ago when it slashed net overseas migration, is now examining ways to put a floor under the housing market, including bailing out property developers.

Canadian housing prices have shed about 20 per cent since 2022. (Reuters: Carlos Osorio)

Many cannot sell without realising enormous losses, but can't afford to sit on finished properties indefinitely.

That has prompted Prime Minister Mark Carney and his British Columbia counterpart to initiate a plan to buy up unsold apartments and convert them into affordable housing.

The great Kiwi real estate slump, meanwhile, has begun to steady but shows little sign of a turnaround.

Housing here is still in short supply. But demand has dropped sharply.

World.title: More than 2.6 million Australians will be living with cancer diagnosis by 2050, say scientists
World.content:
Exclusive NationalHealthcare More than 2.6 million Australians will be living with cancer diagnosis by 2050, say scientists Melissa Cunningham August 18, 2026 — 5:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 2.6 million Australians are forecast to be living with a cancer diagnosis by 2050 – an increase of 1 million people over the next 25 years. For the first time, researchers have used scientific modelling to estimate the prevalence of cancer in Australia in the future, including those in active treatment and people who have survived the disease, but require ongoing care. Naveena Nekkalapudi, pictured with her dog, Laika, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2014. She is now cancer-free, but lives with ongoing nerve pain. Wayne Taylor The study, published in The Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific medical journal, predicted breast cancer would be the nation’s most prevalent cancer in 2050, followed by prostate, melanoma, colorectal and kidney cancer. Almost 1.7 million Australians have cancer or are in the post-treatment phase of the disease, but by 2050, researchers have predicted the total number of people living with cancer will rise by 57 per cent to more than 2.6 million.



Currently, the nation’s population is about 28 million, but by 2050, the Australian Bureau of Statistics estimates it could grow to between 32 and 38 million, depending on fertility rates, migration and life expectancy. Population growth, a rise in ageing Australians and a soaring incidence of certain cancer types is expected to prompt a surge in people being diagnosed. Related Article Cancer Revealed: The radical overhaul of cancer screening to detect most at risk Roughly 44 per cent of the 2.6 million Australians forecast to be living with cancer by 2050 are expected to have an incurable cancer that will require ongoing treatment. “Our projections suggest that in 2050, while more than half of people with a past cancer diagnosis will be potentially cured (1.47 million), about 1.15 million people will be living with cancer (cancers not yet cured) and requiring active treatment or ongoing care,” the researchers wrote.



But in hopeful news, researchers predicted that in the future, cancer survival rates would improve thanks to earlier detection and advancements in treatments such as pioneering immunotherapy. They predicted this would lead to a record rise in people living longer with the disease or being declared “cancer-free” following treatment. Professor Michael Jefford, a co-senior author of the research, and the director of the Australian Cancer Survivorship Centre at Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, said national survival rates had improved remarkably in the past 20 years. “The five-year survival rate for all cancers in Australia is over 70 per cent, which is the highest it’s ever been,” the medical oncologist said. “People are having cancer detected at an early stage and at a stage where it can be cured.”



Professor Michael Jefford says national survival rates have improved remarkably in the past 20 years. Simon Schluter Jefford said while the number of cases diagnosed would continue to climb, the research highlighted a “huge” increase in cancer survivors, many of whom would have other illnesses or ongoing health issues as result of the disease or their age. Melbourne woman Naveena Nekkalapudi was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2014 at age 39. Nekkalapudi is now cancer-free and counts herself lucky. But bouts of intensive chemotherapy permanently damaged her nerves, leading to a condition known peripheral neuropathy. “In my case, it’s ongoing chronic pain, it’s pins and needles, it’s shooting and burning pain,” she said. “I call it the gremlins jabbing a pin into my big toe at night … you can’t do anything about it.”



For more than eight years, Nekkalapudi, 51, needed a pain management specialist, and she continued to take medication to control her symptoms. Jefford warned an overhaul of Australia’s healthcare system was urgently needed to meet the mounting demand. Related Article Good Weekend First we read DNA. Then we edited. Now we’re learning to write He said managing the large numbers of people surviving or living with the disease would require new models of care. This could include care led by general practitioners or nurses, and remote monitoring of lower-risk patients to ease pressure on hospitals and cancer centres. “We know that survivors have significant unmet needs and that existing models of care do not adequately manage these,” Jefford said.



“Survivorship care should focus not just on surveillance for possible recurrence and second cancers but should also focus on the management of physical and psychosocial issues, health promotion and disease prevention, and management of chronic health conditions.” Nekkalapudi, who is a carer for her mum who has also survived breast cancer, called for a focus on early prevention of the disease. She also wanted patients to be provided support “before, during and after” treatment to help them prevent or manage any long-term toxicity complications, which might arise as a result of their treatment. The study was a collaboration between Melbourne’s Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, the University of Sydney, the Daffodil Centre and the Cancer Council NSW. The study’s lead author, University of Sydney’s Associate Professor Qingwei Luo, said the findings demonstrated that cancer was increasingly becoming a long-term, chronic condition rather than a short-term illness.



However, the epidemiologist at the Daffodil Centre, a partnership between Cancer Council NSW and the University of Sydney, warned the largest increase in cancer prevalence was predicted to occur among Australians aged 80 and over, a demographic projected to more than double from 481,000 in 2025 to more than 1 million by 2050. An image of changes in cells indicative of prostate cancer. AP “Many of these [people] will have complex needs, multiple chronic conditions, and long-term treatment effects,” Luo said. Breast cancer is projected to be Australia’s most prevalent cancer in 2050, with more than 485,000 cases up from 298,109 in 2025. This is predicted to be followed by prostate cancer, which researchers estimate will increase from 309,663 cases to 468,991 in the next 25 years. Meanwhile, melanoma cases are forecast to reach 331,909 and colorectal cancer cases are forecast to rise to 237,053. The number of people being given a kidney cancer diagnosis is also set to increase by 121 per cent, soaring from 48,908 last year to 108,101 cases in 2050.



The increase in diagnoses is due to more people living beyond the age of 60, and more people living longer with the disease due to targeted therapies and early detection. Editor's pick Exclusive

Investigation The corrupt relatives behind one of Australia’s richest people These five conditions would account for more than 62 per cent of all Australians living with or beyond a cancer diagnosis by mid-century, the researchers said. World.title: This is, hands down, the most confronting thing I’ve seen on screen all year
World.content:
Alex Gibney is no stranger to challenging material. But his film about the stabbing of Salman Rushdie takes some topping.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This year’s Melbourne International Film Festival has kicked off. Here we take a closer look at some of what’s on offer. See all stories .

As Salman Rushdie lay in hospital after being repeatedly stabbed on stage in August 2022, his wife Rachel Eliza Griffiths started filming. Asking if he was OK with that, he told her yes. “We need to document this.” Now, Alex Gibney has turned that raw, unflinching and often hard-to-watch footage into Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie, one of the most confronting, but ultimately hopeful, movies you’ll ever see. “On this film, I acted mostly as an editor,” says the prolific documentarian who won an Oscar (with Australian producer Eva Orner) for Taxi to the Dark Side in 2007 and has five Emmy wins to his name. “My agent told me Salman and Eliza were interested in talking to me, and I learned they had this footage that Eliza took, starting on day five of his recovery and going right up to when they returned to the scene of the crime. And the first question I asked them was, ‘Why don’t you do it? No one knows more about what happened than you do’. And they said, ‘Well, that’s the problem. We feel too close to it. We want somebody else to come in and see if they can figure out a way to reckon with it.’” Gibney pitched an approach informed by The Singing Detective, the 1986 BBC drama series written by Dennis Potter, in which Michael Gambon played a bed-bound writer in hospital whose medication produces a blurring of his imaginative world and his memories. Despite its complex (and much-praised) structure, the show could be boiled down, says Gibney, to a pretty simple idea: a guy who is sick gets better, but along the way he reimagines his life through hallucinations and his detective fiction.



Rushdie, who had not yet decided to write his own account of the incident (his book Knife: Meditation on an Attempted Murder was released in August 2024), liked the idea, and the film Gibney has made – with Griffiths credited as executive producer and principal cinematographer – serves both as an account of the attack and its aftermath and as a meditation on Rushdie’s life more broadly. Knife opens with a recreation of the attack, with Rushdie asking in voiceover, “Why didn’t I fight back?” It’s a shocking way to start, but it’s nothing compared to what follows. Staff and audience members come to Rushdie’s aid at the Chautauqua Institution on August 12, 2022. AP The Booker Prize winner was in a chair on the stage of the Chautauqua Institution in New York State, about to be interviewed, when a man armed with a knife rushed up the steps and lunged at him. The attacker, Hadi Matar, stabbed the novelist 15 times, landing blows in his neck, stomach, chest and thigh. One of them struck Rushdie, who was 76 at the time, in his right eye (he has lost all sight in it). Matar had been inspired by the fatwa issued by Iran in 1989 in response to Rushdie’s novel The Satanic Verses, which Ayatollah Khomeini and his fellow clerics had deemed blasphemous. (Iran’s position on the fatwa has since become somewhat ambiguous, but it has never officially been rescinded. Last month a trial on terrorism charges against Matar – who has already been convicted of attempted murder – began in Buffalo, New York.) The film also includes real footage of the attack, which was only released during Matar’s first trial in February 2025. It’s horrendous in its brutality, and Gibney admits he wasn’t sure that he should even include it. “I mean, for a documentarian, it would be very hard not to show the actual crime, but I did ponder that maybe we shouldn’t,” he says. What got him over the line was the footage Griffiths had shot of her and Rushdie returning to Chautauqua, “and within that context it seemed to make sense to show it”.



The most challenging scenes in the film, though, are probably the shots of Rushdie’s horribly disfigured eyeball, bulging from its socket, occluded, pointing wildly out of focus. “Trust me,” says Gibney, “in a theatre you can hear the whole audience go ‘aagh’. It’s very difficult to watch.” There was never any chance of not including that footage, though. “Both of them [Rushdie and Griffiths] felt very strongly that they wanted to show this is what terrorism looks like.” For all that Griffiths’ footage was the rock on which the film is built, Gibney knew he had to go beyond it to tell the story he had in mind. “Too much of that, and it’s only about his physical recovery, rather than a deeper kind of mental recovery,” he says. “And once you enter the mind, it’s a chaotic and unpredictable place, and you have to sort of go with the flow.” Rushdie’s wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths, began filming from five days after the attack. They had been married less than a year when it happened. Getty In archival footage, interviews from across the decades and in his own scripted narration, Rushdie reflects on being an outsider in his own family in Mumbai, of feeling the lash of racism at the English boarding school (Rugby) to which he was sent by his father when he was 14, of the cold shoulder some in the literary establishment turned on him when Iran called for his murder, with the offer of a massive bounty (starting at $1 million, it eventually rose to $6 million). There’s a sense overall of a man wounded many times in his life, and of his attempt to stitch himself back together in spite of it all. Whatever you might think of Rushdie, it’s impossible not to be moved by his resilience, his unflinching commitment to free speech, and his refusal of hatred.

World.title: Trump threatens to bomb ally Oman as US-Iran war agreement expires
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war Trump threatens to bomb ally Oman as US-Iran war agreement expires Michael Koziol August 18, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: US President Donald Trump threatened to bomb US ally Oman if it “gets in the way” of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while casting doubt on the possibility of reaching a new deal with Iran after their 60-day interim agreement expired. Next week will mark six months since the US and Israel launched a joint attack on the Islamic Republic. Although the fighting has subsided, the US continues to impose a naval blockade against Iran, and a permanent deal to end the conflict and restore free shipping remains elusive. Donald Trump in the Oval Office on Monday. He said Iran was not willing to make the kind of deal he thought acceptable. AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta In an interview with Fox News, Trump reportedly confirmed the existence of back-channel communications between the US and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the hardline militants responsible for shooting drones and missiles at ships in the strait. Iran and Oman – an American partner on the Arabian Peninsula, which sits across the Gulf of Oman from Iran – have been engaged in talks about management of the crucial waterway, as stipulated by the Memorandum of Understanding signed by the US and Iran in June. That agreement expired on Monday (Washington time).



At a news conference, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said talks with Oman continued. The process was taking longer, he said, as multiple countries were trying to influence the outcome. The parties have suggested an agreement was close for nearly two weeks. Trump told Fox News on Monday: “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them.” Later, in the Oval Office, he struck a different tone: “I don’t think [Oman] behave very well, but we handle them.” Iranian children swim in the Strait of Hormuz as cargo ships are anchored in the distance. Getty Images It is not the first time Trump has made such a threat, as Oman has previously countenanced the idea of setting up a tolling system in the strait with Iran. He insisted November’s midterm elections were not a factor in his thinking, despite many Iran experts arguing that Tehran was trying to run down the clock on Trump’s patience and political capital. Brent crude oil was trading at above $US90 a barrel on Monday.



Trump on Monday repeated his desire to declare the Strait of Hormuz a US territory, having teased the idea at a rally in Long Island, New York, last week. But he offered no explanation as to how that would work, nor what – if anything – it would entail. “We control it with the blockade. I like the idea of declaring it a territory,” Trump told reporters. “[Iran] can be a nuisance, they can put a mine in the water. But the blockade has been very effective.” Trump in the Oval Office on Monday, where he met with lifeguard Ryder Williams, left. AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta The president also cast doubt on whether an acceptable deal with Iran to end the war and reopen the strait was possible. He implied that Iran was in a parlous state, which may lead it to reconsider its position at a later date. “They want to make a deal, but they’re not going to make the kind of deal that I feel is necessary,” he said. “Iran is in big trouble. They have 300 per cent inflation. The country is a mess and their military is totally defeated.”



Meanwhile, the US is relocating the USS George Washington aircraft carrier from the Asia-Pacific to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, which is heading home amid growing concerns about living conditions on-board after a record-breaking deployment. That decision means there are no American aircraft carriers left in the Pacific. Addressing the apparent Middle East stalemate on Monday, Iran analyst Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at the Israel-based Institute for National Security Studies, said the regime would not capitulate. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian with the memorandum of understanding signed with US in June. Iranian Presidency Office via AP “In the choice between submission and escalation, Iran will choose escalation,” he wrote on X. “One can debate its scope, timing, and the tools it will employ, but the expectation that American pressure will bring Tehran to raise the white flag is incompatible with the way the Iranian regime perceives itself and its survival.” Last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent flagged unprecedented sanctions against Iran in an attempt to apply even more economic pressure on the weakened regime. He has not yet announced further measures.



Related Article Updated

Trump diplomacy Trump praises North Korean dictator Kim Jong-un, slashes military drills with Seoul Aaron David Miller, a Middle East analyst who was formerly a long-time State Department negotiator, said it could include secondary sanctions that cut off any country or bank doing business with Iran from the US financial system, or directly targeting Chinese purchases of Iranian oil. “That’s a severe sanction,” he said. “It would involve everybody, including Australia.” But Miller said he did not believe it would make much difference. “I don’t think any of these things will in a reasonable period of time change Iran’s calculation on the core issues.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil prices climb; BHP, CSL results ahead
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street retreats as oil prices climb; BHP, CSL results ahead Stan Choe August 18, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are edging further from their record heights on Monday, ahead of a week where profit reports from the nation’s biggest retailers could give a hint about how shoppers are dealing with high inflation and a slowing job market. The S&P 500 slipped 0.4 per cent but remains near its all-time high set Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 284 points, or 0.5 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.3 per cent lower. Wall Street opened the week with more losses. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 5.58am AEST pointing to a fall of 48 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar is stronger at US71.03¢. Reporting season continues with BHP and CSL results slated to be released today. Wall Street has run to records in large part because profits are booming for US companies. Those in the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver growth of roughly 50 per cent for earnings per share in the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That’s much better than analysts expected and would be the best since five years ago, when the economy was erupting out of the chasm created by the COVID pandemic.



Related Article Exclusive

James Packer James Packer’s bets on AI pay off after sell-down in gaming shares Nearly all the companies in the S&P 500 have turned in their profit reports for the spring. Still to come are big retailers, including reports this week from Home Depot, Target and Walmart. They’re facing pressure. Their customers’ incomes may be turning iffier after US employers surprisingly cut more jobs last month than they added. At the same time, their customers are continuing to see bills rise quickly as inflation remains much higher than anyone would like. A report last week said that shoppers surprisingly spent less at US retailers last month than in June, and CEOs for retailers could give colour this week on what they’re seeing. In the meantime, the wait continues for what the war with Iran will do with oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 2.4 per cent to $US90.62 on Monday, and the losses for stocks solidified in the afternoon as the gains for oil prices accelerated.



Brent zigzagged between $US72 and $US102 last month as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher following their own big recent moves. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.72 per cent from 4.68 per cent late on Friday following a report showing stronger-than-expected growth in manufacturing in New York state. The 10-year yield has shot up from 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran, largely because higher oil prices raised the pressure on inflation and upped the probability that the Federal Reserve will have to hike interest rates. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy and making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. The average long-term US mortgage rate has already jumped near its highest level in a year because of the rise in the 10-year Treasury yield. Reports last week, though, showed that inflation last month was not as bad as earlier in the summer. That raised hopes that the Fed could wait until later in the year before having to decide whether to raise its main interest rate.



Usually around this time of year, anticipation is building on Wall Street to hear from the head of the Federal Reserve about where interest rates may be heading. But the Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, may give little insight at this year’s economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, at the end of this month, according to Thierry Wizman, a strategist at Macquarie Group. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Trump makes America Inc’s grip on the world even tighter Warsh has been adamant about giving Wall Street less guidance about the Fed’s plans for interest rates. On Wall Street, trading was relatively quiet. L3Harris Technologies fell 3.9 per cent after the defense company said Christopher Kubasik stepped down as its CEO and chairman following “certain conduct by Kubasik that was not consistent with the values of the Company.” It gave few details but said the conduct was not related to its financial reporting, controls, customer relationships or operational performance.



Alphabet dipped 0.9 per cent even though Berkshire Hathaway said it increased its investment in Google’s parent company, along with several homebuilders. Berkshire built a reputation for buying stocks at affordable prices under its former CEO, famed investor Warren Buffett. Constellation Brands fell 5.7 per cent after Berkshire said it sold all its holdings in the seller of Modelo beer and Robert Mondavi wine. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped in Europe following a stronger finish in Asia. Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 rose 0.7 per cent after a report said Japan’s economy grew at a slower pace in the April-June quarter than economists expected. Indexes jumped 1.3 per cent in Hong Kong and 1.4 per cent in Shanghai for some of the world’s biggest moves. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: Six simple exercises physios wish everyone would do for lifelong strength
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessFitness Six simple exercises physios wish everyone would do for lifelong strength Danielle Friedman August 18, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In many cases, aches and pains can be a reflection of your daily routines. Habits like sitting at a desk all day, looking down at your phone or even straining to pick your socks up off the floor can lead to a body that feels creaky, tight and sore. Making time to practise good movement habits can keep you feeling limber and strong. Physical therapists say they repeatedly recommend these six exercises to patients. Getty Images Physical therapists know this all too well. “People come in with the same problems over and over again,” said Theresa Marko, a physical therapist in New York City.



She often found herself recommending the same exercises as solutions, she said — exercises that, for example, “counteract, you know, going to see The Odyssey for three hours”. Related Article Wellbeing Joyspan could be the secret to ageing happily. Here’s what to know We asked physical therapists to share the exercises they wish everyone incorporated into their fitness routines. Here are six that came up again and again. Standing on one leg Good balance is important for both fitness and everyday life, but it deteriorates with age, unless you’re “really deliberate about practising it”, says Conor Nordengren, a physical therapist in Wellesley, Massachusetts.



One of the simplest ways to do this is by regularly standing on one leg, experts say. This simple exercise could “strengthen all the muscles in your foot, your ankle, your knee, your thigh”, Marko said. It also helps to build stability — not only in your legs, but also in your hips, pelvis and lower back. “I stand on one leg in the kitchen, waiting for coffee, waiting for the elevator,” she added. If standing on one leg is challenging for you, lightly rest your hand on a chair, a wall or a counter top until you feel stable enough to let go. If the exercise feels easy, close your eyes. Stand on each leg for at least 30 seconds every day. Hip hinges



The ability to properly bend forward, or hinge, at the hips is useful both for daily tasks, like picking things up off the floor, and for exercises like deadlifts and kettlebell swings. But many people struggle with hip hinges, says Dhara Shah, a physical therapist at Emory Healthcare. It’s common to round your back and lock your knees when you bend over, which puts pressure on your spine and can lead to pain or injury. Regularly practising hip hinges can also strengthen your glutes and hamstrings. To do a hip hinge, send your hips backward while bringing your chest forward. Keep your back straight, your shoulders pulled slightly back, your abdominal muscles pulled towards your belly button and your knees softly bent. Practise this movement daily, doing two sets of 15 hinges.



Sit-to-stands Related Article Wellbeing Does the body keep the score? Our brains and bodies are more linked than we knew The act of sitting down and then standing back up may seem simple, but with age, it can become increasingly difficult without proper strength and stability. Making time to practise “sit-to-stand” exercises will pay off by strengthening your quads, glutes, hamstrings, calves and core muscles, and improve your ability to do lunges and squats, the experts say. To do a sit-to-stand, lower yourself into a chair and stand back up in a slow, controlled way. If this feels challenging, practise it several times a day until it feels easier. If it already feels easy, lower your body even more slowly and just barely tap your butt to the seat before slowly standing up again. The lower the surface, the more challenging it will be. “That control piece makes it a little harder,” Shah said.



Do two sets of 20 repetitions several times a week. For more of a challenge, do it while holding weights or a kettlebell. If struggling initially, you can also try a dead-bug with an exercise ball for added stability. Getty Images Dead bugs with diaphragmatic breathing Many people feel the effects of sitting for long periods in their neck, shoulders or back, but the problem often begins in their innermost core muscles, says Carrie Pagliano, a physical therapist in Virginia. “With a lot of these issues, people are just missing fundamental strength,” she said. When your core is weak, your neck and shoulders often compensate to keep you upright. Physical therapists recommend doing the dead bug exercise while practising diaphragmatic breathing to build core strength at the deepest level.



To do a dead bug, lie on your back and raise your legs at a 90-degree angle, then raise your arms straight towards the ceiling. With your spine pressed into the floor, slowly straighten and lower your left leg while also lowering your right arm, until both are fully extended. Return to the starting position, then repeat with the opposite sides. While extending, slowly exhale through your mouth to contract your deep core. While returning to the starting position, inhale and feel your belly expand. Do two sets of eight exercises a few times a week. This breath work helps “stabilise your core from the inside out”, says Alicia Ferriere, a physical therapist in New Jersey. Together with the dead bugs, it can help support your spine and relieve aches in your neck and shoulders. Wall push-ups Push-ups allow you to practise lifting your body weight, which is essential for staying independent as you age and getting up if you fall, Nordengren says. They primarily strengthen the chest, shoulders, arms and core.



Related Article Fitness How three oncologists exercise – and why Unless you’ve regularly been doing push-ups from the ground, experts recommended doing them with your hands on a stable, raised surface such as a wall or a counter top. As you build strength, you can gradually lower the surface until you reach the ground. “I’ll very rarely have people do them from the floor right away,” Nordengren said, especially since “a lot of people struggle with the technique”. Start in a plank position, with your back flat and your feet pressed into the floor. Next, engage your core and slightly tuck your tailbone underneath you to prevent your back from arching. Bend your elbows into a 45-degree angle, while slowly lowering your chest, then push yourself back up. Imagine that you are pushing the floor away, Nordengren says, and be sure to reach your arms long at the top. Do two sets of 10 reps twice a week. Cat-cows



To counter the effects of sitting or standing for long periods of time, many physical therapists recommended the cat-cow stretch, in which you alternate between arching and curving your back while on all fours. Take a few deep breaths in each position to feel a deeper stretch. This classic stretch can help relieve stiffness in your spine, shoulders and neck and improve your mobility. Editor's pick Exclusive

Victoria residential property Real estate agent sacked over allegations he secretly sold properties to his partner When you’re in an all-fours position, you can limber up other body parts, too, Ferriere says. Try reaching forward with each arm or stretching each leg out behind you and doing a few hip circles. Ultimately, these exercises are “giving you a little extra buffer to live your life”, Nordengren says, so your body is strong, steady and prepared for the unexpected. This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: Ange Postecoglou has moved to Saudi Arabia. How should we feel about that?
World.content:
Analysis SportSoccerSaudi Arabia Ange Postecoglou has moved to Saudi Arabia. How should we feel about that? Vince Rugari August 18, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ange Postecoglou has made a career out of taking the road less travelled; of eschewing the easy, obvious thing in favour of the biggest available challenge. Not for the first time, he’s outdone himself. Ange Postecoglou on the job during Al-Nassr’s Saudi Pro League game against Al Fateh. Getty Images It’s been just over a year since he was unceremoniously dumped by Tottenham Hotspur after delivering the club’s first trophy in 17 years, and just under a year since his brutal sacking by Nottingham Forest after 39 disastrous days in charge. Popular wisdom was that, to overcome the perception that he was damaged managerial goods, Postecoglou, now 60, would have to leave the Premier League and rebuild his reputation elsewhere: perhaps a big club in Germany or the Netherlands, where he could re-establish his credibility and set up a swift return to England. But nobody thought he would go this far off Broadway.



Postecoglou’s next chapter began over the weekend, without any of the fanfare that came with the last couple. You may not have even known it happened: in the early hours of Sunday morning (AEST), Al-Nassr opened the new Saudi Professional League (SPL) season with a 3-0 win over Al-Fateh. Loading Cristiano Ronaldo, 41, who increasingly resembles a wax likeness of Cristiano Ronaldo, sported a notable new haircut as he watched on from the stands, not yet ready to play after his recent wedding, having told Vogue (as you do) that this would “probably” be his final season. It will revolve around his pursuit of the 24 more goals he needs to become the first player in history to score 1000 career goals in official competitions. Postecoglou could be the coach who gets him there. He welcomed Ronaldo to his first team meeting of the season by calling him “Cris” and congratulating him on his nuptials. He is now attached to the perpetual CR7 content machine. This is his new world. Postecoglou’s two-year contract with the reigning Saudi champions reportedly gives him a salary of almost $20 million per year. Pretty good work, if you can get it; the road less travelled, in this instance, is also paved with riyals. View post on X



Is this really where we envisaged him taking his managerial talents? And where are we, exactly: does this mark the beginning of the end of the great Angeball odyssey, or is this just a brief interlude before his triumphant resurgence at the highest level? At this point, we should take a deep breath. Australians, in particular, should be very careful about turning their noses up at Postecoglou’s decision to work in Saudi Arabia, lest we engage in exactly the same sort of Eurocentric snobbery that Ange has always railed against. View post on X You can’t, on one hand, accuse English pundits of underestimating Postecoglou’s previous achievements in Australia, Japan and Scotland because of where they took place, and then on the other hand dismiss Saudi Arabia as some sort of barren footballing wasteland. It’s not: Saudi Arabia was a legitimate football country before the Public Investment Fund decided to start spending big a few years ago, and it still is.



The cynical view is he’s only gone there for the cash, which doesn’t quite square with the relentlessly ambitious Postecoglou we know. The generous view is that he has taken arguably the most high-profile job in club football outside of Europe, and is now in charge of a squad with more quality than many top clubs in Europe: beyond Ronaldo, there’s Samu Costa, Sadio Mane, Joao Felix, Inigo Martinez and Kingsley Coman, plus a host of tidy Saudi internationals. This is entirely consistent with Postecoglou’s general worldview: that worthy football exists beyond the borders of Europe, and that coaches should go wherever they feel they can make the biggest impact. Ange Postecoglou is pictured during an Al-Nassr training session. Instagram Cristiano Ronaldo won his first Saudi title with Al-Nassr last season. Getty Images It is, though, possible to be respectful of Saudi football and also acknowledge the undeniable truth that, for Postecoglou enthusiasts, watching the Riyadh derby just isn’t going to hit the same as a North London derby, or an Old Firm clash. Nothing against the Saudi Pro League; that’s just how it is.



But it’s his career, not ours; he has more than earned the right to do whatever he wants, and owes an explanation to nobody. In pure football terms, this is a cracking challenge. Al-Nassr are the reigning champions of Saudi Arabia; this is the first time Postecoglou, who normally specialises in fixer-uppers, has taken charge of a team defending a league title. That’s new. They’ve never won the AFC Champions League, so there’s his big target to aim for, along with winning the league again. He’s also got to adapt his brand of football to new conditions, in a place where it’s never not hot. He has to somehow manage the gigantic ego of a player who is within sight of an unprecedented individual milestone, and who famously doesn’t press – which would be a lot easier to deal with if this player didn’t run the entire show at Al-Nassr. And he’ll do all this in the knowledge that whatever success he has will be downplayed in Europe, because it’s only Saudi Arabia, and his failures will be magnified, because it’s Saudi Arabia. This is not a pragmatic career choice. Ange Postecoglou. Getty Images There are, of course, some uncomfortable ethical considerations. Any player or coach who goes to Saudi Arabia is participating in that country’s efforts to build its public image in a certain way. Does that make this sportswashing? Is every coaching appointment in Saudi really an elaborate act of propaganda? Does sportswashing even actually work if human rights issues are brought up every time someone signs for a Saudi club? Should Postecoglou not get the Tim Cahill treatment, then? Is Socceroo Aziz Behich also guilty, having spent six months on loan at Al-Nassr in 2024? Do we consider Kevin Muscat as doing the bidding of the Chinese government because the club he coaches is owned by a state-owned company?



Or is there another way to view this: that the Saudi football “project” is also a case of a football-mad country which happens to have the means to invest at a staggering scale into the thing that it loves? Are they not engaging in exactly the kind of “nationalistic approach” Postecoglou once said was required to climb the ladder in world football, having given up hope it would ever happen in Australia? Or is any investment from the Saudi government inherently tainted? Where is the line? You can wrestle with these questions at your leisure, but there are no especially satisfying answers. Related Article Premier League Socceroos teenager’s $33m deal sets stage for dream Premier League debut Success there may not win over Postecoglou’s biggest critics, but it can be a road back to the top. We have proof: Matthias Jassle, who has replaced Eddie Howe as Newcastle United manager, went straight to the Premier League from Al-Ahli. After also being sacked by Spurs, Nuno Espirito Santo spent a year at Al-Ittihad before returning to England with Nottingham Forest – so it can be done. And if he can get Ronaldo swooning in public about how good a coach he is, all sorts of doors could open for Postecoglou one day. Who knows? For him, the road less travelled is often bumpy, but it rarely leads to a dead end. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Janice was thrilled to buy her own unit. But she has no idea if she will ever move in
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCity life Janice was thrilled to buy her own unit. But she has no idea if she will ever move in Ellie Busby and Anthony Segaert August 18, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Janice Cahill thought the plans for her cosy second-storey unit looked perfect. Recently widowed, the retiree had sold her family home and spent $60,000 on a deposit for a one-bedroom off-the-plan apartment in a new complex in Kembla Grange, near Wollongong. The location would allow her to live close to her grandchildren, and the building’s lift would help avoid difficult stairs. Cahill was told the building would be ready by December 2025. Then the developer emailed with news it would be delayed until March 2026. Then April. Then August. Then September. She still hasn’t moved in. “It’s pretty depressing,” she said. “It does really and truly affect my mental health.” Janice Cahill is hoping to move in to her new home later this year. Wolter Peeters She signed a contract with UPG 113 Pty Ltd – a company Cahill did not know, and claims she was not informed, was in fact a subsidiary of Bathla Group, one of the state’s most prolific and controversial developers. The firm is now teetering on the edge of collapse as it deals with more than $3 billion in debts and a circling Building Commission investigation into its key properties. Questions have been raised for more than a year about the ability of Bathla Group, and the more than 450 subsidiary companies identified by the Herald, to pay its debts and remain in the market.



In the latest development, the company, which is a major sponsor of the Western Sydney Wanderers, is trying to sell off land in the profitable north-western suburbs. It is advertising a block of undeveloped land in Bella Vista it bought for $15.71 million from receivers for the developer Dyldam, which collapsed in 2020 with debts of half a billion dollars – less than the amount Bathla owes. Building Commission NSW, the state’s construction watchdog, has undertaken more than 40 inspections of Bathla sites over the past few months and has identified defects at sites in Marsden Park, which the commission said have mostly been rectified, and the Kembla Grange development into which Cahill is planning to move. The company’s spokesperson said the company’s records indicated the agency had only conducted five inspections “with no issues noted”. Fed up with the lack of progress on her new home and having heard that the tradesmen had walked off the site because they were not being paid, Cahill contacted an executive at Bathla in November 2025.



“We met for coffee [and] he apologised for the delay and gave all this story about the plumbing issues, and Sydney Water not being connected,” she said. A spokesperson for Sydney Water said there had been no delay at the site. Half-finished copper piping was left undone at Bathla’s property. The basement of one of the buildings at Bathla’s Kembla Grange development appeared to be graffitied by trespassers. Bongs and faces were added to pillars. “He assured me that he would keep in touch with me and keep me updated, which to this point hasn’t happened,” Cahill said. “I’ve emailed him and asked him what the updates are, and I’ve had no response. So I think he’s ignoring me.”



“He said, ‘Oh, tradies will always say they put invoices in that they haven’t done work for, and that’s why they haven’t been paid’. And I just thought, this meeting is useless.” Bathla’s spokesperson said the company had communicated to unit buyers through their purchasing agents and that its executives had been in direct contact with some. They also said “all trades are on payment terms”. When asked why the completion date for the project had been pushed back, the spokesperson said it was “due to unforeseen site delays with some external works … Completion is forecast for November.” The brickwork on one property at Bathla’s Kembla Grange site. In another response, they said buyers would be able to move in during October or November. “On completion the project will be handed to the buyers in great condition.”



When Marie Sinclair, whose elderly parents bought an apartment in the same building, visited the site in September last year, she was shocked to find doors with keys left unattended, graffitied walls, half-finished copper piping and multiple broken surfaces. Her parents had sold their home after pressure from the developer’s salesperson to prepare to move into the block, she said. “They were homeless. We couldn’t find a rental [within budget]. So they have to live with me,” she said. “A spotlight needs to be shone on this.” Sue Mancuso and daughter Marie Sinclair stand in front of the fenced-off development. Wolter Peeters Empty worksites reveal extent of crisis



A Creditor Watch report shows Bathla’s main corporate entity, Universal Property Group, is at high risk of not being able to meet its financial commitments or insolvency within the next 12 months. The spokesperson said Bathla and all its related entities would pay off the debt accrued, and that the developer would finish building the 3500 houses, apartments and subdivision lots that are currently under construction in Australia. “We do not believe Universal Property Group is at high risk of an insolvency event,” he said. Parts of Bathla’s Castle Hill site have been flooded. Wolter Peeters But a lack of work across many of the company’s sites gives insight into the crisis. In Castle Hill, one of the company’s key projects, the 68-unit Ashford Rose development exists only as a hole in the ground. When the Herald visited last week, no construction work was occurring and no workers were seen on the property. Parts of the site have been flooded with water.



Bathla’s website shows apartments available for sale at Ashford Rose, but the company’s spokesperson said no units had been sold off the plan. “We are awaiting a further staged construction certificate to recommence work on site,” they said. “The water [onsite] is due to heavy rainfall. This will be dealt with appropriately.” The reserve remains fenced-off because Bathla is yet to hand over ownership to Blacktown City Council. Wolter Peeters In Marsden Park, a “drainage reserve” was meant to be turned into a place to play for the tens of thousands of new residents moving into the area. But the park hasn’t opened to the public, remaining fenced off because Bathla, which completed the bulk earthworks for the site, has yet to hand over ownership of the plot to Blacktown City Council. Frustrated locals have resorted to breaking in to get access to the promised green space, while the council waits for Bathla to complete the settlement process. The spokesperson for Bathla said all parties were working to finalise the contract, with settlement to occur shortly after. Builder’s track record in spotlight



At the heart of Bathla Group is a corporate structure that makes it difficult for prospective buyers to know who they are dealing with. Each development is owned and sold by a subsidiary company of Bathla, which is officially called Universal Property Group. Corporate filings show Universal Property Group has hundreds of subsidiary companies, all listed as numerical variations of UPG: UPG 1, UPG 2, up to UPG 460. Bathla, or Universal Property Group, is also closely connected to the company Raj & Jai Constructions. Documents lodged with the corporate regulator show the two companies share the same business addresses, have identical auditor and agent details, and the co-owners of Bathla and the owner of Raj & Jai are all listed as living in the same Girraween apartment block. Building Commission NSW considers Raj & Jai as an associated entity of Bathla. In response to questions about Bathla, its spokesperson said the company was “an independently owned and operated entity”. When the Herald sent questions to Raj & Jai, the spokesperson provided the same response. In 2011, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission found Universal Property Group engaged in “unconscionable conduct” after offering vendor finance to people who were mostly immigrants and came from non-English-speaking backgrounds. As part of the enforceable undertaking, the company agreed to a scheme whereby vendor finance borrowers would be entitled to seek compensation.



In 2018, Universal Property Group pleaded guilty and was fined $135,000 by SafeWork NSW after a worker at a Doonside site fell through a sheet of unmarked plywood and became impaled on upright concrete reinforcing bars. He was seriously injured. Universal Property Group expressed remorse for the incident. Related Article City life Starting a family, Mohammed bought his dream home. Two kids later, he still can’t move in Bathla and its subsidiary companies have also regularly taken up cases in the NSW Land and Environment Court, pursuing legal action against councils over “deemed refusals” for development applications, which occurs when a council has failed to decide on an application within 40 days (high-impact plans get 60 days, and state-significant projects get 90). In 2020, then-Blacktown mayor and current state MP Stephen Bali criticised Bathla, saying the group simply wanted to “ram through acres of development” within 40 to 60 days. Meanwhile, the council has refused to comment on how much its recent appeals have cost. Despite Bathla’s financial problems, the developer continues to propose new housing projects across the state. In recent years, more development applications have been submitted in south-western Sydney that follow a similar pattern to Blacktown. Liverpool City Council’s annual report for 2023 to 2024 revealed there were a total of 15 appeals in the Land and Environment by Bathla’s subsidiaries for development applications.



Of these 15 appeals, 14 were deemed refusals because the 40-day time period had passed. There were also two appeals by Raj & Jai Construction. Building Commission NSW is encouraging home owners concerned about their contracts with Bathla Group to call the agency for advice. Cahill, who is due to have a double knee operation next month and will struggle to walk up the stairs to the studio she is renting, has been emailing Bathla asking if she’d be able to move in by the time of her surgery. She hasn’t heard back. “I just want my bloody apartment,” she said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: I rarely drink alcohol, but I make an exception for one particular cocktail
World.content:
InspirationFoodie travel Opinion I rarely drink alcohol, but I make an exception for one particular cocktail Lee Tulloch Travel columnist August 18, 2026 — 5:00am

August 18, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The search for optimum health means I’m not a regular drinker of alcohol. But there are two drinks I find hard to resist – a martini with a twist in a New York bar, and a Bellini in Venice. Martinis can pack a punch and Bellinis provide a pleasant hit of dopamine. But it’s not about the alcohol content or even the taste of the drink. It’s about the sense of place. The arrival at Hotel Cipriani. In Venice, you’re automatically offered a Bellini or an Aperol Spritz when you sit down for a drink at a restaurant or bar. Both are specific to the city.



The spritz was created in the early 19th century for Austrian soldiers stationed in the Veneto region who liked a splash of water added to their wine. 



Most visitors don’t care or notice if the Bellini isn’t made with fresh peach. But I think there’s something wrong if you’re served the same sickly drink they serve at hens’ parties back home. Pouring Bellinis at Harry’s Bar in Venice. Alamy On my last trip to Venice, I tried to figure out what the perfect Bellini might be. The starting point in this pilgrimage is Harry’s Bar, tucked away on a narrow street near St Mark’s Square. It was opened in 1931 by bartender Giuseppe Cipriani, who went on to establish one of Venice’s finest hotels, The Cipriani, and invented the dish carpaccio along the way.



The cosy bar is a designated Italian National Monument, and is most famous for being the place where Ernest Hemingway liked to drink – and for the Bellini, which Cipriani invented in 1948, naming it for the Renaissance painter, Giovanni Bellini. I had never been there until this year when friends, visiting from Melbourne, invited me for a drink. I’d avoided it because I heard it was touristy. And it is. But it was fun to be somewhere so steeped in history, even though the legendary Bellini was a bit of a disappointment. It may have been made from real peach, but it was made in such volumes it didn’t taste hand-crafted. A small glass sets you back about €22 ($36) at the bar. For those who think the Bellini is a woman’s drink – Hemingway apparently drank both martinis and Bellinis at Harry’s. Across the water at the Hotel Cipriani, A Belmond Hotel, on Giudecca Island, Gianfranco of the hotel’s Bar Gabbiano makes a Bellini for me using fresh peaches.



The white peaches from the north are best, he says, the juice often hand-squeezed. Gianfranco pours the fresh puree into a special glass jug, then tops it with prosecco, waiting until the froth settles before adding more peach. Related Article Venice Luxury Italian hotel where George Clooney got married enters a new era One part peach to two parts prosecco is the approximate recipe, although Gianfranco says it’s a bit like cooking, the proportions can be varied to taste. It’s elegant and not too sweet and all the better for being served poolside by the lagoon. To my surprise, another excellent Bellini I tasted in Venice didn’t have Cipriani associated with it. Hotel Heurekais a charming, independent hotel in untouristy Cannaregio. A small palazzo of 10 guest rooms, it has a beautiful private garden and an intimate bar in the lobby, where Alessandro, who spent 34 years as bartender at the now-closed Bauer Hotel, presides.



One evening, he was making a jug of Bellinis for two other guests, so I joined in. It couldn’t have been fresher. He pureed the juicy peaches on the spot and topped them up with a medium-dry prosecco. It was perfection, fruity but barely sweet at all. You could, if you liked, buy a “peach-flavoured” Cipriani Bellini at a bottle shop in Australia for about $30. But a true Bellini needs to be enjoyed in summer in Venice, its place of invention, when the peaches are ripe. Everything else is a sugary cocktail. The writer was a guest of Hotel Heureka and the Hotel Cipriani.

World.title: More than 2.6 million Australians will be living with cancer diagnosis by 2050, say scientists
World.content:
Exclusive NationalHealthcare More than 2.6 million Australians will be living with cancer diagnosis by 2050, say scientists Melissa Cunningham August 18, 2026 — 5:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 2.6 million Australians are forecast to be living with a cancer diagnosis by 2050 – an increase of 1 million people over the next 25 years. For the first time, researchers have used scientific modelling to estimate the prevalence of cancer in Australia in the future, including those in active treatment and people who have survived the disease, but require ongoing care. Naveena Nekkalapudi, pictured with her dog, Laika, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2014. She is now cancer-free, but lives with ongoing nerve pain. Wayne Taylor The study, published in The Lancet Regional Health Western Pacific medical journal, predicted breast cancer would be the nation’s most prevalent cancer in 2050, followed by prostate, melanoma, colorectal and kidney cancer. Almost 1.7 million Australians have cancer or are in the post-treatment phase of the disease, but by 2050, researchers have predicted the total number of people living with cancer will rise by 57 per cent to more than 2.6 million.



Currently, the nation’s population is about 28 million, but by 2050, the Australian Bureau of Statistics estimates it could grow to between 32 and 38 million, depending on fertility rates, migration and life expectancy. Population growth, a rise in ageing Australians and a soaring incidence of certain cancer types is expected to prompt a surge in people being diagnosed. Related Article Cancer Revealed: The radical overhaul of cancer screening to detect most at risk Roughly 44 per cent of the 2.6 million Australians forecast to be living with cancer by 2050 are expected to have an incurable cancer that will require ongoing treatment. “Our projections suggest that in 2050, while more than half of people with a past cancer diagnosis will be potentially cured (1.47 million), about 1.15 million people will be living with cancer (cancers not yet cured) and requiring active treatment or ongoing care,” the researchers wrote.



But in hopeful news, researchers predicted that in the future, cancer survival rates would improve thanks to earlier detection and advancements in treatments such as pioneering immunotherapy. They predicted this would lead to a record rise in people living longer with the disease or being declared “cancer-free” following treatment. Professor Michael Jefford, a co-senior author of the research, and the director of the Australian Cancer Survivorship Centre at Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, said national survival rates had improved remarkably in the past 20 years. “The five-year survival rate for all cancers in Australia is over 70 per cent, which is the highest it’s ever been,” the medical oncologist said. “People are having cancer detected at an early stage and at a stage where it can be cured.”



Professor Michael Jefford says national survival rates have improved remarkably in the past 20 years. Simon Schluter Jefford said while the number of cases diagnosed would continue to climb, the research highlighted a “huge” increase in cancer survivors, many of whom would have other illnesses or ongoing health issues as result of the disease or their age. Melbourne woman Naveena Nekkalapudi was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2014 at age 39. Nekkalapudi is now cancer-free and counts herself lucky. But bouts of intensive chemotherapy permanently damaged her nerves, leading to a condition known peripheral neuropathy. “In my case, it’s ongoing chronic pain, it’s pins and needles, it’s shooting and burning pain,” she said. “I call it the gremlins jabbing a pin into my big toe at night … you can’t do anything about it.”



For more than eight years, Nekkalapudi, 51, needed a pain management specialist, and she continued to take medication to control her symptoms. Jefford warned an overhaul of Australia’s healthcare system was urgently needed to meet the mounting demand. Related Article Good Weekend First we read DNA. Then we edited. Now we’re learning to write He said managing the large numbers of people surviving or living with the disease would require new models of care. This could include care led by general practitioners or nurses, and remote monitoring of lower-risk patients to ease pressure on hospitals and cancer centres. “We know that survivors have significant unmet needs and that existing models of care do not adequately manage these,” Jefford said.



“Survivorship care should focus not just on surveillance for possible recurrence and second cancers but should also focus on the management of physical and psychosocial issues, health promotion and disease prevention, and management of chronic health conditions.” Nekkalapudi, who is a carer for her mum who has also survived breast cancer, called for a focus on early prevention of the disease. She also wanted patients to be provided support “before, during and after” treatment to help them prevent or manage any long-term toxicity complications, which might arise as a result of their treatment. The study was a collaboration between Melbourne’s Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre, the University of Sydney, the Daffodil Centre and the Cancer Council NSW. The study’s lead author, University of Sydney’s Associate Professor Qingwei Luo, said the findings demonstrated that cancer was increasingly becoming a long-term, chronic condition rather than a short-term illness.



However, the epidemiologist at the Daffodil Centre, a partnership between Cancer Council NSW and the University of Sydney, warned the largest increase in cancer prevalence was predicted to occur among Australians aged 80 and over, a demographic projected to more than double from 481,000 in 2025 to more than 1 million by 2050. An image of changes in cells indicative of prostate cancer. AP “Many of these [people] will have complex needs, multiple chronic conditions, and long-term treatment effects,” Luo said. Breast cancer is projected to be Australia’s most prevalent cancer in 2050, with more than 485,000 cases up from 298,109 in 2025. This is predicted to be followed by prostate cancer, which researchers estimate will increase from 309,663 cases to 468,991 in the next 25 years. Meanwhile, melanoma cases are forecast to reach 331,909 and colorectal cancer cases are forecast to rise to 237,053. The number of people being given a kidney cancer diagnosis is also set to increase by 121 per cent, soaring from 48,908 last year to 108,101 cases in 2050.



The increase in diagnoses is due to more people living beyond the age of 60, and more people living longer with the disease due to targeted therapies and early detection. Editor's pick Exclusive

Investigation The corrupt relatives behind one of Australia’s richest people These five conditions would account for more than 62 per cent of all Australians living with or beyond a cancer diagnosis by mid-century, the researchers said.
