World.title: Off-grid stories during F1 mid-year break as racing returns
World.content:
Formula 1's mid-year hiatus ends this weekend, as the racing series returns to action with the Dutch Grand Prix in Zandvoort.

The five-week break has given drivers and teams a chance to refresh ahead of a long and gruelling run to the finish line, with the drivers' and constructors' championships well and truly alive in 2026.

While there has been no action on the track, there has been news off it during the break.

Ahead of this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix, here are a few stories you may have missed during the hiatus.

1. No contract announcements

The first news is no news.

Drivers off contract at the end of 2026 Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes

George Russell, Mercedes

Isack Hadjar, Red Bull

Carlos Sainz, Williams

Alex Albon, Williams

Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls

Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin

Oliver Bearman, Haas

Esteban Ocon, Haas

Nick Hulkenberg, Audi

Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi

Franco Colapinto, Alpine

The mid-year break usually signals the start of F1's silly season, where teams and drivers formalise contracts for future seasons.

The 2026 silly season is set to be busy, with as many as 14 drivers off contract at the end of this year.

And there are big names who are yet to finalise deals for 2027 and beyond, including Mercedes drivers' championship leader Kimi Antonelli, and two-time world champion Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin).

There has also been wild speculation of a potential driver swap between McLaren and Red Bull, with Australia's Oscar Piastri and four-time world champion Max Verstappen changing teams as early as next year.

But, thus far, there have been no announcements.

This will change in the near future, and just because no contracts have been announced does not mean no work behind the scenes.

2. Piastri confident McLaren can 'make that step' back to the top

After the highs of the previous two seasons, McLaren's 2026 campaign has resembled more of a yo-yo.

McLaren have won the previous two constructors' championships, while Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri both won seven grands prix last year, a campaign where Norris became drivers' world champion.

Piastri blasts 'f***ing stupid' backmarker, Norris wins Hungarian GP Oscar Piastri retired from the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix, won by his teammate Lando Norris, but not before he blasted a "stupid" backmarker and slammed his team for a poor strategy at the Hungaroring.

But in 2026, with a new era of regulations, McLaren has had mixed results.

It started the season poorly, with Oscar Piastri failing to start the opening two grands prix of the season (Australia and China), while Norris also failed to start the Chinese Grand Prix.

Both drivers have been plagued by reliability issues, but have also produced promising results.

Piastri has twice finished on the podium (Japan and Miami), while Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix — a race Piastri led before being hit by a backmarker and then suffering an issue that forced his retirement.

Despite not being in the championship picture thus far in 2026, Piastri is confident McLaren will return.

In an interview with the team during the break, Piastri cited McLaren's early struggles in 2023 before their rise up the grid to become back-to-back champions.

"When you look at the previous experience of what we've been able to achieve as a team, and how we've been able to make progress through the year, it's good," the Australian said.

"In 2023, we were in a much worse position than where we are now, and we were able to really jump up the order to fight for podiums.

"The way that Lando and I worked together during that period to try and focus on making the car quick, so that we could then fight for the results that we wanted, hasn't changed. It's still strong, with productive conversations together with the team — we are all pushing toward the same goal.

"I feel like for me I've already seen it play out more than once. I think that's a real strength of the team. Yes, things are different, the cars are different, maybe the way we will make that step will look different. But we've made that step before, and I'm confident we can do it again."

3. Bahrain Grand Prix back on calendar, in Malaysia

While the official mid-year break is coming to an end, F1 had an unofficial hiatus earlier this year when the Bahrain and Saudi Arabia weekends were called off due to unrest in the Middle East.

That left an unexpected gap between the Japanese Grand Prix and Miami Grand Prix weekends, with F1 holding onto hope that they would be able to bring those races back onto the calendar.

Well, they have brought one back, in a different country.

The Bahrain Grand Prix will be held in 2026, but thousands of kilometres away in Malaysia.

Sepang International Circuit will host the event from October 2-4, between the grand prix weekends in Azerbaijan and Singapore.

F1 is no stranger to Sepang, first racing there in 1999, while the last F1 race held there in 2017 was won by Max Verstappen.

"We are delighted to confirm that Malaysia will host the Bahrain Grand Prix in 2026. Once again, the sport has demonstrated its ability to adapt, find solutions, and deliver, creating an exciting moment for everyone who follows Formula 1," F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali said.

4. Cadillac has a team principal change

While there was no change in the driver market, F1's newest team made a change on the pit wall.

Cadillac announced Marcin Budkowski would become the American squad's new team principal, replacing Graeme Lowdon.

Lowdon was the team principal from 2024 and an instrumental figure in preparing Cadillac for its debut season in 2026.

Budkowski has been around F1 for many years, and was once the executive director at French outfit Alpine.

"Marcin's appointment marks another important step in the continued evolution of the Cadillac Formula 1 Team," said Dan Towriss, CEO of the Cadillac team.

"As we enter this new era for the Cadillac Formula 1 Team, Marcin brings exceptional F1 experience, technical expertise and strategic leadership that will strengthen our organisation and help us develop the winning mindset, tools and processes required for long-term success.

"We're grateful to Graeme Lowdon for his leadership and the role he played in forming the Cadillac Formula 1 Team from the ground up. His contributions helped establish a strong foundation in our build-up phase, and we thank him for his commitment and wish him well."

World.title: Shock defeat to Bangladesh reveals bigger picture hiding in plain sight
World.content:
You could pick a handful of moments during the first Test at Marrara Oval in Darwin where it was clear not everything was as it seemed on surface level.

On day two, Marnus Labuschagne sprinted off with his usual exuberance from the infield to chase down a shot that trickled towards the boundary.

The immaculately manicured outfield, offering a playing surface that was nigh on pristine, had already been praised for its lawn-like quality.

Mark Waugh on Fox Sports noted you could probably play bowls or tennis on it.

Yet as soon as Labuschagne slid for the ball, the ugly truth was revealed, as a huge clump of turf was ripped up in a heaped mass of mud and grass and injury potential.

This was a pattern repeated throughout the match: The outfield's undoubted beauty was only surface deep.

Australia's standing at the top of the Test match rankings may only be surface deep, as deep fissures have been revealed in Darwin. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

An analogy to what transpired over the next four days, as the number nine-ranked Test team that were missing two of their best bowlers, thumped the world number one side at full strength on their own turf, could not have been clearer.

Bangladesh's stunning victory in Darwin has delivered Australian cricket the shock that it undoubtedly needed.

A team that arrived without fanfare or pedigree has slapped down the world's number one Test playing nation by playing simple, sensible Test cricket.

The bowling was slow but accurate. The batting, unspectacular but patient and disciplined.

The Tigers' attitude was exceptional.

As the growth of the big three has accelerated inequalities between the haves and have-nots of Test cricket, Bangladesh are one of those teams that have been left firmly on the outer, yet proved in Darwin that the paucity of opportunities that have come their way has in no way blunted their potency or hunger for success within the format.

They were here to play Test cricket and play it well.

Najmul Hossain Shanto led his team with skill and composure throughout. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Given it had been 23 years since they last played a Test on Australian soil, their commitment to playing such an impressive style against a country that has snubbed them for so long was more than admirable.

Credit for that has to go to coach Phil Simmons and unflappable skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto.

Shanto made correct decision after correct decision on the pitch, Bangladesh never succumbing to the pressure or enormity of what was transpiring around them right up until Mominul Haque crushed Beau Webster through the covers to seal victory, a simple hug between the two not out batters sufficing as the bench finally exploded in joy on the boundary.

Bangladesh's historic win deserves all the praise that will undoubtedly be heaped upon it, the context of which will forever be extraordinary.

Bangladesh held their nerve throughout a tense contest. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Legendary English cricket writer Neville Cardus once wrote that to properly consider Test cricket, you need to see the big picture.

"I wish to present the Test matches in their setting," he wrote in the introduction to his book chronicling the 1936/37 Ashes series.

"To me cricket must be put against a background."

So what is the background here for Australia?

Australia is about to embark on as busy a Test match year as they have ever had, playing as many as 20 Tests in the next 12 months.

From the Top End, the men's Test team will head to South Africa, play New Zealand and England at home, then face overseas tours to India and England for the Ashes in 2027.

It is a demanding schedule both as physically gruelling and mentally taxing as they come.

Steve Smith and Australia have a lot of thinking to do ahead of the next Test. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Starting off with a two-Test series against Bangladesh, a country Australia has only deigned to host once before for a Test series and only played against in red ball cricket six times in total before this week was considered by most to be a friendly warm up, a competitive practice during a winter sojourn in the Top End sun.

It is, of course, incredibly admirable Cricket Australia is taking Test matches to regions that cannot ever hope to host an Ashes contest.

For financial reasons as much as from a societal responsibility, playing these sorts of Tests in this continent's more remote, northern reaches is undoubtedly the right thing to do.

But maybe there is a sense that this is considered a form of benevolence to the lesser-populated areas of the nation.

Perhaps, for some, even playing Bangladesh is a form of charity to a nation that simply does not have the financial pull of the major nations, little more than an obligation to the World Test Championship.

Maybe, despite protestations to the contrary, that attitude sneaks into the minds of the players, so subliminally that they themselves do not even notice it.

Pat Cummins defended the team's preparation, but perhaps they didn't even realise they were underdone. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

For how can playing in front of about 5,000 spectators in a venue where only half the oval is bordered by a grandstand compare with the cathedral-like cavernous majesty of the MCG, or the lack of pressure contrast with the parochial furnace of a packed Gabba?

Marrara Oval offers neither the stately splendour of the Adelaide Oval or SCG, nor the admittedly under-populated grandiosity of the new Perth Stadium.

Darwin is definitively off-Broadway.

And although Australia's defeat didn't seem to be for lack of effort, the application and necessary quality was lacking throughout the match.

Horror drops from Steve Smith and Nathan Lyon were surely aberrations, but the lazy stroke play and jittery, muddled thinking of the batters was very not.

Steve Smith was not his usual best in the field. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

This shock to a team that has been creaking under the weight of their own success for a number of years now is one that has probably arrived eight months too late.

It was due last summer against England before those Bazballers tripped up over their own hubris.

A papering of the cracks was the result of that emphatic 4-1 Ashes victory, the foundations of sand upon which the top order was built were never tested, the supposedly seismic impact of a fired up England bowling attack never coming to bare, self-sabotaging itself amidst a storm of recriminations in the boozy sand of Noosa.

So on we continued. Australia's brittle batters went off to earn their coin in meaningly limited overs matches and failed to address the issues that have plagued them in red ball cricket, perhaps even accentuating the problems by promoting angled bats and rash shots.

Now the show moves to Mackay and presents Australia with an ever-bigger list of questions and problems to face.

Jake Weatherald's status as opener has to be looked at. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia were rusty and not up to speed in Darwin.

Even if Mackay's Harrup Park, the newest venue to host a men's Test in Australia, provides a suitably refreshed outlook and attitude from Australia next Saturday, will victory there do anything else other than to plaster even more paper over gaps that are swiftly turning into chasms?

It's been eight years since a rambunctious tour almost boiled over, a sorry spectacle that was quickly overshadowed by a sandpaper-scraping that was barely as coarse as the friction generated by two teams flirting on the edge of respectability throughout.

Any weakness in Australia's psyche will be ripe for exploitation in southern Africa, and the venom is unlikely to be as hidden as it was in the far north of Australia.

World.title: Quick hits: Das's redemption and Mehid's Messi attempt
World.content:
Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them, as Mitch Starc's desperate review spoke volumes and Cameron Green's redemptive arc proved to be in vain.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test, as Bangladesh claimed a stunning victory, their first ever in a Test on Australian soil.

1. Das's day four redemption

Das made amends after missing a chance early on day four. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Australia began the day still 67 runs in arrears, knowing that any early slip-ups could prove fatal to their hopes of pulling off an unlikely escape.

So, Alex Carey's heart was surely in his mouth as the excellent Hasan Mahmud had him edging during the fourth over of the day.

It was a tough chance, but one experienced Bangladeshi wicketkeeper Litton Das would have been hopeful of gobbling up.

Das was too slow to react, and the ball flew past his outstretched left glove and to the boundary.

But Carey was unable to profit from that early slice of fortune, finding himself walking back to the pavilion just three overs later.

This time, Das made no mistake with what, probably, was a more difficult chance, with Carey feathering one through off the bowling of spinner Mehidy Hasan Miraz.

It was a superb delivery from Mehidy, pitching and gripping and turning away from the Australian wicketkeeper.

Das had his redemption and Bangladesh was on its way.

2. Webster falls to a beauty

Mehidy produced a peach to dismiss Webster. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

Spin bowling is an art form built on deception, with guile and sleight of hand as important as pin-point accuracy.

On a pitch offering few surprises and only the minimum of turn, it is the impetus of a genuine spinner to trick their way into the minds of their rivals.

Beau Webster had played sensibly through the first 20 balls of his innings, alert to the threat of Mehidy Hasan Miraz's off spinners.

Mehidy was probing at the off stump of Webster, but the ball that deceived him was simply wonderful.

Angling the ball so that the seam would not bite, Mehidy just pushed the ball through a couple of kilometres per hour faster than the balls before.

With no seam to grip, the ball skidded on, perhaps a little lower, and took the top of his off stump.

A master magician couldn't have disguised his intents better and Australia's tail was exposed.

3. Starc's desperate review

Australia began the second session with a 15-run lead and just three wickets in hand, requiring something very special from both Cam Green and Mitch Starc.

So, when Starc nicked off in the third over after lunch, the final nail was well and truly closing in on the Australian coffin.

There was a clear noise and a dramatic deviation, but Starc, well aware of the value of his wicket, decided to send the call upstairs.

Unlike Steve Smith on day three, who had so defiantly called for a review even before Kumar Dharmasena had raised his finger, Starc questioned this decision with embarrassment.

He began his walk from the middle with the review still underway.

There were no ghosts in the machine, no undetected front foot no ball, and Australia was in touching distance of a chastening defeat.

4. Mehidy's footwork lets him down

Given the magic that had been cascading from Mehidy's right hand all day, you wouldn't have put it past the off spinner from doing something special with his foot.

But Mehidy was more messy than Messi when presented with opportunity.

Nathan Lyon, new to crease, was slow to take off for a single, and there was a real chance of a run out, with a Bangladeshi fielder circling in the infield.

But the throw was off target, and Mehidy was forced to improvise, attempting to sidefoot the wayward effort towards the pegs.

Instead, the ball thudded into his ankle and fell limply to earth, Mehidy wincing as he returned to his mark.

It looked like a really painful one, but, thankfully, he was right to continue.

5. Green's drought-breaking ton

Cameron Green scored his first Test century since February 2024. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having not passed 50 in his previous 13 Test innings, Cameron Green's position in the side was very much a topic of conversation heading into this Test.

A jittery run-a-ball 13 in the first innings would have done little but amplify those calls for him to be replaced.

But on days three and four at Marrara, Green delivered everything that he has promised, a third Test century and first on home soil.

There was some luck, Green didn't look good last night and was delivered some divine intervention when an inside edge onto his leg stump didn't produce a wicket, the bail held in place by some benevolent force far in excess of that provided by mere gravity.

But since that fortuitous slice of relief, Green made hay, playing the ball teasingly late from under his eyes, and with the balance and poise of a man who deserves to be batting in Test cricket.

It was his first Test century since he scored 174 not out against New Zealand in Wellington back in February 2024.

Tech.title: Wordle meets Clippy in this new word game
Tech.content:
Like many of us, Sam Rosenthal plays games like Wordle every day, chasing after good scores and sharing the results with friends and family. But he’s also a game designer, the creative director at Blaseball developer The Game Band, and so this regular habit got him thinking about what else could be done in the space. “When I was a kid and I played word games with my family, they weren’t the New York Times puzzle games,” Rosenthal explains. “We were sitting in a car on a road trip playing these really loose games that couldn’t be made digitally before. Things like the alphabet game or our own riffs on 20 questions. That felt like a really interesting space to explore.”

This led to Dartwords, a new daily word game that launches today on the web. Dartwords is a word guessing game: Each day there’s a secret word, and you have 10 chances to figure out what it is. To start, you have no hints. You simply type in a word — any word — and from there a little Clippy-like character named Darty will respond with clues based on your guess. For instance, you might guess a type of animal, and Darty might respond saying that the answer is bigger, or maybe that it’s manmade. With each guess a dart hits a board on the screen, getting closer to the bullseye as you get closer to the right answer.

The success of Wordle has led to a deluge of daily puzzle games, particularly in the word game space, and Rosenthal says the goal of Dartwords was to create an experience that was “more conversational” compared to its contemporaries. In order to make it work, he says that the studio built a bespoke hint engine utilizing a local LLM trained on the English dictionary. He explains that Darty’s clues are a combination of broader hints generated by the LLM and, as you get closer to the correct response, clues written by the developers. “It’s this interesting mixture of using hand-authored work and local models to get us to where we want to be,” he says.

(On the subject of AI, Rosenthal says that all of the art and UI / UX in the game is handmade, while “we do use tools like Claude Code to speed up day-to-day coding tasks, but we pair them with our taste, judgment, and careful reviews.”)

Image: The Game Band

For me at least, it took a few rounds to get the hang of it. The open-ended nature of Dartwords can be almost paralyzing, as you have to try to think of a word that will get you a good hint. But eventually I started to have a better feel for how to follow up the game’s hints, and this morning I managed to get the right answer in just three guesses, a personal record. The hope is that if Dartwords becomes a success with a large player base, things will improve based on feedback and data. “Over time, with more people playing the game, our system will get better and better and hopefully serve better clues,” says Rosenthal.

Dartwords joins an increasingly eclectic lineup of games from the studio. The Game Band got its start with the narrative puzzler Where Cards Fall before launching the surreal baseball simulator Blaseball that went viral during the pandemic. More recently, the studio released Dead Man’s Party, a Knives Out-themed party game that’s part of Netflix’s current push into TV games. But with Dartwords, the studio is entering a particularly challenging and crowded space buoyed by the breakout success of Wordle. Since then, everywhere from LinkedIn to The Atlantic has started launching daily puzzle games, while platforms like Puzzmo provide their own alternative.

Rosenthal believes that one of the differentiating factors for Dartwords is Darty itself: a goofy sentient dart with big, expressive eyes and tiny hands for clapping. “Darty was literally inspired by Clippy,” he says. “The whole intent is that we wanted it to be a loose word game. It’s more improvisational, it feels more conversational. And because of that, we need something for people to get mad at if it gives you a bad clue. We want this game to feel charming and fun, and have a little more character to it than you traditionally get in word games.”

Tech.title: YouTube is changing how it counts views to give the numbers a boost
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

YouTube will soon count a view as soon as a video starts to play, lining up with the system used by Instagram, TikTok, and its Shorts videos. The update will go into effect on August 24th, “which means creators will likely see their total view counts increase faster moving forward,” the platform says.

Instagram and TikTok similarly add a view to a video when it starts to play or replay, while X counts a view when a user watches a video for at least two seconds. YouTube applied Instagram and TikTok’s view-counting method to Shorts last year.

YouTube says it’s going to keep its original view-counting method under an “engaged views” metric in its Analytics dashboard. As my colleague David Pierce notes, it’s not entirely clear how YouTube counted views before this, but “it’s generally accepted wisdom that you have to watch 30 seconds of a standard YouTube video for it to count.”

The change won’t impact creators’ earnings or how they’re eligible for the YouTube Partner Program (YPP), according to the blog post. Creator earnings will also still be based on “engaged Short views” and “engaged watch hours.”

This isn’t the only creator-related update YouTube has made lately, as the platform is also upping the requirements needed to join the YPP next year.

“Historically, we’ve used multiple view counting systems across different formats,” YouTube says in its update. “However, we’ve heard that creators want to eliminate this metric confusion and accurately understand their true exposure… We hope that having metric parity across all formats gives creators a clearer picture of their overall exposure.”

Tech.title: Sonos finally added Live Activities controls for your iPhone lockscreen
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sonos released an update to its mobile app that finally introduces support for iOS’ Live Activities, giving iPhone users quick access to playback controls on their lockscreen. The added functionality is a “much requested, anticipated, and needed feature,” according to a post Sonos shared to Reddit today that was spotted by 9to5Mac.

While some features like displaying album art are not available, the Sonos Live Activity provides basic details and controls when listening to music or podcasts through a Sonos system without having to fully unlock your iPhone and open the app.

Support for Live Activities and lockscreen controls similar to what’s already available in the Android version of the Sonos app was teased by the company’s CEO Tom Conrad during an interview with Bloomberg last February. And following backlash to a major Sonos app update in 2024, support for Live Activities is off by default but can be enabled by navigating to both the Sonos app’s preferences as well as the Sonos app section of iOS’ settings.

Once it’s turned on, the Live Activity will appear “after you initiate playback and then close the app” and displays the name of the group or room where audio was last playing from and the title of what you’re listening to. After playback stops, the Live Activity will automatically disappear from your lockscreen after 15 minutes.

Support for the Apple Watch and CarPlay is included, but while the Live Activity will be displayed on your wrist or in your car, the controls aren’t supported there. It’s not known if or when those controls will ever work, but Sonos says its team is still working to improve the new feature, and when it comes to album art, the company is exploring “alternative ways to enhance the lock screen experience.”

Tech.title: Trump’s dumb border wall
Tech.content:
is a policy reporter at The Verge covering surveillance, the Department of Homeland Security, and the tech-right.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

About 22 miles south of the former mining town of Patagonia, Arizona, down a winding, unpaved mountain road that passes cows grazing on open range, stands a cottonwood tree believed to be at least 200 years old. The “grandmother” tree, as some locals call it, is imperiled and already showing signs of stress, almost as if it knows its fate. The leaves are yellowing prematurely, falling to the ground at the height of summer. On July 27th, a construction crew felled three neighboring trees to build an extension of President Donald Trump’s wall along the US-Mexico border.

An activist climbed up the last tree standing two days later and ever since, someone has sat on a platform hoisted onto the tree’s branches. They say they’ll sit there as long as it takes, because as long as someone is in the tree, it can’t be cut down.

The protest is about more than one cottonwood. “This tree represents a literal line in the sand against border militarization in general,” said Russ McSpadden, the Southwest conservation advocate for the Center for Biological Diversity.

In recent weeks, the Department of Homeland Security has revived its effort to wall off the border, dispatching construction crews to remote parts of Texas, Arizona, and the Tohono O’odham Nation’s reservation lands to finish Trump’s wall — and has waived environmental laws to get it built, causing backlash from the tiny desert town of Ajo to the even tinier ghost town of Terlingua.

This latest construction push is happening despite record-low encounters along the southwestern border. In fact, encounters at the southwest border dropped almost immediately after Trump took office — not because of any new infrastructure, but because he effectively shut down asylum. Despite the steep decline in migrant crossings, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which passed along party lines in 2025, gave Trump an additional $46.5 billion to finish building the wall.

The border wall is more than just a wall; it’s a vast surveillance network of interconnected drones, towers, and cameras. Even in areas where there’s no visible barrier separating the United States and Mexico, CBP relies on this “virtual wall” to track migrants. This vast surveillance apparatus is far more effective than a wall, and it’s already largely in place.

In the ghost town of Lochiel, Arizona, activists from surrounding communities have set up an encampment on private property near the cottonwood tree to support the protest. They take turns cooking meals and use a pulley system to transport food and water to the person sitting in the tree. They know they’re being watched. Trucks from Vision Quest Solutions, a private security firm that advertises itself as veteran- and Native American-owned, roll up and down the fresh dirt road just south of the tree. The activists track the various contractors that are building the road: Fisher Sand & Gravel, BJ Drilling, Stinger Bridge & Iron, and others.

Homeland Security contractors drive past an ancient cottonwood tree in Lochiel, Arizona. Activists have been occupying the tree since July 29th. Photo: Gaby Del Valle / The Verge

Henry, a community organizer from Tucson who is participating in the encampment, said that a DHS helicopter flew “dangerously close” to the tree on August 10th.

“This movement was started and held down for a long time by local environmentalists who care really deeply about these ancient cottonwood trees,” said Henry, who asked to be referred to by a pseudonym. He is among a newer group of activists “who see it as an opportunity to physically stop border wall construction.”

The planned construction projects differ by region. In Arizona’s San Rafael Valley, where an older fence already divides Mexico and the United States, DHS is building a wall featuring 30-foot-tall steel bollards. The plan is to have a “double wall” throughout the Arizona-Mexico border — one that runs through the Tohono O’odham reservation, Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, and the San Rafael Valley. To achieve this, DHS contractors are tearing down the old fence, replacing it with the new bollards, and building an entirely new wall a few dozen feet away. The cottonwood tree sits directly in the path of the second wall.

“They’re approaching the tree from both sides with their work crews,” Henry said. “I don’t really know what their plan is once they don’t have anything else to do.”

In Big Bend National Park, Customs and Border Protection is building what it calls a “Technology & Patrol Road,” or a “smart wall” system of sensors, cameras, and surveillance towers accessible via a new road — even though there’s an existing road that cuts through the park.

Responding to mass outcry about recent construction in Big Bend, CBP chief Rodney Scott said that DHS isn’t building a wall. “CBP is building one new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology, and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations,” Scott said in an emailed statement. “What people are seeing right now is survey and design work—NOT construction of a wall through the park.” (The statement was also posted near-verbatim on DHS’s X account. )

Unlike in other areas along the border, Scott said, CBP isn’t building a 30-foot wall or installing stadium lighting in Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area.

On August 17th, Scott announced that CBP is pausing all construction in Big Bend National Park while he conducts a “personal, on-the-ground evaluation.” Reporters with Marfa Public Radio who flew over the park this morning saw staged construction vehicles, but noted that the crews weren’t working, according to station manager Travis Bubenik.

Outraged locals, joined by environmentalists from across the country, charge that CBP doesn’t need to build a 30-foot wall to destroy local ecosystems. Over the weekend, contractors started digging into Mariscal Mountain, a massive limestone ridge, ostensibly as part of the survey and design work needed to build its patrol road.

You can call it what you want. You’re destroying what we’re trying to protect. — Billy Miller, a river guide and landowner in Terlingua, Texas.

CBP maintains that its goal is to ensure Big Bend remains open to the public. According to agency spokesperson John Mennell, the “smart wall” CBP plans on installing in the area is proactive, not reactive. Though the national park and Border Patrol’s greater Big Bend sector — which encompasses 165,154 square miles — has historically seen fewer crossings than other parts of the border, Mennell said that the buildup of security elsewhere could push migrants into Big Bend.

The Center for Biological Diversity sued the Trump administration last year, arguing that waiving environmental laws to build Trump’s wall “violates the foundational principle of the separation of powers rooted in the US Constitution.” But a federal judge effectively closed the case in March, citing two laws that let DHS disregard nearly three dozen federal laws — including the Endangered Species Act, the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, and the Clean Air Act — to “ensure expeditious construction of the barriers and roads” along the border. A separate lawsuit, filed by the Center for Biological Diversity, a local church, and Billy Miller, a river guide and landowner in Terlingua, Texas, is ongoing.

“Their lawyers — the contractor’s lawyers, the federal government’s lawyers — told us they would give us 30 days’ advance notice before any ground disturbance,” Miller, who has been a river guide in the area for 22 years, told The Verge. “But they just started destroying the river corridor this past week without telling us anything.”

The government’s attorneys, he said, countered that there hasn’t been any ground disturbance, since what they’re doing is “grubbing and pioneering to create access roads to the river.”

“You can call it what you want,” Miller said. “You’re destroying what we’re trying to protect. Y’all were supposed to tell us about it.”

Miller said that he and other locals have been told that the new CBP roads won’t be open to the public; only Border Patrol will be able to use them. “That’s heartbreaking. You’re going to destroy our national park, or take away private landowners’ property, and create roads nobody can use?” he said. According to Mennell, the CBP spokesperson, the National Park Service will decide whether the roads will be open to the public.

“You’re taking a wilderness area that’s really hard to get through, really hard to walk through on foot, and now you’re creating a brand-new road? They’re creating roads that smugglers could use, if there were smugglers out here in the first place.”

People protest the plans by US President Donald Trump’s administration to build a section of the border wall at the Big Bend National Park in Study Butte, Texas, on August 15, 2026. Photo: Ronald Schemidt / AFP via Getty Images

CBP also plans on installing vehicle barriers that locals say will block their access to the Rio Grande, which would threaten Miller and other river guides’ livelihood. In addition to destroying landscapes, jeopardizing livelihoods, and endangering migrants, the border wall threatens migratory species across the Southwest, including Sonoran pronghorns and Mexican gray wolves.

Over the last two weeks, the small, tight-knit community has been invaded by hundreds of construction workers. “Some businesses, like the Starlight Theatre, which is the most popular restaurant in town, have put up a sign that says they refuse to serve border wall workers or border barrier construction workers,” said Miller.

Though Trump received 55.6 percent of the vote in Texas’ Brewster County, the community is almost universally opposed to the wall. Miller has friends and relatives who “voted for Trump without really thinking that he would ever try to build a wall out here,” he said. “And now they are kicking themselves in the ass for voting for him.”

Locals share the opinion that the wall isn’t about border security or immigration. It’s about money. Some of the contractors, they point out, are run by major Trump donors. Fisher Sand & Gravel, one of the contractors working on the wall in Arizona, reportedly lobbied Trump directly, and was awarded a nearly $1.3 billion contract during his first term.

On Wednesday, over 100 people attended a protest in Big Bend National Park’s Santa Elena Canyon. Their chants of “no road, no wall, no wire, no way” echoed off the surrounding cliffs.

Michael Ryan, a retired National Park Service river ranger who attended the rally, said some people he talked to drove more than 100 miles to be there. “We never thought we would see anything like this,” said Ryan, who has lived in the Big Bend region for 35 years. “We used to think more Airbnbs in the area was about the worst thing that could ever happen to us, and now the scope and scale of this construction is mind-boggling.”

In Arizona and Texas alike, locals see the wall as not only wasteful but destructive.

“They could spend this money on more agents if they wanted to, more infrared cameras, more motion sensors, more drones,” said Miller, the Big Bend river guide. “Even though that’s, to everybody out here, a complete waste of money, that would be more effective than what they’re planning.”

Update, August 17th: After publication, CBP announced it would pause construction in Big Bend National Park. The piece has been updated to reflect the announcement.

Tech.title: Apple ordered to stop scaring iPhone and iPad users away from third-party apps
Tech.content: In its preliminary assessment, the Bundeskartellamt considered that the current design of the [App Tracking Transparency] prompt steers users towards refusing consent, whereas the design of the [Personalized Ads] prompt steers them towards giving their consent to the use of their data for advertising purposes. Factors that contribute to this steering effect include the symbols used (for example, a warning hand symbol), different wordings (“app tracking” versus “personalised advertising”), partially ambiguous descriptions of how the data will be used, differences in the space available to explain the advantages of allowing data use, and the order in which the selection options are displayed.

Tech.title: Uber partners with Zipline on Eats drone deliveries
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Uber is teaming up with drone company Zipline to start airborne takeout deliveries later this year, with the goal of reaching one million daily drone deliveries by 2029.

Uber also said it was making a strategic investment in Zipline, a California-based company that has been orchestrating drone deliveries in Texas since 2025. The news comes as Uber’s delivery rivals begin to step up their own drone deliveries, thanks to easing government regulations that allow companies to fly farther and cheaper.

The Uber Eats deliveries will start in Zipline’s existing market of Dallas-Fort Worth, before eventually expanding to dozens of additional cities. Zipline, which has made two million deliveries so far, also operates overseas, including Rwanda, Ghana, Japan, Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, and Kenya. The company first started operations in Rwanda in 2016, delivering medical supplies in minutes to remote locations. The deal is similar to one Uber made with drone company Flytrex last year, which also included an investment by the ridehail giant.

Uber says that Zipline’s drones can bring a customer’s order to their front lawn in a “matter of minutes.” The company claims it is building the world’s largest hybrid network of human couriers, sidewalk robots, and drones, in which customers are matched with the best, most efficient method of delivery, depending on where they live.

But while Uber partners with third-party drone operators, its rivals are seeking regulator approval to deploy their own drones. Last month, DoorDash launched its own drone delivery program called DoorDash Air, after receiving approval from the Federal Aviation Administration.

Thanks to a 2025 order from President Donald Trump, the FAA has proposed new rules to expand the deployment of drone delivery operations. As such, drone operators are scrambling to secure partnerships with grocery chains and major retailers in the hopes of claiming their share of what could be $7.7 billion market by 2031, according to one analysis.

Tech.title: Higgsfield raises $400M Series B, quadrupling its valuation in 8 months to $5.4B
Tech.content:
In Brief

Higgsfield announced Monday that it has raised a $400 million Series B at a $5.4 billion valuation. This new round is just eight months after nabbing a $1.3 billion valuation.

Higgsfield, founded by former Snap exec Alex Mashrabov in 2023, lets users create AI images and videos. It made headlines this past year for premiering AI-generated movies at both Cannes and in New York. It has tools like the Cinema Studio to help filmmakers direct AI films and the Marketing Studio for marketing and advertising teams. In a release announcing the round, the company touted $700 million in annualized revenue and 30 million users across 200 countries.

One growing market for the company has been enterprises. It is now working with 390 of the Fortune 500, it said. Mashrabov told TechCrunch that Higgsfield expects “enterprise adoption of video AI to become much more deeply embedded in everyday marketing and creative workflows.”

The fresh capital will fund the usual business needs like hiring and product development. But it will also help pay for compute. “Video is one of the most compute-intensive domains in AI,” Mashrabov explained. Just one minute of video is like processing 60,000 words. Securing reliable compute capacity has therefore become a necessary expense to remain competitive with others in the industry like Synthesia and Runway.



DST Global led the latest round, with many other investors piling in including Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Valor Capital, and Tribe Capital.

Tech.title: Reddit begins testing a new audio and video experience, similar to popular TikTok videos
Tech.content:
Reddit recently said it would bring most viral stories to life through a new “video Reddit” experience, allowing users to listen to Reddit posts in the background while doing other tasks and activities. On Monday, Reddit will begin testing an initial version of this experience with both video and audio posts across select communities to see which type of posts resonate with its users and have the potential to scale.

The company first announced its plans for narrated Reddit videos during its second-quarter earnings call in July, when CEO Steve Huffman told analysts on the quarterly call that people were already consuming Reddit content like this on other platforms.

He was referring to how other social media platforms, like TikTok and Meta’s Reels, often feature popular Reddit stories narrated through a text-to-speech feature or read aloud by creators. Some of those videos display the words on screen as they’re read or are accompanied by unrelated footage, like video gameplay or cooking content.

Screenshot of TikTok’s Reddit stories Image Credits:TikTok screenshot

“There is an emerging content type elsewhere on the internet of, basically, podcasts where people read Reddit content,” Huffman explained on the call. “I think this version of, like, listened-to or spoken Reddit can be really engaging, as well,” he added.

Reddit tells TechCrunch the initial tests are early, limited experiments meant to provide the company with a better understanding of how these formats can be useful to users, and whether they can be done in a way that feels authentic to Reddit. Users will be able to choose whether they want to “read” or “play” a post, when available.

The test will focus only on select English-language posts for the time being, and will be accessible through Reddit’s iOS and Android apps.

The different formats will not replace the original, text-only post, Reddit notes. Both the original post and the comments can still be viewed and engaged with as before. Instead, Reddit suggests that people may sometimes want to listen to Reddit audio while exercising, walking, or running errands, while others might want to watch written conversations come to life through video and audio combined.

This isn’t the first time Reddit has experimented with video. The company in earlier years rolled out native video hosting and tried various iterations of a TikTok-style video feed. More recently, Reddit launched support for video in comments, which it says now accounts for more than 10% of video posts on its platform.

Tech.title: Sound-powered fire protection startup gets $15M to snuff out fires before they turn catastrophic
Tech.content:
For over a century, fire protection has been limited to water and chemicals. And while they can prevent catastrophic fires, the cleanup bills can be significant.

But maybe not for long. Sonic Fire Tech is testing a sound-powered fire protection system, which it says snuffs out fires within seconds while also sparing properties from messy water and chemical damage. The company announced Monday that it has raised a $15 million round led by The O.H.I.O. Fund with participation from Khosla Ventures. The startup previously raised a $3.5 million seed in October.

The fresh funding will help the Ohio-based startup hire more employees and run the battery of tests needed to earn approval from the National Fire Protection Association, which writes model codes adopted by fire departments around the country.

Approval typically takes about three years, but co-founder and CEO Geoff Bruder told TechCrunch he thinks that Sonic Fire Tech’s process will be “significantly shorter than that.”

Part of Bruder’s optimism stems from the fact that Sonic Fire Tech’s system doesn’t leave a mess after a fire suppression event, which should speed up the process. The tests are conducted in a lab and preparation can take hours. With Sonic Fire Tech’s system, “they don’t have to do cleanup,” he said.

That advantage in the lab could pay dividends in the real world. Commercial kitchens, for example, can face months of cleanup and restoration following a fire. Some 75% of them don’t reopen, Remington Bixby Hotchkis, Sonic Fire Tech’s COO, told TechCrunch.

Sonic Fire Tech’s acoustic fire suppression system uses a sound generator to pump inaudible sound through PVC pipes in the ceiling. When sensors in a room detect a fire, the generator kicks in and infrasonic waves, around 20 Hz, bombard the flames.

“We are the only technology that creates its own suppressant without collateral damage. False alarms are less of a concern for us,” Hotchkis said. “We deploy within seconds.”

That speedy response could stop fires before they cause significant damage, which has the insurance industry interested. The startup is in talks with insurers about whether the system will qualify for premium discounts. The insurance industry’s acceptance could speed adoption of the company’s product.

The system also shows promise when applied to lithium-ion battery fires, which are among the most challenging to put out. In the few tests Sonic Fire Tech has run so far, “we don’t put out a lithium-ion fire, but we contain it,” Bruder said. “If we’re able to keep the outer casing from lighting fire, we can potentially stop cell-to-cell spread and limit the size of the fire.”

Sonic Fire Tech is working on systems to protect the interiors of commercial buildings, kitchens, and homes, both for new construction and retrofits. The company has also been working on a system to safeguard the exterior of homes in wildfire country, though development of that has progressed more slowly as the startup waits for time at a suitable testing lab.

In addition to quicker fire suppression, Sonic Fire Tech’s system promises to lower restoration costs, if any are needed.

Today, about 500 jurisdictions mandate interior fire protection systems. But Bruder points out that 50% of home fires start in the kitchen, whether they be grease or electrical fires. Even a small Sonic Fire Tech system, focused on the kitchen, could go a long way to minimizing the risk of catastrophic house fires, lowering premiums in the process. “Sprinklers that they’re putting in now can’t handle those fires,” Bruder said.

Tech.title: YouTube will now count a view as soon as a video starts playing
Tech.content:
YouTube announced on Monday that it’s changing how views are counted on its platform, with a view now counting as soon as a video starts playing or someone enters a live broadcast. Although the Google-owned platform never disclosed how it previously counted views, it was generally understood that a view was counted after a user watched at least 30 seconds of a video.

The change comes a year after YouTube applied the same approach to counting views on Shorts videos. It’s worth noting that rivals TikTok and Instagram also count views as soon as a video starts playing.

“Historically, we’ve used multiple view counting systems across different formats,” the company wrote in a YouTube Community post. “However, we’ve heard that creators want to eliminate this metric confusion and accurately understand their true exposure, which is why we’re making this update.”

The shift could lead to significantly increased YouTube view counts, especially for videos that only briefly capture viewers’ attention. That means public view counts may no longer be a useful tool for creators and advertisers to determine how popular a video may be.

YouTube says it will keep the original view metric, now called “Engaged views,” accessible to creators through its Analytics tools to allow them to see how many viewers chose to continue watching their videos.

The company notes that the change won’t impact creators’ earnings or how they become eligible for monetization through the YouTube Partner Program.

The update, which goes into effect on August 24, comes a week after YouTube made another creator-focused change, announcing that new creators will have to meet higher thresholds to begin earning money from ads and subscriptions starting next year.

Creators who want to start earning on the platform will need at least 8,000 qualified watch hours over the past year or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days. Currently, creators need 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 watch hours over the past year or 1,000 subscribers and 10 million Shorts views over the past 90 days. Additionally, creators need to maintain 10 million Shorts views over a 90-day period to earn money.

The decision has drawn backlash from users, as it will make it harder for creators to enter and remain in YouTube’s monetization program.

Tech.title: Feedly attributes weeklong slowdown to bug, not its AI pivot
Tech.content:
Bad news for those who get their updates through RSS feeds: Feedly, the largest stand-alone RSS reader worldwide, has experienced technical issues for over a week, and paying users are upset that the web app has been “unusably slow.” Some users have also reported that the company has ignored their support requests. Uh-oh.

Feedly, the heir to the market ceded by Google when it closed Google Reader in 2013, is today among the most successful RSS newsreaders globally with 15 million users, according to its website. That makes it larger than competitive products like the web-based Inoreader as well as various desktop apps like NetNewsWire, Reeder, and others.

And yet, the app is experiencing a number of ongoing issues that are affecting users and paying subscribers alike. The most critical problem is a significant slowdown on its web app, which has made browsing feeds quickly and efficiently very frustrating. Users on Reddit reported the app running “extremely” slow, making it “unusable.”

Further, users said that the company’s iOS app, including on iOS 27 beta, has not been working, and the classic version of Feedly’s mobile app (preferred by a small subset of customers) was shut down without warning weeks ago.

As most consumers now keep up with news through dedicated apps, like Apple News by browsing the web and sources like Google News, and through posts on social media, the market for RSS readers has always been relatively small. However, Feedly has been working to shift its focus to AI, offering businesses a way to track emerging threats and keep up with tailored intelligence through its app.

With the latest issues, it begs the question as to whether Feedly is still focused on its core RSS customers amid its pivot to AI, which is the product the company now advertises via its homepage.

TechCrunch reached out to Feedly for an update on these issues, given that multiple customers on Reddit said their requests for technical support had been ignored.

In response, Feedly CEO Edwin Khodabakchian reassured TechCrunch that RSS was still a focus.

“Despite the pivot to cyber threat intelligence, fixing the basic RSS functionality is still a priority because our CTI community uses the news-reading capability,” he said. “Our goal has been to maintain the Feedly News Reader as fast and streamlined as possible.”

In addition, the CEO said the company was aware of the issues with its web app, which were attributed to a bug, and said the front-end team had been testing a fix. Currently, the team believes the issue was related to using “Mark as Read” on accounts with a lot of folders, and a fix for that was released Friday. The company is still confirming whether this has resolved the problem for all users.

Khodabakchian also confirmed that the Feedly Classic app was “retired two weeks ago because it “no longer met some iOS and Android requirements,” though it had been removed from the App Store long before that. At the time, the app had only a few hundred active users, he noted. The team did not notify those existing users before its final shutdown.

In addition, Khodabakchian said he was not aware of the iOS app issues, which prevent the app from loading, but said Feedly would investigate. He also promised it would be fixed quickly, noting that the company still actively invests in its main iOS and Android app.

Tech.title: Amazon, which started off selling books, is destroying rare texts to train AI
Tech.content:
In Brief

Amazon is buying tons of rare books, cutting off their spines, and scanning them for AI training, according to 404 Media, which placed a tracking device in a rare book that ultimately arrived at an Amazon facility in Las Vegas.

The facility, known as VGT3, identifies itself with a symbol of a dinosaur holding a book in its claws. Amazon told 404 Media in a statement that it “purchases books through commercial channels to improve the products and services customers use.”

Companies like Amazon need unfathomably large amounts of text to train their LLMs, which have already ingested what they can from the internet (and, in Anthropic’s case, illegally pirated books). Rare books, especially ones that are out of print or impossible to find on the internet, offer a new source of coveted training data.

These texts are especially valuable since there’s no chance that anything published before 2022 was written by an LLM. When LLMs train on AI-generated text, they risk “model collapse,” which can occur when the quality of an LLM’s outputs degrade after ingesting too much AI-generated text.

Tech.title: Groq raises $350M to fuel its pivot from AI chips to neocloud
Tech.content:
Startup Groq has raised $350 million as it continues to pivot from an AI chipmaker to a neocloud company that provides powerful GPUs and AI infrastructure services.

The new capital, led by investment firm Disruptive with planned participation from Nvidia, values the company at $3.5 billion. That’s down from the $6.9 billion Groq was valued at last September, just a few months before Nvidia hired the startup’s founder and CEO, Jonathan Ross, and other top talent as part of a $20 billion licensing deal that the company paid out to investors.

A spokesperson for the company told TechCrunch that despite the difference in valuation, the company doesn’t see it as a down round, but rather as establishing a new valuation for the “post-Nvidia-licensing-deal version of Groq.”

Groq was focused on building its own chips, dubbed LPUs (language processing units), to compete with Nvidia on inference — the type of compute needed to run AI workloads in real time. After it lost its star team, Groq shifted from being a pure AI chipmaker into a cloud and data center provider that operates Nvidia systems.

In June, Groq raised a $650 million round to kick off its pivot. Groq intends to scale from 54 megawatts to more than 200 megawatts in 2027.

Today, Groq operates 13 data centers across North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia Pacific, serving more than 6 million developers, enterprises, and AI-native companies. Groq says the fresh funds will support “those seeking usage of medium and larger sized clusters of Nvidia accelerated computing for training and inference.”

“We are building Groq into the world’s leading AI inference cloud,” Alex Davis, Groq’s chairman and CEO of Disruptive, said in a statement. “Inference will without a doubt become the largest and most critical layer of AI infrastructure.”

While inference is in high demand as enterprises scale AI workloads, it’s an open question whether neoclouds will be a profitable enough business to provide returns on their considerable investment in the long term. CoreWeave reported strong second-quarter revenue growth and recently landed major contracts, including with Meta and Anthropic. However, investors remained concerned about the company’s high capital expenditures, heavy reliance on debt, and exposure to rapidly depreciating hardware, and its ability to turn growth into free cash flow.

Groq’s financials are still private for now, but its pivot puts the company directly inside Nvidia’s AI infrastructure ecosystem. That’s not exactly a unique relationship among neoclouds today. Nvidia supplies the GPUs powering clouds from CoreWeave, Lambda, and Nebius, while also investing billions into some of those companies as they race to build more capacity.

TechCrunch has reached out to Groq for more information.

Tech.title: Nvidia investing $1.5B in SoftBank data center developer behind OpenAI project
Tech.content:
In Brief

Nvidia said on Monday that it will invest $1.5 billion in SB Energy, a data center linked to SoftBank and OpenAI.

The investment ensures that Nvidia will be the sole supplier of compute infrastructure at OpenAI’s Ports-Pike data center near Cincinnati, Ohio. Nvidia will also provide up to $105 billion in credit to help build the facility, which could scale from an initial 4.25 gigawatts to 8 gigawatts in size, according to documents the company filed with the SEC.

SB Energy’s existing investors include SoftBank and OpenAI. SoftBank had previously held $5.8 billion worth of Nvidia stock, which it sold in November to help fund other AI investments.

The data center and power developer will build a 9.2 gigawatt natural gas power plant on the site, which is land owned by the U.S. Department of Energy. The site previously enriched uranium for the U.S. nuclear arsenal and for U.S. Navy submarines.

The power plant is expected to cost $33 billion. The steep sum reflects the skyrocketing costs of building natural gas power plants, which have risen 66% in the last two years, according to BloombergNEF.

By the time SB Energy’s power plant and others are completed, they’ll be competing for natural gas with export markets, a confluence that could triple natural gas prices in some parts of the country.

Tech.title: 7 Best Cheap Laptops to Buy in 2026 (and Some to Avoid)
Tech.content:
Compare Top 7 Budget Laptops

Other Budget Laptops to Consider

Here at WIRED, we never recommend products we haven't tested ourselves—and I’ve tried hundreds of laptops over the years. I left many laptops off this list due to price, quality, or both. While I stand by my top-pick recommendations above, there are a few additional laptops I've tested that are still worth buying for a particular use case.

Photograph: Luke Larsen

Lenovo LOQ 15 for $1,400: This fantastic gaming laptop used to sell for $900, despite coming with an RTX 5060. And unlike so many other affordable gaming laptops, this one comes with a solid IPS panel that has not only a fast refresh rate but also great image quality. So no, it's not extremely cheap, but it's worth considering because it remains the best value in gaming laptops right now.

Acer Chromebook Plus 516 for $479: Chromebooks are really at their best when they cost less than $500. They thrive as cheap laptops that don't feel cheap. The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 has one primary advantage over other laptops around this price: its touchpad. I care a lot about touchpad quality, as it's an area where budget laptops tend to make compromises despite being a component that can impact day-to-day laptop use. Poor touchpad quality can make simple things like drag-and-drop or text selection frustrating. The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 has a really nice touchpad with a smooth surface for your finger to swipe or drag across. It makes a huge difference.

Acer Nitro V 16 for $900: No gaming laptop selling for this price is going to be perfect. Far from it. The Acer Nitro V 16 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) has a big compromise that I need to warn you about up front: its 135-watt power adapter. It's just not enough to keep the Nitro V 16 fully powered during many of the GPU-heavy games I tested, such as Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong. That means even if the laptop is plugged in, it'll start to drain the battery when you tax the GPU hard enough. That sounds awful, and it is. Acer could have easily sold the Nitro V 16 with a larger adapter. But the battery only drains in certain games and only when playing in Turbo or Performance modes. Stick to Balanced mode, and you'll be fine, as it only drops performance by around 5 percent. All said, I still think the MSI Cyborg A15 is the better laptop for this reason.

Lenovo Chromebook Duet Gen 9 for $379: Lenovo’s Chromebook Duet Gen 9 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) quickly became one of my favorite gadgets of 2024, despite its small size. That’s the whole point of this 11-inch detachable laptop, which is incredibly fun to use around the house and throw in a bag when it’s time to go. The keyboard detaches from the screen, so it makes for a nice tablet when paired with ChromeOS's Android apps. With the keyboard attached, you can get some work done. At nearly 10 hours on average, its battery life will easily get you through the day, too.

Cheap Laptops to Avoid

Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1. Photograph: Luke Larsen

Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1: 16-inch laptops tend to be more expensive than smaller options, making them hard to find at a cheap price. The Lenovo IdeaPad 5i 2-in-1 (6/10, WIRED Recommends) is a 16-inch laptop that tried to squeeze out just enough quality to make it worth the price. While the display has typical deficiencies (such as poor color coverage), I do appreciate that it doesn't have a matte finish, which brings out more clarity in the panel. I also found the keyboard tiresome to type on, and ultimately feel the OmniBook 3 is the better laptop for the price.

Asus Vivobook 14: As one of the first cheap laptops to use the Snapdragon X, I praised this laptop through 2025 for its excellent battery life. But once the OmniBook 5 and OmniBook 3 came along, I stopped recommending the Vivobook 14. That's primarily because of how much better the OLED screens are on the OmniBook devices compared to the washed-out display that comes on the Vivobook 14. But if you ever see this drop to below the price of the OmniBook 3 and want the cheapest Windows laptop possible, it might be worth considering.

What Are Important Specs in a Cheap Laptop? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Read our guide on How to Choose the Right Laptop if you want all the details on specs and what to look for. In short, your budget is the most important factor, as it determines what you can expect out of the device you're purchasing. Next, you should consider display size, chassis thickness, CPU, memory, storage, and port selection. While appropriate specs can vary wildly when you're considering laptops ranging from $200 to around $1,000, there are a few hard lines I don't recommend crossing. For example, don't buy a laptop if it doesn't have a display resolution of at least 1920 x 1080. In 2025, there's just no excuse for anything less than that. You should also never buy a laptop without at least 8 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. Even in Chromebooks, these specs are becoming the new standard. You're selling yourself short by getting anything less. Another rule is to avoid a Windows laptop with an Intel Celeron processor—leave those for Chromebooks only. Specs are only half the battle, though. Based on our years of testing, laptop manufacturers tend to make compromises in display quality and touchpad quality. You can't tell from the photos or listed specs online, but once you get the laptop in your hands, you may notice that the colors of the screen look a bit off or that the touchpad feels choppy to use. It's nearly impossible to find laptops under $500 that don't compromise in these areas, but this is where our reviewers and testers can help. How Much RAM Do You Need in a Cheap Laptop? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The simple answer? You need at least 8 GB of RAM, but you'll likely want at least 16 GB. These days, lots of Windows laptops that fall into the “budget” category come with 16 GB of RAM standard t, as part of the Copilot+ PC marketing push. That's a great value that ensures you'll get the best performance out of your laptop, especially when running heavier applications or multitasking. Either way, it's important to factor in the price of the RAM because manufacturers will often charge $100 or even $200 to double the memory. On Chromebooks, there are some rare occasions where 4 GB of RAM is acceptable, but only on the very cheapest models that are less than $200. Even budget Chromebooks like the Asus Chromebook CX15 now start with 8 GB of RAM. Prices are constantly shifting, however, largely because of the ongoing memory shortage. We are starting to see the return of 8 GB in laptops like the MacBook Neo and Dell XPS 13, but I recommend opting for 16 GB if at all possible. Are There Any Good Laptops Under $300? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Yes, but you need to be careful. Don't just go buy a random laptop on Amazon for less than $300, as you'll likely end up with an outdated, slow device you'll regret having purchased. You might be tempted by something like this or this, but trust me—there are better options, some of which you'll find in this guide. For starters, you shouldn't buy a Windows laptop for less than $300. That price puts you solidly in cheap Chromebook territory. These Chromebooks are budget-level in terms of quality, but they're still better in almost every way than their Windows counterparts of a similar price. A good example is the Asus Chromebook CX15. If you want a Windows laptop that won't give you instant buyer's remorse, you'll need to spend at least a few hundred more. Once you hit $500 or $600, there are some more solid Windows laptops available, such as the HP OmniBook 3. Even in that case, though, you're making some compromises in features like touchpad quality and chassis thickness. But as a general principle, Windows laptops only start to become worth buying in the $500-plus range. Should You Get a Cheap Windows Laptop or Chromebook? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The eternal question. If you're looking for a laptop for less than $500, I highly recommend that you opt for a Chromebook. I know that won't be a possibility for everyone, as some people require certain applications that require a Windows laptop or a MacBook. If you do decide to get a Chromebook, make sure all of your connected accessories and other devices are compatible. Chromebooks give you access to a full desktop Chrome browser, as well as Android apps. While that leaves some gaps for apps that some may need, you might be surprised by how much you can get done without the need to install any software. Most applications have web versions that are every bit as useful. While Chromebooks are most well-known as junky student laptops, the “Chromebook Plus” designation has filled in the gap between dirt-cheap Chromebooks and $800 Windows laptops. You'll find some great Chromebook Plus options in the $400 to $600 range that have better performance and displays and look a bit more like a modern laptop. The Acer Chromebook Plus 514 is a great example of this. You can read more about the differences between Windows laptops and Chromebooks here.

Tech.title: CookUnity Prepared Meal Delivery Review (2026): Chef-Centric Meals
Tech.content:
But, of course, Raj's meals are available only to those served by the Seattle hub. Others, near Los Angeles or Atlanta, may have other local chefs who offer similarly compelling arguments. I wouldn't know.

Local Mileage May Differ

CookUnity Beef Stroganoff with Truffle & Pappardelle from chef John DeLucie Photograph: Matthew Korfhage

The strength of CookUnity is that each regional hub is basically local. But this is also a potential weakness: Each regional hub is different. Each hub has greater or lesser variety. Each also has a different selection of chefs and meals.

But my good experience with the Seattle hub might translate to what you'll find in a different kitchen, with different cooks. This may be true even if the same chef's name and face are on your meal box. Some chefs operate four or five kitchens at different hubs, and different kitchens may have different results, even with the same recipes. And heck, I've had different results even from the same chefs. I can only speak to my own good experience and the good experience of my colleague Louryn Strampe, who ordered out of the Chicago hub.

Note that while CookUnity offers a much bigger caloric range than most prepared meal kits, usually the big feasts are heavily carb-loaded: rice, noodles, pasta. Those looking for a focus on proteins and veggies can find them easily, but usually in more moderate portions. Food cost is food cost. Starches are cheap.

But I have reason to believe that CookUnity's other hubs also offer good cooking—and that has a lot to do with CookUnity's business model. The overall factor that I think makes CookUnity work is healthy competition.

Each CookUnity chef making prepared meals is, essentially, a competing food business within the same big commissary kitchen. Their name is on each box, and a good number of the chefs have restaurants and reputations to protect. There are many incentives to make each meal interesting and delicious. My experience bears this out.
